L.DUIS CLAU.!JJE DRAPEAU
Grand Master
Louis C. Drapeau was born near Live Oak, California, August 30,
1885. His mother, whose maiden name was Virginia Lynds, and his
grand parents, J. B. Lynds and Katherine Lynds, are buried in the old
cemetery at Gridley, California.
Bro. Drapeau moved to Oakland at an early age, and attended
grammar and high school in that city. He worked for Past Grand
Master and United States Senator Geo. C. Perkins, as messenger, clerk,
and finally private secretary, and went to Washington, D. C. with the
Senator.
While in Washington Bro. Drapeau graduated from the law department of Georgetown University, with the degree of L.L.B.
In 1913 Bro. Drapeau went to Ventura, California. For a year he
was official shorthand reporter of the Superior Court there. Then he
practiced law in southern California until October 4, 1937, when he
was appointed judge of the Superior Court in Ventura County.
Judge Drapeau served on the Superior Court until March 31. 1949,
when he was elevated to be associate justice of the District Court of
Appeals in Los Angeles, a position which he now holds.
Justice Drapeau was married to Julia Irene Mead in 1906. Three
children were born to that union, Virginia Lynds Wegis, Louis C.
Drapeau, Jr., and Jack Drapeau. The passing of Julia left them motherless at an early age.
In 1923 Justice Drapeau married Dorothy Julia Reese. Dorothy is
the eldest daughter of the late Past Grand Master David John Reese
of Ventura. Of that marriage two children were born, David Rhys
Drapeau and Jerry Drapeau. Dorothy took over the unfinished task of
raising this large family, and today is loved and revered by her husband
and all the boys and girls, now men and women grown.
Judge Drapeau had the thrill and pleasure of assisting in the conferral of the 3d degree of Masonry upon two of his sons, Louis C.
Drapeau, Jr.• and David Rhys Drapeau.

LOUIS CLAUDE DRAPEAU
Grand Master
1951 - 1952

Judge Drapeau has been active in community and civic affairs. He
is past president of the Ventura Rotary Club, and of Cabrillo Parlor,
Native Sons of the Golden West; Past Exalted Ruler of Ventura
Lodge No. 1430, Benevolent & Protective Order of Elks; life member

Parent-Teachers Assodation: and for many years member of the
American Legion and Independent Order of Odd Fellows.
Judge Drapeau also served three years as Building and Loan Commissioner of the State of California from 1934 to 1937.
·
His Masonic History is as follows:
Made a Master Mason in Oakland lodge No. 188 May 20, 1907.
Master of San Buenaventura Lodge 214, two years.
Charter Master of Poinsettia Lodge 633, and served two years.
Inspector for the Grand Lodge two years.
President Southern California Past Masters Association, one year.
In Grand Lodge, Bro. Drapeau served on the Homes Endowment
Board,· the Committee on Grievances, and the Board of Trustees for
the Masonic Homes. He was elected to and passed through the several
stations of Junior and Senior Grand Warden, and Deputy Grand
Master, becoming Grand Master in October, 1951, and serving until
October, 1952.
Bro. Drapeau's other Masonic affiliations are as follows: Member
of and Past High Priest of Ventura Chapter No. 50, Royal Arch
Masons of California; Member of and senior Past Commander of Ventura Commandery, No. 17, Knights Templar: Member of Santa Barbara Consistory, Scottish Rite Masons: coroneted a 33d degree Mason
in 1952. Member of Royal and Select Masters of California: Order of
Sciots: Al Malikah Temple, Order of the Mystic Shrine: Order of the
Red Cross of Constantine: honorary member of the Legion of Honor
of the Grand Council of the Order of De Molay.
Due to the nature of Grand Master Drapeau's judicial duties it was
possible for him to devote an extraordinary amount of time to the
affairs of the Office of Grand Master, and he heeded the call of his
Brethren without thought of conserving either his time or his strength.
He visited the Brethren in the metropolitan cities and in the out of the
way places.
His friendliness, the human touch so peculiarly his, and his down to
earth treatment of the problems confronting him, endeared him not only
to the Craft at large but to the Officers with whom he was closely associated. He was, and will always remain, one of the most popular Grand
Masters in the last quarter of a century.

The House of Life
Very Reverend THOMAS GRICE, Grand Chaplain
Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Members of the Grand Lodge,
Delegates to the 103d Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Masons of California
As I look upon you and feel something of the high privilege of this
hour, I am wondering, as I speak my message, if I shall receive your ap~
proval and approbation . I covet that.
At least I can say that I come to this high privilege not by my own
worthiness, but by the blessing of our Most Worthy Grand Master who
has given to me a place among you as your Grand Chaplain. I regard this
office as the highest and the noblest that a minister of any church may
attain. It has been a great and wonderful year for me to have gone up
and down the State with our Grand Master and to have witnessed the
sincere and cordial reception of his message, to have listened to his in~
terpretation s of the teachings and landmarks of Free Masonry. I want
to say I wish I could have had this experience 25 years ago. It would
have made me a better minister and interpreter of the Book on the altar.
I want to thank him for this great year of life and to say in your pres~
ence that because of it I am a better Mason, a better man and a better
American.
And now may I submit for your approval this simple devotional
talk with which we may begin the 103rd Annual Communica tion of the
Grand Lodge of Masons of the State of California.
I begin with a text from the Bible. Without an open Bible upon its
altar a lodqe can neither receive, nor initiate candidates, nor transact
business. There are 75 references to the Bible in our Ritual and every
name in the Ritual is from the Bible. I quote these words from its sacred
pages:
"By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out
unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance and he
went out, not knowing whither he went for he looked for a
House which hath foundations , whose builder and maker is God."
I know that old man, or it might have been his younger brother. He
lived back in the northern part of the state of Minnesota. Today, when
you come upon that settlement you find the land cleared, the swamps
drained, and acres of smiling farms. And on each one there stands a
neat, two story farm house. The landmark, however, which attracts the
attention of every traveler, is a great brick house which stands on a hill
and is three stories high. Its architecture is pretentious, the walks of

years of life"-an unfinished house-Micha el Angelo, immortal painter
and architect, at eighty-nine .years of age said, "I am dying, when I
have scarcely learned the ABC of art. I was just getting ready for my
real work,"-an unfinished house. Victor Hugo, the great French writer,
said, "For fifty years I have been writing my thoughts in prose and
poetry; but I feel that I have not said a thousandth part of what is in
me." Yes, life is like an unfinished house for most of us. That is why
every Master Mason is directed to the Hour Glass in our Ritual.

noticed on the other side of the bed another chair and said, "I see I'm
not your first visitor, Alec." "Oh," Alec said, ''I'll tell you about the
chair. It's like this. Years ago, I couldna pray. I fell asleep on my knees.
And even if I kept awake, my thoughts would wander. And I worried
about it and I spoke to the minister about it. And he told me not to
trouble my head about kneeling down. Said he, 'Just sit you down, Alec,
and put a chair agen ye, for the Lord, and talk to him-just as though
He sat beside ye,'-and I've been doing it ever since. So now you know
what the chair is doing, standing the way it is." A week later, the
daughter came into the parsonage. As soon as I saw her, I knew something had happened. She said, "Father died last evening. I had no idea
that death was so near. He had just gone to lie down for an hour. He
seemed to be sleeping comfortably. I left him for a few minutes. When
I came back, he was gone. He didn't seem to have moved, except that
his hand was on the chair. Do you understand?" And I said ,"Yes, I
understand." Alec Fraser had been living on the third floor of the House
of Life and had gone out from that room to have a still closer fellowship with his God. To the Home where sight takes place of Faith.
"BUILDING A HOUSE/" ls there a better description of human
life than that? I think not. That's the reason why our home is so dear to
us. One of the sweetest songs ever sung tells the same story. Some
years ago, an American died in a foreign land and they buried him in
foreign soil. He slept his sleep for thirty years. In 1883, a company of
Americans stood by his grave in Africa and they opened it. They took
his body out, and wrapped that body in the Stars and Stripes and put
it in a coffin and brought it to New York Harbor. They put it on a
special train. Took it to Washing ton and marched down Pennsylvania
Avenue, headed by a band. Out came the President, the Vice-President ,
the Members of the Cabinet. Congress adjourned and the Supreme
Court-all the great men of the nation came out to welcome that body
home.

"Behold how swiftly the sands run and how rapidly our
lives are drawing to a close. Thus wastes man. Today he puts
forth the tender leaves of hope. Tomorrow blossoms and bears his
blushing honors thick upon him.· The next day comes a frost
which nips the shoot and when he thinks his greatness is still
aspiring, he falls like autumn leaves to enrich our Mother Earth."
Yes, I say, Masonry teaches, warns us, that human life is like an
"unfinished house."
And, now, let us go inside the House we are building.
3. The Soul Hath Its First Floor: It is here that most people live
and die. To them, life is toil, laughter, tears, holiday, game of profit and
loss, to give a little, to get much for the stomach, and the back, and the
pocketbook. That is the tale. Most of us know there ought to be other
floors in the House of Life. Some of us have even built the walls and
the stairway, but we rarely ever climb the stairs. How seldom we read a
great book? Or hang a picture? How many of us, when asked, say,
that the Bible is dry and that we have no time to pray?-We're so
busy that we never have time to think. "We are so occupied with the
stones of the street that we never turn our eyes to the stars."
Then, like the old man's house, the "House of Life" should have a
second floor. Suppose we go up the stairway. In this chamber there is
more room, less furniture and fewer inhabitants. The society is choice
and the conversation fine. When you and I have gone-we liked it so
much that we said we would go back some day and make it home.
And, then, there is the third story to the "House of Life." This is
the Upper Chamber. It's the glory of the House and the crown of all
the rest. The experience of that Holy of Holies we cannot put into
words. The life lived in that room is not dependent on activity but on
fellowship, faith and prayer. It is the life we live with God. Not much
furniture in it sometimes, but what there is, is useful. I wonder/ I wonder/
-do we all have a third floor in the House of Life?
Let me tell you the story of Alec Fraser. He is an old Scotsman.
The minister of the local church called, for Alec Fraser was sick and
confined to his room. The daughter placed a chair, and the minister

13

Who was he?
What battle had he fought? None. What picture had he painted?
None. What invention had he given to the world? None at all. But
he had written a little song, sung by millionaire and artisan. Sung by
the farmer at the plow, sung by the man in the trenches of Flanders
Fields. and dug-out of Iwo Jima, sung by the sailor on the high seas.John Howard Paine had written
"Home, home, sweet home
Be it ever so humble, there's no place like home."
Yes, building a house and making it home is dear to the heart of
every American-bu t especially so to every fine Mason.
4. As we close this simple narrative, may I make these observations?
You can call it the exhortation, if you like. Jn the building of the House

we work with God. Then we may discover that we live in a house that
hath foundations whose builder and maker is God. And thus,

of Life, will you remember that God and man are partners. Free Masonry reminds us of this truth again and again. Remember that we are
builders. Savages are not. As soon as they start to build, they get away
from savagery.

"Through the deep caves of thought we hear a voice that singsBuild thee more stately mansions, oh, my soul,
As the swift seasons roll!
Leave thy low-vaulted past!
Let each new temple, nobler than the last,
Shut thee from heaven with a dome more vast,
Till thou at length art free,
Leaving thine outgrown shell by life's unresting sea."

Remember-that our whole planet is a place of labor and that we
are builders together-with God. The Master Mason learns this lesson
in the Third Degree. One of the hierographyical emblems is the beehive. "The beehive is an emblem of industry and recommends that
virtue to all created beings from the highest seraph in Heaven to the
lowest reptile of the dust." All effort does not accomplish anything.
There must be togetherness. So we do not go to the butterfly for an
example. We go to the bee. "As busy as a bee," working for the community in the hive.

Oliver Wendell Holmes
"Amen-So Mote it Be."

Remember- God is a builder. He loves to build. He lives to build.
The Creator is transforming chaos into unity. discord into harmony,
darkness into light, raw materials into spiritual perfection.
And God is building Humanities. He is busy building Civilizations.
He is also building in the realm of mind and spirit as well as of matter.
He is building universal spiritualities. In all of this, we Masons are
working with the Master Builder, the Supreme Architect. We are
workers together with God.
God sketches the plans, puts them on the trestle board, as we would
say, gives us the blueprints and then it is up to us. He leaves it to our
initiative to put things together by our own purpose and skill and training. Roughly speaking, we ask for bread and He gives us a handful of
seed and points to the soil. We ask for fish and He leads us to the river.
We ask for a mast for our ships and He points to the forest. We ask for
a house and he gives us a handful of clay. We ask for a temple and he
gives us an unshaped rock. But-mind you, and remember, we are
workers together with God. Whether we build a house, a temple or a
city, we must work with God.
Remember-no task will fail that has God for a partner. Man is a
spirit, a child of the Infinite, and the resources of the Infinite are His.
The hand that carved a war club can be trained to carve an altar and
build a temple. The mind that split the atom can be trained to build
the City Four Square.
The earth is not man's goal. It is a starting place. We haven't tried
all our powers, even in this world-let alone reached their limit. When
Victor Hugo was dying, he said, "I know that I am the Chrysalis of an
archangel." But let us remember this can only be brought about when

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
Lams C. DRAPEAU, Grand Master

pie is of such great promise. Every one of these ceremonies gave me a
feeling of satisfaction and delight.
On March 15th, however, Mother Nature failed to cooperate. She
sent a deluge. It has been said that the Grand Master floated those two
cornerstones in. And one Past Grand Master opined that they were
seen a day or two later out in the illimitable reaches of our broad Pacific
Ocean, halfway to Catalina Island. However, the cornerstones are still
there, and the buildings to rest upon them are progressing apace.

Brethren, another Masonic year has come and gone. In conformity
to the usages of our Craft, it now becomes my duty to render an account
of my stewardship from the close of Grand Lodge in October, 1951,
until this Communication.
It has been a pleasant and busy year.
To the brethren, living and dead, who made it possible for me to
occupy the high office of Grand Master of Masons in California, I
tender my heartfelt thanks.
NEW LoDGES CONSTITUTED

I constituted four Lodges: Los Altos Lodge, No. 712, October 26,
1951: Castro Valley Lodge, No. 713, November 1, 1951; Blue Lakes
Lodge, No. 714, November 2, 1951: and Magnolia Park Lodge, No. 715,
November 15, 1951.
Each one of them has made an auspicious beginning. and each one
of them goes forward with the good wishes and good will of all Masons
everywhere.
NEW LODGES INSTITUTED

The following new Lodges were instituted:
January 7, 1952, Belmont Shore, U.D., Seal Beach:
May 26, 1952, Research Lodges, U.D., in Northern and Southern
California:
July 1, 1952, Wayfarer Lodge, U.D., Whittier;
August 8, 1952, Estero Lodge, U.D., Cayucos;
August 16, 1952, San Lorenzo Valley Lodge, U.D., Boulder Creek:
August 23, 1952, Home Lodge, U.D., North Hollywood;
September 13, 1952, Mineral King Lodge, U.D., Visalia.
Each one of these Lodges under dispensation has my sincere best
wishes. I am sure each one of them will demonstrate an ability to work
in Masonry which will warrant Grand Lodge in granting a charter. Research Lodge in San Francisco was instituted by our Deputy Grand
Master; all of the others by me.

CENTENNIAL CELEBRATIONS

I participated with the brethren in the observance of eight Centennial Anniversaries of Lodges of this jurisdiction:
November 1, 1951, Eureka Lodge No. 16, at Auburn:
February 21, 1952, Washington Lodge No. 20, at Sacramento;
April 29, 1952, Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, at Honolulu;
May 8, 1952, Georgetown Lodge No. 25, at Georgetown;
May 9, 1952, San Joaquin Lodge No. 19, at Stockton;
May 10, 1952, Madison Lodge No. 23, at Grass Valley:
May 22, 1952, Occidental Lodge No. 22, at San Francisco;
June 27, 1952, El Dorado Lodge No. 26, at Placerville;
July 26, 1952, Martinez Lodge No. 41, at Martinez.
These were great occasions. What a history of Masonry each of
these Lodges in its hundred years of existence represents. It was a privilege indeed to join with the good men of the present day in commemorating the work of the good men of a hundred years ago.
Unfortunately I missed one Centennial, that of Mountain Shade
Lodge No. 18, in Downieville. This was due to conflicting dates, and
was a matter of regret to me.
NEW TEMPLES DEDICATED

The following new Temples were dedicated by Grand Lodge:
November 17, 1951, Greenleaf Lodge No. 670, at Whittier;
November 24, 1951, Canoga Lodge No. 611, at Canoga Park:
November 30, 1951, Blythe Lodge No. 473, at Blythe:
F~bruary 1, 1952, Vista Lodge No. 687, at Vista:
February 9, 1952, Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625, at Los Angeles:
June 4, 1952, Glendale Lodge No. 544, at Glendale;
July 31, 1952, Fontana Lodge No. 653, at Fontana;
August 1, 1952, Point Loma Lodge No. 620, at San Diego:
August 2, 1952, Oceanside Lodge No. 381, at Oceanside:
September 6, 1952, The Gardens Lodge No. 621, at Los Angeles:
September 17, 1952, Callayomi Lodge No. 282, at Middletown.
This wonderful record demonstrates how California Masonry is
really on the march. Eleven new Temples completed by our brethren in
one year.
Moreover, in every one of these Temples the brethren have built
themselves into the edifices. We are again engaging in operative, as

18

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

well as in speculative Masonry. Our own brethren laid out the work
and dug the footings; mixed the concrete and laid the foundations; built
the walls and put on the roofs; finished and decorated the interiors. That
is a record which any Masonic jurisdiction has the right to be proud of
and to rejoice in. I predict a glorious future for every one of these Lodges.
Another interesting trend too in the building of these Temples is
that they are all on one floor. They are not two~story buildings. With
ample parking spaces, this type of architecture seems to fit the modern
trend in both urban and suburban communities.
GRAND MASTER'S BREAKFASTS

Grand Master's breakfasts, generally on Sunday mornings, have been
very interesting. Generally under the auspices of Masters and Wardens
Associations or Boards of Relief, I attended the following:
October 14, 1951. San Francisco;
March 2, 1952, Santa Maria;
March 16, 1952, Los Angeles;
March 30, 1952, Long Beach;
April 6, 1952, Sacramento;
May 17, 1952, Los Angeles;
May 25, 1952, Berkeley;
June 22, 1952, (Anchor Lodge, Compton-St. John's Day); and
September 14, 1952, Fresno.
Each of these functions was well programmed and well attended.
Indeed they afford the Grand Master an opportunity to meet a great
number of Masons.
ATTENDANCE AT SISTER GRAND LoDGES

It was my privilege to attend the Annual Communications of the
Grand Lodges of Oregon and of Nevada. As has been our custom, our
Junior Grand Warden attended the Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Arizona, and our Deputy Grand Master attended the Communication
of the Grand Lodge of Washington.
As I look back through the past four years I think one of the greatest
pleasures you have given me has been the opportunity to attend these
Communications of our sister Grand Lodges as your representative. I
met such fine people; such friendly people. I enjoyed every bit of it.
The last Communication of our sister, Oregon Grand Lodge, was
their Centennial year. So our Deputy Grand Master and our Grand
Secretary also attended. Because of delay in plane service which kept
me away that afternoon, our Deputy Grand Master, for me, laid a
wreath upon the grave of the first Grand Master of Oregon who was
our first Grand Treasurer in California.

19

GRAND MASTER'S CONFERENCE WITH THE OFFICERS OF
GRAND LoDGE AND THE PAST GRAND MASTERS

Our Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems was the originator of
this custom. I thought it a particularly good idea, and continued it,
calling the elective Grand Lodge Officers and the Past Grand Masters
together in San Francisco January 19, 1952.
The conference functions something like that of the executive of
a corporation with his vice~presidents and past presidents. The inter~
change of views and suggestions from all the brethren who attended
was of great assistance.
GRAND MASTER'S CONFERENCE IN WASHINGTON, D.C.

Together with our Deputy Grand Master and our Grand Secretary
I attended the Conference of Grand Masters of North America held at
Washington, D. C.; also the meeting of the directors of the George
Washington Memorial at Alexandria, Virginia. Both conferences were
held during the week of the birth date of the father of our country.
The experience was well worth while. Our Grand Lodge has many
matters of business to transact with other Grand Lodges. So I think it
highly desirable that our Grand Secretary and other Grand Lodge
elective Officers should become personally acquainted with like officers
of other jurisdictions.
INSPECTORS CONFERENCES

I was able to attend but two of our Inspectors Conferences, one at
Del Mar, and the other at Lake Tahoe. I missed the other districts.
These conferences are of great value to California Masonry. Indeed
I cannot leave our Inspectors without comment upon the unselfish de~
votion and service which every one of them renders. This is the working
body of Masons who teach our esoteric work to officers of our Lodges
and who supervise Masonry in all its work throughout the year.
THE GRAND MASTER'S VISIT TO HAWAII

Following our annual custom I spent two delightful weeks in Ha~
waii last April. visiting the Lodges and our brethren in the enchanted
isles. Masonry there is in a healthy condition.
I was met with the traditional courtesy and entertained in the tra~
ditional manner of the Islands. I am indebted to all of the brethren in

MEMORIAL SERVICES FOR DECEASED PAST GRAND MASTERS

I suppose every Grand Master has had some one particular project

I have had that experience in laying wreaths at the places of rest

"undiscov'rd country from whose bourne no traveler returns."
In this work I have had the invaluable assistance of our Committee
on History. Graves have been located, pictures taken of the ceremonies
and a proper record made. None of all of our Past Grand Masters was
overlooked.
While in the District of Columbia last February, with the assistance
of the Grand Master and Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia,
wreaths were laid upon the graves of our third and of our fifth Grand
Masters. One is in the old Congressional Cemetery in East Washington; the other in Arlington.
We were unaible to find the exact place of rest of Past Grand Master
Howard in the old cemetery at Virginia City, Nevada. Vandals have
destroyed or carried away his headstone. But we laid a wreath for him
at a monument erected in memory of another celebrated California and
Nevada Mason, Brother Storey.
I find that at the graves of some of these Past Grand Masters there
is no headstone or marker whatever. Some are buried in family plots
with only the name of the family on a monument. Most of the headstones
make no mention of the fact that our departed brother was Grand Master of Masons in California. I am wondering if it might not be a good
idea for Grand Lodge to inscribe the Masonic record of these distinguished men on markers or on existing monuments in these plots. I suggest that the Committee on History make some study of this idea.
May I leave this subject with one personal comment. Nearly fifty
years ago, as a boy, I worked for the Honorable George Clement Perkins, Grand Master of Masons in California in 1871. First I was his
messenger boy; then his clerk; and finally his private secretary. He was
the only man I ever worked for, for when I left him I went into the
practice of the law for myself.
Without his encouragement, without his patience with me, without
his belief in me, I doubt if I should ever have attained the high honor
with which you have entrusted me.
So it was with a particular thrill that as Grand Master this year I
laid a wreath upon the grave of this our Past Grand Master, former
Governor of California; and United States Senator from this State for
many years. May he rest in peace.

EARTHQUAK E DAMAGE

I had a visit to Tehachapi Lodge set on my calendar for July 26th,
1952. This was to have been another of the famous annual meetings
of that good old Lodge, to which in years gone by Masons have come
from all over California.
On July 22nd came a destructive earthquake in the southern San
Joaquin section of our State. Our Masonic Temple in Tehachapi was
demolished.
Our good Brother, our Senior Past Grand Master, Oscar Lawler,
telephoned me on the morning of the earthquake and told me that he
stood ready to do anything for our brethren in the earthquake area. He
got in touch with the Master of Tehachapi Lodge and proffered immediate assistance of Grand Lodge. Fortunately this was not necessary.
Then I called a meeting in Bakersfield for July 25, 1952. All of the
Inspectors, and the Masters and Wardens of the Lodges in the area were
present, together with Past Grand Master Oscar Lawler, Past Grand
Master Arthur Crites, Arthur M. Warren, Deputy Grand Master,
Ray Taylor, Assistant Grand Lecturer in the District, Ralph C. Hine,
Grand Orator Henry D. Oliphant, Assistant Grand Secretary, and
Arthur Triggs, Grand Marshal. A hurried survey of the damage indicated what had happened to Tehachapi Lodge; also that considerable
damage had been done in Maricopa, and some damage in Taft, Bakersfield and in Ventura. I appointed a Committee of the following brethren
to make a more extensive survey of the damage, to keep in touch with
the situation in the several places named, and to report to you at this
Communica tion: Past Grand Master Oscar Lawler; Past Grand Master
Arthur Crites; Assistant Grand Lecturer Ray Taylor, together with
our Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, Grand
Orator and Grand Marshal.
Another severe earthquake followed later, destroying the Temple at
Maricopa and doing further damage. This situation will be covered in
more detail by the Committe e's report. The Lodges most seriously
stricken have been asked 'by the Committee to submit full particulars
as to damage suffered and plans for restoration. lt is hope the data will
be available for consideratio n at this Communica tion of Grand Lodge.

RECOMMENDAT ION AND RuLING No. 1-THE OVERGROWN LODGE

It is my considered opinion that there comes a time when Lodges
become too large. When that happens. Masonry in general suffers. And
the opportunity to participate in our work is denied to many qualified
and well-deserving brethren. The more members a Lodge has, the less
opportunities there are for Masons to go through the chairs.
When a Lodge gets too large its membership tends to divide into
cliques. Sometimes the officers have their own private parties, and draw
away from the membership. It becomes difficult if not impossible for
the brethren to know one another.
Some Lodges tend to become business. rather than fraternal organizations. Average attendance goes away down. Membership in numbers
alone does not make good Lodges; big bank balances and holdings of
securities do not reflect Masonry at its best.

(a) Placing a limitation upon the number of candidates which
Lodges with over a certain number of members may have in a given

RECOMMENDATION AND RULING No.

27

5

Was the 1951 legislation relating to forfeiture of fees for failure
of an applicant to present himself within 5 years for the second and
third degrees, prospective or retroactive?
In my opinion the law is retroactive so that it is applicable, but so
that in computing the 5-year period there should be included any time
of such failure preceding as well as after the passage of the legislation.
Thus, it is immediately applicable to anyone who at this tiine has permitted 5 years to go by.
My reasons for so thinking are as follows:
Grand Lodge has the power under Section 6 of the Constitution to
pass such legislation. The question, therefore, is whether such was the
intent of Grand Lodge. That this was the intent of Grand Lodge is
apparent from the history of the legislation, since it was intended to
cure a long standing and irritating situation.
The retroactivity of by-laws calling for forfeiture of dues paid has
been the subject of civil law. Generally speaking, of course, a new law
of a society will not be interpreted as retroactive unless it was so intended
( 4 Am. Jur. 461 ) : but if a constitution of a society reserve the right to
amend the by-laws then it may be retroactive if reasonable (Robinson v.
Templar Lodge, 117 Cal. 370: Power v. Sheriffs Relief Assoc., 57 Cal.
App. 2d 350). Considered abstractly as a statute which operates retroactively. an analogy may be found in Helvey v. Security-First Nat.
Bank of L.A., 99 Cal. App. 2d 149 ( 1950), in which it was held that
the abandoned property act would permit escheat of unclaimed bank deposits.
In Masonic law we recall that amendments to the constitution are
effected immediately on close of the annual communication (Section 27,
Constitution), and ordinances are similarly so effective (Section 350,
Ordinances). It has been held that an applicant who refuses to go forward after initiation is not entitled to return of any portion of the fee
(Section 573, Edicts and Resolutions). Also, Section 2 of Article IV
of our uniform code of by-laws provides that the fee paid by an applicant for the degrees does not come forward to be initiated within three

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

months, the fee shall be forfeited. A somewhat analogous situation is
also presented in respect of dues paid in that, regardless of payments
of dues in advance, a lodge may enact legislation for additional dues
(Section 531, Edicts and Resolutions).

Moreover, a lodge should never publish so as to reach the profane
that which should 'be kept within its tiled precincts (Sec. 696 R.D.)
In any event, no Mason should ever use Masonry for his business
advertising or purposes (Section 748 R.D.), nor ask the profane to assist
Masonic charities (Secs. 795, 795a).

RECOMMENDATION AND RULING

No. 6

May a lodge purchase the official Grand Lodge publication "One
Hundred Years of Freemasonry in California," or subscribe to the magazines "New Age," or "Channel Counties Mason?"
As a general rule, a lodge may spend its funds for the purchase of
books, and for the maintenance of a library, for the benefit of its members. Thus, the purchase of the set of the official "One Hundred Years
of Freemasonry in California" is proper. (Section 608.)
With respect to magazines, it would be impracticable and unwise
at this time for the Grand Master to rule thereon. The lodge and not
the Grand Master should in the first instance, at least, and in light of
Masonic law and Masonic policy and current directives of the Grand
Master, examine any such proposed item for purchase and see whether
it is proper for inclusion in the lodge library.
This would seem to be especially true now in view of the current
activities of the Committee on Publications. Reference is made to the
letter dated October 23, 1951, from the Grand Secretary to all Masters
and Inspectors, setting forth the report of the special Committee on Publications and the law adopted by the Grand Lodge; the letter dated November 6, 1951, from the Grand Secretary to all Masons of this jurisdiction; and the letter dated November 30, 1951, from the Grand Secretary to all lodges of this jurisdiction and all other interested parties.
These indicate the problem in California and the process by which publications may be cleared by the Committee on Publications, in a prescribed manner, subject to the limitations of the law and the policy laid
down. These are the channels that the Grand Master has requested be
followed.
It would appear, therefore, that any ruling by the Grand Master
with respect to any specific magazine might unwisely intercept the work
of the Committee on Publications, and might well be misconstrued as
an oblique official blessing where none was intended.

May Lodge funds be used to sponsor a public Christmas tree in the

No. 10
May Lodge funds be used to maintain recreation facilities for Masonic servicemen and members of the DeMolay, primarily, but possibly
also used by other persons; and, may such funds, for that purpose, be
obtained from the proceeds of a picnic to be sponsored by the interested
Lodges? The answer is no.
Aside from the administrative difficulties, it appears that such activities are prohibited by Masonic law. For example, a lodge may not sponsor widows' and orphans' funds (Section 912). Such undertakings are
collateral to the purposes of a Lodge, and hence, the financial undertakings are collateral, however worthy may be the motives of the movers. There are numerous dangers inherent in such sponsoring by Lodges
of collateral undertakings, and in related commercial activities.

No. 11
Where a member dies, and his dues are paid in advance for one or
more quarters (not fractions thereof), may or should the Lodge return
to any proper person the unearned dues?
The answer is that the Lodge may and should return to the proper
estate representative the mentioned unearned dues.
Under Section 133, Article IX, Section 1, the dues of a member are
payable quarterly in advance.
Membership in a Lodge is terminated by death (Section 174). As
analogies, it has been held that liability for dues ceases immediately on
demit (Section 534) and on expulsion until restoration (Section 535).

RECOMMENDATION AND RULING No. 12
May Lodge funds be used to compensate an inspector for his time
spent at Grand Lodge, or for speakers at Public Schools Week programs and Constitution Month observance programs?

31

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As to compensation of inspectors, the answer, given on the assumption that the question assumes the inspector will receive payment of
permissible expenses, is no. Section 68 provides for the payment of an
inspector's expenses. Such expenses are defined to be "necessary expenditures for transportation to and from each annual communication
of the Grand Lodge. in the same manner as ordered for the officers or
representatives of lodges." The same section prohibits payment in more
than one of those capacities and the section also provides the conditions
of attendance required for payment.
As to the use of lodge funds for such speakers as are included in the
question, it would appear that this comes within the scope of social
purpose, the expenditures of which are authorized by Section 159,
subject to the terms and conditions thereof and provided the Lodge in
good faith uses the funds for the "promotion of fraternal intercourse"
(Section 637).

RECOMMENDATION AND RuLING No. 16
May life membership funds be invested in building and loan associations.
The answer is no, as to California building and loan associations.
but yes as to federal building and loan associations.
Under the laws of the State of California, savings banks may not
invest in California building and loan associations. Certain persons or
firms, as estate representatives, trustees and insurance companies, who,
under the law must invest in funds legal for savings banks, may, by
reason of special legislation, and under certain conditions, so invest certain funds. But, savings banks, as such, may not invest in California
building and loan associations. ( Deerings General Laws, Act. 652, Section 61: Statutes 1949, Chapter 202.)
The California Building and Loan Association Act provides: "All
shares issued by any duly chartered Federal savings and loan association shall be legal investments for the funds of executors. administrators, guardians, and trustees of every kind and nature and for the funds
of all insurance companies, cemetery associations and savings banks and
are acceptable and may be used as security for the faithful performance
of any public or private trust or obligation; provided, such association
shall be an 'insured institution' as defined in Title IV of the National
Housing Act." ( Deerings Act 4241, Section 1.)
Therefore, since under Section 152 a Lodge may invest its funds only
"in securities prescribed as legal for savings banks," and since there
has been no change under the new Section 152.1 so far as this question
is concerned, it follows that a Lodge may not invest its funds in California building and loan associations, but may invest its funds in federal
building and loan associations.

30

No. 13
May Lodge funds be used for the purpose of paying an organist?
The answer is no if the payments are as salary: and the answer is
yes. however, if the payments are as expenses within the limitations of
Section 159.
There is no specific provision in Masonic law for payment of salary
to an organist of a Lodge (Section 620).
Considered in the category of expenses, however, a different situation is presented. For example, a lodge may buy an organ as a necessary expense within the category of Section 157 (Section 608 (a) ) .
The expense of an organist would be fully authorized and justified,
however, as necessary expenditures from the entertainment funds of a
Lodge, in furtherance of fraternal intercourse, and subject to the limitations on the use of such funds ( Section 159) The social purposes authorized by this Section, namely. "the promotion of fraternal intercourse," is a very comprehensive expression. The expense of Public
Schools Week has been authorized for such promotion (Section 637).

RECOMMENDATION AND RuLING No. 17
May El Dorado Lodge contract with other fraternal orders to conduct and provide perpetual care of a cemetery in which all these respective orders have various allotments of graves? The answer is no.
It appears that dating from 1871 the Lodge and certain of the other
fraternal orders acquired land for burial purposes of their respective
members at Placerville. Later, other fraternal orders acquired adjacent
properties. Then there was formed the Union Cemetery Association,
composed of trustees of these orders. It was discovered in 1951 that some
perpetual funds had been erroneously used for operating expenses. One
of the fraternal orders, the Redmen, some years ago disbanded and its
property became the property of the Association itself. Current activities are directed toward a reorganization.
In the over-all picture, presented by the present request for a ruling.
it appears that it would be unlawful and improper for the Lodge thus

32

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to enter into the proposed cemetary organization, such as partnership,
or joint venture, or corporation, to be bound by contract in that manner
and thus obligate the Lodge membership in the future, to become subject to State laws and civil courts, possibly be tempted to draw upon
the funds of the Lodge to meet liabilities, and possibly do all this in
connection with graves of the other fraternal orders. (Sections 155 to
159; 616 a to 617; 627.)
In the portion of the cemetery which was set apart for Masonic purposes-that is, to provide a suitable place for the burial of the dead of
the Lodge-it would be proper for the Lodge to expend necessary funds
to obtain proper places for such burial of its own dead and also to keep
that portion in good condition. (Section 605.)

No. 18

May the Master of King David's Lodge declare rejected an applicant on the report of an investigatin g committee which contained one unfavorable report by a member thereof1
The answer is yes (Sections 228, 675, 678).
The Master could review the acts of the committee and satisfy himself as to the reasons assigned for the reports ( Section 669). While the
conclusions of the committee members without giving any supporting
facts may be lawful. the better policy is to require the committee of investigation to report the facts upon which the favorable or unfavorable
conclusion is based (Sections 674, 675). Also, the Master could have
referred the report again to the committee for further investigation (Section 677). Or, if it appeared that new evidence was available or that
further inquiry was desirable, a committee which might not have performed its duty could have been discharged and another appointed to
do the work more faithfully or more exhaustively (Section 677).
From. the facts reported on the question presented, however, it appeared there was a basis stated for the unfavorable report, albeit the
basis may in the opinion of some have been insufficient; but, in any event,
apparently the Master was satisfied and the Master declared the applicant rejected.
Under these circumstances, no new application from this applicant
may be received by any Lodge within twelve months of such rejection,
unless by dispensation of the Grand Master (Section 219). Such a dispensation should not be granted, however, unless it appears to the Grand
Master that a mistake was made, or that extraordina ry circumstances
exist (Section 428 ) .
Only the Lodge that rejected the applicant can ask and receive such
a dispensation (Sections 432, 705, 108).

34

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

It is recognized that meritorious work is being done among boys by
the Order of DeMolay. Also, that such a great and good movement and
its growth should be carefully developed and safeguarded. In order that
there may be among Masons information and cordin.ation as to the Order
of DeMolay, but not sponsorship, the Grand Lodge created and has
continued a Committee on DeMolay (Grand Lodge Proceedings, 1946,
pages 66, 198; 1947, page 161: 1948, page 137; 1949, page 158; 1950,
page 136; 1951, page 217).
It has been reiterated, that according to the Masonic law as viewed
in California, our traditional Masonic policy and ancient landmarks wiJI
not permit sponsorship of a DeMolay Chapter by the Grand Lodge or
by a Lodge thereof. Neither Grand Lodge nor any constituent Lodge may
assume any responsibility in connection with any sponsorship of a DeMolay Chapter (Sec. 521 R.D.).
It is a maxim of jurisprudence that what cannot be done directly,
cannot •be done indirectly. Accordingly, any group or club of Masons
which does sponsor a DeMolay Chapter should not convert this to an
indirect Lodge activity or affiliation. It would stem that taking a part
of a Lodge name, such as the number of the Lodge, might be construed
erroneously in some quarters as an oblique blessing direct from a Lodge.
(Secs. 748, 750 R.D.).
The Master of a Lodge is charged at his installation "to avoid all
dissimulation." A club or group of Masons from a particular Lodge
should not associate to sponsor a DeMolay Chapter if such association
is merely a device or pretense by which the Lodge itself actually is doing the sponsoring. The group or club should be separate and apart
from a Lodge, and so conduct itself that no claim could fairly be made
that it is in fact a Lodge activity or affiliation.

It is recognized that this may work a financial hardship on the
Brother, but under Masonic Law, such hardship would not justify an
exception. Secs. 947, 887 R.D.).

RECOMMENDATION AND RuLING

No. 30
Does conviction of a felony make ineligible to membership an applicant for degrees, where no time was served and restitution was made
and rehabilitation seems apparent?
The answer is yes.
In 1875 Grand Lodge decided that one who has served a term in
the State Prison was not "Under the tongue of good r~port" and hence
could not petition for the degrees (Sec. 208, 875 R.D.).
In 1948 there was presented to the Grand Lodge a resolution to
amend Section 208 to provide by express and specific statute that a
person convicted of a felony could not apply for the degrees. Grand
Lodge rejected the resolution.
This resulted in decision Number IV in 1951 by Past Grand Master
Paulsen recommending that the decision of 1875, as reported in Section
875 R.D. be set aside and disapproved and that the question of whether
an applicant is "Under the tongue of good report" be left to the disRECOMMENDATION AND RULING

36

PROCEED INGS OF THE

cretion of the Lodges. The decision did concede, however, that as the
law then existed a person who had been convicted of a felony, or at
least had served a term in the State Prison, was not entitled to apply
for the degrees. The Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes disapproved this decision and recommendation and the report of disappro val
was approved by Grand Lodge.
Consequ ently it is now the law, in accordan ce with our long-esta blished policy, that an applican t for degrees be ineligible to membership
if he has been convicted of a felony or has served a term in the State
Prison.

RECOMM ENDATIO N AND RuLING No. 32
Under Sec. 301, as amended, R.D., must the Grand Master, or one
of his deputied and authoriz ed officers appoint in every case the Master,
or a Past Master of this jurisdiction to preside at the trial; and, must
the Grand Master, or his said officers ascertain whether the person to
preside at the trial is qualified?
Sec. 301, as amended, R.D., requires that the Grand Master, or one
of his deputed and authoriz ed officers must, in each case, appoint the
Master, or any Past Master of this jurisdiction as Trial Master to preside at the trial. The Master may, without such appointment, act in respect of certain procedur al steps, as specified in Sec. 301.
It is required by Sec. 301, as amended , R.D., that to preside at the
trial, the Master, or Past Master, be in good standing , skilled in Masonic
law, qualified fairly to try the case, and be not a witness. It is not incumbent on the Grand Master , or his said deputed officer, to ascertain
whether the Master, or Past Master, be so qualified, but in the event
the Master, or Past Master, is not so qualified, he should report the facts
to the Grand Master or to his deputed and authoriz ed officer, who can
then appoint another to preside (Sec. 957, R.D.)

What procedur e should be followed on a candidat e who, during the

adherenc e to the Ancient Landmar ks of the Order." Landmar k Eighteenth requires the qualification of the candidat e for initiation. Sec. 650
R.D. enjoins us to remember always that "the ritual itself constitutes
binding law."
Thus, the ritual must be adhered to by all Lodges and Masons. ( R.D.
Sec. 247).
RECOMM ENDATIO N AND RULING No. 35
1. May a Lodge receive an applicati on for the degrees of Masonry
from the owner of a bona fide restaura nt who sometimes acts there as
a barkeeper?
The answer is no. (Sec. 210, R.D.). The mere fact that this person
only occasionally serves cocktails does not alter the fact that he at those
times is a barkeepe r. The word "barkeep er" should be defined to mean
a person who tends a bar where alcoholic drinks are sold.
2. May a Lodge receive an applicati on for the degrees of Masonry
from one who is not presently but who was formerly a barkeeper?
The answer is yes. (Sec. 210, R.D.) The fact that the applican t was
formerly engaged as a barkeepe r is not in itself a ground of disqualification under Section 210.

RECOMME NDATION AND RULING No. 40
Is there any violation of the prescribed regulation s relating to the

on the ultimate petition, and which number on the ultimate petition do
conform to the number as provided by Section 101, R.D.?
The answer is no.

the notice of intention. 1£, therefore, they exceed in number the ultimate
and legally numbered petitioners, it is merely superfluity which does not
vitiate.

by Section 101, R.D .. and if they give notice of intention as prescribed
by Section 105, R.D. It is assumed that they did this and that there has
been compliance with this phase of the regulation s.
No. 41
May an Officers Association compel its member Lodges to contribute
toward an Association treasury, including the cost of decorating Masonic
graves on Memorial Day? To this question I answered no.
If an Officers Association thus by resolution could compel payment
of Association expenses, whether for authorized or unauthori zed purposes, it would give to the Association control over the funds and property of its member Lodges, and thus violate Section 151 R.D. This reads:
"A Lodge must retain the control of its own funds and property."
Moreover , it appears that the cost of decorating Masonic graves on
Memorial Day does not come within the purview of the instructive purposes of an Officers Association. (Sections 864, 864 (a}, R.D.)
The Lodges themselves may voluntaril y and by agreemen t contribute
to an Officers Association treasury for authorized purposes. (Section 864
(a) R.D.)
The Lodges themselves also may expend their funds for the purpose of decorating Masonic graves since this is within the authorized
activities of a Lodge. (Section 649, R.D.) Such expenditu res, of course,
must be within the limitations of Se~tions 157 to 159, R.D.

RECOMMENDATION AND RuLING No. 42
Is it sufficient compliance with Section 240 R.D., after objection is
made kl the advancement of a Fellowcraft, if there was not read to the
Lodge members the part of the Committee report setting forth the cause
assigned, but merely that portion which contained the conclusions of the
committee that the objection was well taken and which, as thus presented,
was sustained by vote of the members so that the Fellowcraft was denied advancement?
The answer is no.
Since the cause assigned was not presented to the members then they
could not have voted thereon. Consequently, the Lodge failed to follow
the provisions of Section 240 R.D.
One who has been made a Mason occupies an entirely different position from one not yet initiated. He is entitled to certain rights and privileges, including the right to be advanced in the absence of sufficient
cause to the contrary. The cause assigned should of necessity be specific in nature, showing something done or omitted to be done by him,
which goes to his character or fitness. And when any such objection is
investigated, the cause assigned must of necessity, under Section 240
R.D .. be disclosed to the members of the Lodge before the vote on
whether such cause assigned is a valid and Masonic one. (Sec. 807 R.D.)
Hence, the vote of the Lodge was a nullity.

In our ancient charges of 1722 (Ross, P. 573) appears the following:
"Therefo re, no private piques or quarrels must be brought within the
door of the Lodge; far less any quarrels about religion, or nations, or
State policy, we being only as Masons, of the Catholic Religion above
mentione d; we are also of all nations, tongues, kindreds , and language s,
and are resolved against all politics, as what never yet conducte d to
the welfare of the Lodge, nor ever will."
So until Grand Lodge modifies or repeals it, we are forbidde n to
bring "within the door of the Lodge" quarrels about state policy, and
all politics.
In 1875 a report of the Jurisprud ence Committ ee was adopted by
Grand Lodge. The report was with reference to a circular letter expressing sympath y of Masons with the struggle f~r independen~~ of
the Cuban people. The following language appears m that report: · •
It is an inflexible rule of this Grand Lodge not to interfere or meddle
with political or religious matters, at home or abroad. Its members may
represen t all shades of political and religious opinion, but when they
are assemble d in subordin ate or Grand Lodge, they cannot so much as
discuss such opinions. Masonry has its own proper objects and purposes ,
and those must be consider ed by us to the absolute exclusion of all others,
and particula rly of such as would certainly arouse contentio n a~d confusion. Of religion we only desire to know that each one asking .a.dmission is a sincere believer in God and a future existence. Of politics
we only ask if the applican t is a good citizen."
I agree with you that it may well be said that this language i_s dictum. However , I am of the firm conviction that it is so rooted m. t.he
tradition s and law of this jurisdicti on as to be fundame ntal that politics
or discussio n of state question s in our Lodges are forbidde n, and that
political action by the Grand Lodge, or by subord~nat~ Lodg.es, or by
any officer of any such Lodges, in his official capacity, ts forbidden.
The ancient charges of 1722 are part of our written la.w. (Sec. 650,
p. 273, Ross). That law continue s in binding force until. repealed or
modified by Grand Lodge. (Sec. 656 Edicts and Resolutio ns, P. 280,
Ross).

that Grand Lodge at its annual communication in 1920 too~ such. act10n
that our law was amended with respect to any matters which m~ght ~e

and that. therefore , matters affecting the referend um measure here m
question do not come within the pr~hibitions ~hove set forth, at least
insofar as discussion of the measure m Lodges ts concerne d.

My Dear Bro. Adams:
Referenc e is made to a conferen ce with your good self and several
other Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of Californ ia in San
Francisc o last May 23rd; also to the letter which you personal ly delivered to me at that time. It was my understa nding that you presente d
the matter of participa tion by Masons in Californ ia in the present campaign concerni ng the propositi on to exempt private schools from taxation to me as Grand Master for a formal ruling.
So I shall most cheerfull y put myself on record as fully and complete ly as I know how.
In 1951 the Californ ia legislatu re enacted legislatio n exemptin g private schools from taxation. Pursuan t to provisions in the Constitu tion
of the State of Californ ia that legislatio n was held up and referred to a
vote of the people, as to whether it shall or shall not take effect. So the
measure is now under consider ation by the people of this state, and will
be decided by them at the presiden tial election in Novemb er.
As the debate upon the proposed legislation has progress ed, serious
question s of Masonic law have been presente d to me.
Should the Masonic Order in Californ ia officially take a position
one way or the other and declare itself for or against the measure?
Should the Grand Master, or other officers of Grand Lodge officially
make a declarati on for or against the legislation? Should Masonic Lodges,
their Masters or other officers declare themselves for or against it?
Should Lodges, in commun ications on lodge letter heads, solicit funds
for campaig n purposes in connecti on with this legislatio n or present
argumen ts to their members for or against it? Should the measure be
discusse d in lodge meetings or at social affairs precedin g or following
such meetings?
So far during the campaig n many Masons, as individu als, have expressed themselves, contribu ted money for campaig n purposes , and
otherwis e endeavo red to present to the voters their views relative to
this legislation. I think I can confiden tly say that neither the Grand
Lodge nor the Grand Master ( in the recess between the annual communicati ons of Grand Lodge) may have anything to say relative to
such conduct. Masonry does not dictate to its members what any one
of them shall or shall not do or say in any political matter.
So we come to the question as to what we may do as Masons, not as
individu als; what our Lodges may do as Lodges; and what the Grand
Master may do as represen tative of the Grand Lodge.
The written law of Masonry consists of the Constitu tions, Regula-

because I feel that Grand Lodge in its wisdom may conclude that the
time has come to make exceptions to the old rule absolute ly forbidding
politics; that in modern times we should have a more modern Masonic
rule.
Therefor e I adopt the suggestio n of these brethren , and rule that
the referend um measure exemptin g private schools from taxation may
be discussed in meetings of tiled Lodges and at social meetings before
or after such meetings.
I do this because I think the time has come for Grand Lodge to re~
examine the whole question. I have been told that in some Lodges dis~
cussions of political measure s and even of political candidat es have
been had for years.
If I have gone too far, at its next annual communication Grand
Lodge can disappro ve the ruling. Or if Grand Lodge shall so determine,
the whole matter may be explored and other and different law enacted.
This ruling does not contemplate that discussil'.>ns may be had of
other measures which will appear upon the ballot, or of any candidat e
for political office.
Neither the Grand Master nor the Master of any Lodge shall, in
his official capacity , endorse or condemn this or any other measure on
the ballot. Nor may any Lodge adopt any resolution or take any other
action in favor of or against this or any other measure.
Nor shall any Mason circulate an official Masonic communication,
asking financial aid for or against this or any other measure, or seeking
political support for or against it. (Ordinan ces Sec. 126, p. 51 Ross).
Nor shall any Lodge roster be used for any other than a Masonic pur~
pose. (Sec. 732, Edicts and Resolutions, p. 339 Ross).
With sincere fraternal greetings. I am,
Very truly yours,

May 22, 1952

My Dear Grand Master:
I am taking the liberty of writing you with respect to what I under~
stand is your position with reference to the discussion of the proposed
tax exemption.
It is probably unnecess ary to remind you that (as Judge Lucien
Shaw once told me) a decision in a particula r case is controlling au~
thority in another only where the facts are the same-o r at least similar.
Now the facts in the matter with which we are now concerne d are so
radically different from those in both of the cases discussed in Sec. 815
and 816 of G. M. Ross' Digest that it seems to me those utterance s could
ibe entirely disregar ded-or in any event, distinguished, as they easily
can be.
The question of whether or not Grand Lodge should accede to a re~
quest to join with a Lodge in South America in using its influence to
induce the Spanish Governm ent to grant Cuba its independ ence is a
far cry from whether or not members of our Lodges should be permitted
to discuss proposed legislation materiall y affecting our public schools,
and encourag ed to do what they can as individuals in the arduous and
ominous campaign· to be waged: and the question of whether or not
membership in a particula r denomination, society, or sect is a valid
reason for denying advancem ent to an Entered Apprent ice is just about
as foreign.
Over a long period of years, I have given considerable thought to
what a Lodge should or should not do; and I am strongly of the opinion
that those reports of our Jurisprud ence Committee set forth in Sections
815 and 816 have not been as carefully considered as they should have
been.
In the first place it should be noted that in the Cuba matter what the
Jurisprud ence Committee really found objectionable was the request for
some action-s omethin g to be done by Grand Lodge. The phraseol ogy
concerning the inhibition against discussion was pure obiter dicta. This
is obtrusive ly apparen t from the language concluding the report.
"As individuals, doubtles s many of the members of this Grand Lodge
feel a deep interest in the success of the struggle for the independ ence
of Cuba, and would be very glad to do anything in their power to assist
in securing the establish ment and recognition of that independence; but
not one of them would be willing that Grand Lodge should in any way
interfere, or so much as entertain a proposition for interference. Your
Committ ee is of the opinion that the Grand Lodge should take no action
in the premises."

48

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In the other case it was the action taken in forbidding the advancement of the Entered Apprentice that the Grand Master and the Jurisprudence Committee found objectionable; and what was said about
''.discussion" was absolutely unnecessary to the decision, and was simply
lifted (almost the identical words) from the report made in 1875.
It is to be noted, too, that in that report it is said, "Masonry has its
own proper objects and purposes and these must be considered by us
to the absolute exclusion of all others, and particularly such as would
certainly arouse contention and confusion."
Here in these words is the crux of the matter. Both decisions of course
stem from the ancient charges with the tabu on "politicks." Now let us
look for a moment at the language of that inhibition. It is found in the
f,\ncien~ Charges approved in 1722, and in the paragraph concerning
Behavior After the Lodge is over and the brethren not gone." Here it is:
"We are resolved against all politicks as what never yet conduced
to the welfare of the Lodge nor ever will." But to understand and appreciate its real meaning, it should be read in connection with the words
immediately preceding that phrase. They furnish the reason; and you
know that when the reason fails, the rule fails: "Therefore, no private
piques or quarrels must be brought within the door of the Lodge, far
less any quarrels about religion, or nations, or State policy, we being
only as Masons of the Catholic Religion above men~ioned; we are also
of all nations, tongues, kindreds and languages.
In other words, the charge actuaily was against saying or doing
anything which might result in a quarrel among the members who would
have 'been "enjoying themselves, with innocent mirth, treating one another according to ability" and possibly "fired up" where they would
take offense at something which under different conditions would have
been unnoticed. For like reason they were also cautioned (in the same
paragraph) against "doing or saying anything offensive or that may
forbid an easy and free conversation; for that would blast our harmony
and defeat our laudable purpose"-or as was said by our Jurisprudence
Committee in 1875 "certainly arouse contention and confusion."

Now is there any Mason who will hazard the opinion that the discussion of proposed legislation materiaily affecting our public schools
would "certainly arouse contention and confusion" or "blast the harmony
of the brethren of a Lodge"?

The Grand Master has sought to impress upon Masons throughout
the jurisdiction the importance of informing themselves, as individuals,
with reference to public affairs. He has urged them to a quicker interest
in the duties of citizenship. He has commended to them certain specific
subjects as especiaily deserving of their attention. The facilities of the
Institution have been employed to impart inspiration and enlightenment
to the individual, but with no intent that any individual should in tum
seek to commit the Institution to the formal support of persons or particular measures. The Grand Master has spoken in terms so clear and
explicit that misconception would appear to be weII nigh impossible:
and yet, the thought of some brethren has experienced confusion.

Masons everywhere, in every American jurisdiction profess their
great interest in, and their championship of. our public schools. Here
is an opportunity to make our practices square with our professions.
Whatever may be forbidden, or permitted elsewhere, it does seem to
me that here in California where Public Schools Week had its origin,
and where for more than thirty-two years it has been sponsored by
Grand Lodge which each year caIIs upon its constituent Lodges to join

from individual Masons and Masonic Lodges, and, also to make gavels

Temple, and to offer for sale and sell such articles to Masons and Masonic Lodges, and to apply the proceeds of the sale thereof and contributions received to defray costs of rebuilding and refurnishing the
Temple of Tehachapi Lodge, upon the adoption of this resolution.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, for many years prior to 1951 Section 127 of the ordinances
read as follows :
"A Lodge shall not sponsor, or by resolution or otherwise sanction, or permit the use of the name of the Lodge in connection with,
or for the purpose of furthering any collateral financial undertaking,
or commercial venture, whether for profit or not, which shall not
have been approved by the Grand Master, nor shall any member of
any Lodge be permitted to do so except in his individual capacity,
and without the use of the name of the Lodge," and
Whereas, in 1951, Section 127 was amended by adding the following
paragraph:
"No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction
of Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by
or for any body, order or organization requiring affiliation as a condition to membership", and
Whereas, for over fifteen years prior to the 1951 Amendment of this
section, District and Area Publications have come into being and with
implied approval under this section, have rendered, in the opinion of
the Lodges and their members in the districts and areas served, a much
needed and worthwhile service without in any manner being detrimental
to the good name of Masonry in their area of circulation, and
Whereas, publication of Lodge Name and number, lists of Officers,
schedules of meetings and pertinent and lawful news items, a complete
Trestleboard, is the means through which these publications, in our
opinion, have been able to render a worthwhile Masonic service, and
Now Therefore be it Resolved, that Section 127 be further amended
by adding thereto a third paragraph, as follows:
"A Lodge or member of a Lodge, may insert its Trestleboard,
Notices of Meetings, News items or Advertising in a publication approved by Grand Lodge. or, by the Grand Master during the recess

METHOD OF VOTING

MILEAGE FOR LODGE MAUI 472

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, it is required that proposed amendments to the constitution
or ordinances and business of all kinds be ref erred to a committee or
committees, which committees must report back to the Grand Lodge before any action is taken, and
Whereas, the vote of the Grand Lodge is frequently taken on the
committee report rather than on the amendment or business as originally
presented, and
Whereas, confusion frequently arises where it becomes necessary to
vote in the negative on a report to express approval on an issue, and
Whereas, this confusion can be eliminated merely by providing that
the vote shall always be on the amendment or business as originally
presented.
Now Therefore be it Resolved: that Section 26 of the Constitution
and Section 349 of the Ordinances be amended by adding to each Section the words: When the report of the committee, or committees, is
presented the vote shall be taken on the amendment.
Be it Further Resolved: that Section 69 of the Ordinances be amended
by adding thereto the words: When the report of the Committee, or
Committees, is presented the vote shall be taken upon the business as
originally presented.
Respectfully Submitted,
RALPH

c. HINE, P. M.

Magnolia Lodge No. 242
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General

REPEA L OF SECTI ON 501
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
RESOL VED: THAT SECTI ON 501 OF ROSS DIGES T BE
REPEA LED.
This section appears to erroneo usly hold that a Master may omit a
portion of the usual ceremo ny of opening and closing a Lodge and should
be repealed for the following reasons :
( 1 ) This Section is predica ted upon the report of a special com~
mittee of Grand Lodge which examin ed the record book of Tuolum ne
Lodge No. 8. Among a number of serious charges leveled against the
Master of the Lodge, Charles M. Radcliff who was Grand Master in
1853) was the charge that said Master on Jan. 20. 1861 " ......................... .
declare d his Lodge duly open and in order for busines s by the authori ty
in him vested. waiving all ceremo ny ................... .''. Said committee in the
narrativ e part of its report, but not as a part of the specific charges , nor
of the resolution, commen ted "A Master may. if he choose, omit a portion
of the usual ceremo ny of opening or closing a Lodge. but your com~
mittee is not acquain ted with the regulati on which authoriz es an entire
waiver of all these ceremonies." The subject before the committee was
"waivin g all ceremon ies" not waiving a portion of the ceremonies. The
commen t of the committee on waiving a part was, therefor e, surplusa ge.
or as the lawyers would call it, "pure dictum" .
In 1861 Grand Lodge was operatin g under the constitu tion, regula~
tions, by~laws and standin g resoluti ons of 1858, none of which contain ed
any authori ty to waive any portion of the opening and closing ceremonies. Certain ly there was no definition of what portion of said cere~
mony might be waived by the Master. If this were the law. and it definitely was not, each Master could determi ne the portion which he would
waive and indeed might waive the whole portion except "I declare the
Lodge open or closed.' ' This. of course. connote s the ability of the Mas~
ter to actually waive all such ceremonies. which would be repugna nt to
all Masoni c practice s at that, and previous, time. The constitu tion was
amende d by Grand Lodge in 1861, the actual year in which the foregoing report was made. Neither this constitu tion nor the previous one of
1858 made any provisio n for Grand Lecturer, Ritual Commit tee or in~
structio n in the work.
( 2) Since 1861 many changes have been made in our constitu tion
and regulati ons with respect to ritualistic matters and our current laws
respecti ng the ritual. which, of course. include s the opening and closing
ceremonies, are as follows:
a. "It shall be the duty of the Grand Lecture r: .................... to require
conform ity with the adopted ritual and work." ( 50 Ross Digest
1st.)

62

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

b. "It shall be the duty of each Assistant Grand Lecturer ................. .
to perform such other services as may be deemed necessary to insure proper instruction to the officers and strict compliance with
the adopted work." ( 51 Ross Digest.)
c. "The Grand Lecturer and the six Assistant Grand Lecturers shall
constitute the Ritual Committee and the Committee as so composed from time to time shall be the custodian of the Esoteric
work." ( 52 Ross Digest.)
d. "The Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize any changes in
the ritual for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed
down from time immemorial." ( 248 Ross Digest.)
Our Ritual Committee for decades has held, and it now holds, that
no part of the Esoteric work in the opening and closing ceremonies of our
Lodges can ever he waived by the Master or any other person.

MANDATORY ~ROFICIENCY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, Frequently, newly raised brethren are loathe to visit
Lodges other than their own through fear of inability to pass a satisfactory examination and as sojourners in other jurisdictions they are often
lost to Masonry, and,
Whereas, We now require proficiency in the lecture of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees before advancement, and,
Whereas, A brother's knowledge of Masonry is usually limited to
that which he is taught,

Therefore, be it Resolved: That before a receipt for dues may be
issued a candidate, he must have given satisfactory evidence, by strict
examination in open Lodge, that he is entirely proficient and well qualified in the candidates lecture of the Degree of Master Mason.

MILEAGE FOR SECRETARIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I most respectfully present the following Resolution for your consideration:
Whereas, It is my most sincere judgement that the Secretaries of
Lodges of less than 200 membership should be in attendance at our Annual Communications, and,
Whereas, The majority of these Lodges are not financially able to
send their Secretaries, and,
Whereas, It is just as important and necessary for the Secretaries
of said smaller Lodges to receive first hand those valuable instructions
from our Grand Secretary as larger membership Lodges, thereby enabling them to more efficiently handle their duties, and,
Whereas, The Masters of Lodges are only in authority for one year,
and,
Whereas, The Secretaries, almost without exception, carry on year
after year giving their best to uphold the dignity of their office, to the
aid of the ever changing Masters and the welfare of their respective
Lodges, and,

64

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Whereas, By referring to Schedule A herewith attached, showing
the name and number of the Lodge, there is only 210 Lodges in this
Grand Jurisdiction of less than 200 membership as shown in Grand
Lodge report of 1951, and,
Whereas, As shown by Schedule B herewith attached only the sum
of $4,865.67 was paid as mileage to the attending Masters or Wardens
of these said 210 Lodges, and,
Whereas, As this represents the approximate additional amount
required of Grand Lodge to cover the mileage of Secretaries of said 21 O
Lodges of less than 200 membership, and,
Whereas, This amount would fluctuate according to Lodges meeting
this 200 quota in the year and also by the inability of Secretaries attendance owing to circumstances beyond their control:
Be it Therefore Resolved: That the Grand Lodge of California,
knowing the great benefit to small Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction, by
having them get First Hand instructions from their Grand Secretary at
the Annual Communication, do hereby grant the same mileage to Secretaries, as is allowed to Masters and Wardens, of Lodges of less than 200
membership.
Fraternally submitted,
PERCY E. JOHNSON

SIGN OF DISTRESS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Because we feel that Masonic Officers and Brothers under the California Grand Jurisdiction, as a whole, are lax or uninformed as to the
correct way of giving the Masonic Sign of Distress, and because of this
fact might not recognize the sign if a Brother in need should give it,
certainly not if the Brother gave it incorrectly. And since we feel that
this particular sign is one of our most important signs, that it might mean
life or Death for a Brother Master Mason, we resolve - That the
Masonic Sign of Distress and the words of Distress be included as a
part of the Third Degree Proficiency Examination.
ROBERT LEE HARPER

Senior \Varden
Crossroads Lodge No. 696

Ritual.

ENDOWMENT FUND FOR LODGE ASSISTANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Be it resolved, that in recognition of the fact that every building used
strictly for Masonic purposes and labeled as a "Masonic Lodge Hall" is
an advertisement and a visible manifestation of Masonry and of Masons
generally, and that in all cases such buildings are hist.orical .mon~ments
to pioneer Masons and/or of the Masonic movement m. Cah~orm~, and
further, that because of limited membership and/or financial distress
there is at times a need for outside financial assistance, it is the will of
this Grand Lodge that there be and hereby is established an EndowmentTrust Fund for the repair, maintenance, and/ or rehabilitation (but not
expansion) of buildings used for Masonic Lodge purposes in the State
of California.
Be it further resolved, that this fund shall be established by the levying of the sum of One Dollar ( $1.00) on each petition for th~ d~gr~e~ of
Masonry and for Affiliation when transferring from another Jurisd1c~1on,
from this date forward, together with such other funds donated to 1t or
otherwise set aside for it from such other sources as may appear in future.
Further, that only the interest derived from the investment of this
fund may be expended except that forty per cent ( 40% J of the principal
sum may be loaned to constituent Lodges to be repaid on a deferred
basis with interest where such loans are warranted and repayment can
be assured.
Further, that interest-earnings may be given as an outright grant or
may be loaned with interest as the needs and circumstances may warrant.
Further, that the principal sum of sixty per cent ( 60%) set asid~ for
investment purposes only, be invested by the same investment committee
of the Grand Lodge which handles other investment funds of the Grand
Lodge and that the interest rate charged the constituent Lodges be the
current rate of interest charged by banks for real estate loan.
Further, that it is the intent of this resolution, and at all times shall be
the intent, that a measure of relief be provided for such Lodges as upon
a proper showing may require such relief, that their bur~ens ~ay ?e
eased rather than increased, that the fraternity may share m their misfortune and "join in promoting each other's welfare" which is the true
and real objective of Masonry.
Further, that any constituent Lodge in need of financial assistance
for the purposes as set forth herein shall make application upon a suitable
form, to be provided, and
Be it finally resolved, that said application shall be forw~rded to t?e
Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Finance for final processing ~nd disposition under their rules of procedure and who shall have authority over
