TAX EXEMPTION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, Freemasonry is founded upon doctrines and teachings of
brotherhood, morality. temperance, tolerance, justice, education, good
citizenship, loyalty to civil government. and freedom of ideas and expression, and requires of the individual Mason a dependency on and
belief in God; and,
Whereas, Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California
and its subordinate lodges, practice the aforementioned doctrines and

67

Whereas. Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California,
and its subordinate lodges was ruled, on November 18, 1940 and on
July 17, 1944. by Commissioner of Internal Revenue to be ex em pt from
income tax under Section 101, Subsection ( 3} of the Internal Revenue
Code; and,
Whereas, under provisions of Section 23, Subsection ( o) ( 5).
contributions. by an individual, during the taxable year, to or for the
use of a domestic fraternal society, order or association operating under
the lodge system, are deductible from income (subject to the present 20%
limitation) but only if such contributions or gifts are to be used exclusively for religious. charitable, scientific, literary or education] purposes,
or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals; and,
Whereas, no specific ruling has been requested or obtained by Grand
Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California and its subordinate
lodges, from Commissioner of Internal Revenue, that contributions made
to such domestic fraternal order are deductible by individuals from
income for the reason that the proceeds therefrom are used exclusively
to further the religious, charitable and educational purposes of such
order and for the prevention of cruelty to children;
Whereas, subordinate lodges are authorized to organize corporations under Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code of
the State of California for the primary purpose of acquiring real and
personal. property to erect, construct, equip and maintain Masonic
Temples for their uses, which corporations, upon proper application to
Commissioner of Internal Revenue, may be exempted from Federal
Income Taxes under provisions of Section 101, Subsection ( 14) of the
Internal Revenue Code; and,
Whereas, it appears that contributions to Grand Lodge, Free and
Accepted Masons of California or to any of its subordinate lodges, or
to any wholly owned and controlled building association thereof, do
come within the purview of Section 23, Subsection ( o} ( 5) of the
Internal Revenue Code, namely, the such contributions are used exclusively in the furtherance of Masonry in its efforts to promote religion,
charity, education and prevention of cruelty to children (see attached
Exhibit "A", containing references to Ross' Digest of Constitutions,
Ordinances, and Edicts and Resolutions); and,

Now therefore be it resolved: That Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted
Masons of California, take steps at its 103rd annual communication, to
be held October 13, 1952 to October 17, 1952, inclusive, to make full
and complete representation of the true and worthy nature of the purposes and activities of the Order of the Commissioner of Internal Reve-

68

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

nue, to the end that rulings be obtained that contributions to Grand
Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California, and its subordinate
lodges, or to their wholly owned and controlled corporations, owning
and operating, or proposing to own and operate, Masonic Temples for
use of such Grand Lodge or subordinate lodges, are deductible from
income under Section 23, subsection ( o) ( 5) of the Internal Revenue
Code.

PLURAL MEMBERSIIlP
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas our ordinances encourage dual membership in different
Grand Jurisdictions but forbid membership in more than one Lodge in
this Jurisdiction, and
Whereas the distinction is not generally understood and clarification
is needed, and
Whereas no good reason appears why multiple membership cannot
be authorized under proper conditions either within or without this jurisdiction, substantially in the manner permitted by other Grand Lodges,
Now, therefore,
Be it resolved that Section 163 of the Ordinances be amended to read
as follows:
Multiple Membership. Sec. 163.
This Grand Lodge recognizes and authorizes membership in more
than one Lodge under the following conditions:
1. A member of a Lodge of this jurisdiction residing in the jurisdiction of another Grand Lodge which allows dual membership may affiliate
with a Lodge in that jurisdiction while retaining his membership in this
jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member.
2. A member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction which
allows dual membership may, if residing in this jurisdiction, affiliate with
a Lodge under this Grand Lodge while retaining his membership in such
other jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member.
3. A member, in good standing, of a Lodge in this jurisdiction may
retain such membership and affiliate with any one or more other Lodges
under this Grand Lodge or join in the petition for a Dispensation for a
new Lodge and may present a paid up dues receipt in lieu of a demit or
demand for demit. Such a member becomes a plural member.
4. Upon the election of a plural member or the formation of a new
Lodge containing one or more plural members, the Secretary shall
immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which the plural member holds membership.
S. A plural member shall pay all dues required by each Lodge

71

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

wherein membership is held and shall have all the rights and privileges
of membership in each of the Lodges except that he shall not be Master,
Warden or Secretary of more than one of such Lodges at the same time
and except that the burden of the relief of a plural member, his wife,
widow and orphans shall rest on the Lodges in which he holds membership in proportion to the length of membership in each.
6. Suspension for non-payment of dues or otherwise, or expulsion
of a plural member shall immediately, and of itself, terminate his membership in all Lodges in this jurisdiction and the Secretary of the Lodge
suspending or expelling such a member shall immediately notify the
Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in which the plural member
holds membership. Like notice shall be given in case of reinstatement
and shall immediately and automatically restore him to membership in
each other Lodge.
7. Failure to sign the By-Laws within 30 days after election to
membership in another Lodge shall void such election and terminate
membership therein.
8. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to prevent a plural
member from receiving a demit if otherwise entitled to the same.
9. The Grand Secretary shall keep a record of all brothers holding
plural membership and shall provide forms to cover this Section.

any stated period, nor in advance, except as herein provided.
Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and
General Purposes.

Proposed by the Grand Secretary
A Lodge may annually remit the accrued dues of those of its members
who are unable to pay them.
.A Lodge may remit in advance the dues of those of its members who
have been members in good standing in a Lodge or Lodges of this Jurisdiction for a period of 40 years or more.
A Lodge may remit in advance the dues of those of its members over
the age of 75 years who have rendered special service to the Lodge and
who merit such remission.
Remission of dues in advance as herein provided must be by special
resolution, applicable only to the particular member or members, whose
dues are to be remitted.
A Lodge shall not remit the dues of its members, or any of them, for

Proposed by the Grand Secretary
Each Lodge, whether chartered or under dispensation, shall pay with
its Annual Returns, the following Contributions:
1st: For every Degree it shall have conferred during the year
a sum of $1.00.
2nd: For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of July 31,
the sum of 50c.
3rd: For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of July 31,
such Per Capita sum as the Grand Lodge shall levy for its
general activities.
4th: For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of July 31,
such Per Capita sum as the Grand Lodge shall levy for the

Capita sums as, in its judgment, may be required.
The Per Capita sums levied under 2, 3 and 4 herein shall not apply

1 ) Master Masons whose accrued dues for the preceding 12 months

years of age, and merit such remission as provided for in Section

DISCUSSION OF PUBLIC QUESTIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas: One of the highest duties devolving upon a Mason is the
duty he owes the State as a citizen; and it becomes increasingly evident
that the preservation of the Republic depends upon an intelligent electorate, and,

72

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Whereas: One of the historic methods in America of developing
and imparting factual information is by discussion and the presentation
of all sides of public questions in groups, churches, forums and similar
organizations; and for a Mason there is no better place than his Masonic
lodge to obtain that honest information, enlightenment and inspiration
which will better enable him to discharge his duty as a citizen, and,
Whereas: Not only in this jurisdiction, but in others, the Ancient
Charges and Regulations have been differently construed and inter~
preted at different times, it seems proper that Grand Lodge should now
construe and interpret them as they relate to a citizen'e duty today.
Now, therefore be it resolved: That none of the Ancient Charges or
Regulations ( specifkally including the Charge approved in 1722 with
respect to "Behavior After the Lodge is Closed and the Brethren Not
Gone" )-and no edict or decision of any Grand Master or any edict
or regulation, or other action of Grand Lodge heretofore given, made,
taken or adopted-shall be so construed or interpreted as to prevent a
free, full and open discussion in Grand Lodge, or in any constituent
Lodge, of any question directly or indirectly affecting Masonry, or any
object, purpose or activity of the Grand Lodge of California, or the
discussion of any public question to be submitted to the people, and
upon which Masons, as citizens, in the discharge of their civic duties
will be required to express an opinion: PROVIDED, HOWEVER
That there is to be no discussion of sectarianism, as such, or of
partisan politics, or of any particular candidate for public office; and no
pending or proposed legislation is to be endorsed or disapproved by the
adoption of a resolution, or any other action by the lodge.
And, be it further resolved that this resolution be adopted and
recorded among the standing resolutions of this Grand Lodge.
CHAS. ALBERT ADAMS
Past Grand Master
Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

ADDITIONAL LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, The regular attendance of our membership at the various
lodges is important to the continued well being of Masonry; and
WHEREAS, The Junior Wardens of the San Diego area have studied
the attendance records of several lodges; and
WHEREAS, These studies do disclose that the smaller lodges enjoy a
larger attendance at both regular and special meetings in relation to
total membership than do the larger lodges; and
WHEREAS, The area studied has twice doubled in population in the
last two or three decades with the addition of a single new lodge; and
WHEREAS, The membership of this Grand Jurisdiction is rapidly in~
creasing both by new members and by members of other Jurisdictions
attracted to California;
Now Therefore be is Resolved, That it is the consensus of opinion
of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of The State of California that there is a need for additional lodges in
many communities and that every proper encouragement should be
afforded to the formation of new lodges.

INTERPRET ATION OF SECTION 127
Resolved: That it be and is the determination of Grand Lodge that

a Lodge does not engage in a commercial enterprise by placing adver~
tising matter in any bulletin issued by it, provided that the revenue
derived from such advertising matter shall not materially exceed the
cost of publishing and distributing such bulletin; that a Lodge may
lawfully agree with the publisher of any publication that all or any
portion thereof shall constitute the official bulletin and calendar of such

76

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

lodge, and that the same may be distributed to the membership of such
Lodge by such publisher, using the roster of said Lodge for that purpose,
but for no other purpose, and that such Lodge may lawfully pay to the
publisher an agreed price for such publication and the distribution
thereof; that the matter provided by the Lodge for publication in such
bulletin may include the list of its officers, a calendar of its meetings, and
official statements by its officers.
That it be and is the determination of Grand Lodge that the foregoing are not prohibited by the provisions of Sections 126 and 127 of
the Ordinances or by Section 732 of the Edicts and Resolutions.
Proposed by
ROBERT F. SHIPPEE, Past Master,
HENRY S. ORME LoDGE No. 458.

Purposes, and on Publications.

PROPOSED NEW SECTION ON PUBLICATIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Resolved: That a new section be added to the Ordinances of Grand
Lodge reading as follows:
The owner or owners of any publication, (other than bulletins issued
and distributed by Lodges to their members). devoted to the interests
of the Fraternity, may obtain the sanction of Grand Lodge to publish
and distribute any such publication subject to the following conditions:
I . The owner or owners thereof shall be Master Masons and members in good standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction.
2. The owner or owners thereof shall not be incorporated.
3. No advertising therein shall be solicited by telephone.
4. Any solicitor of advertising employed by the owner or owners
shall be a Mason in good standing in his Lodge.
5. Any such solicitors shall not be compensated for their services
upon a commission basis.
6. Any such solicitors shall not knowingly make any untrue statements or misrepresentation of facts in connection with their
solicitation of advertising in any such publication.
7. The owner or owners thereof shall be solely and entirely responsible for any untrue statements or misrepresentation of facts
knowingly made by solicitors of advertising employed by them.
8. Each issue of such publication shall contain the name, business
address. residence address and telephone number (if any) of
the owner or owners thereof.
9. No owner or owners shall represent or shall agree that any
portion of the advertising charges .. subscriptions or profits of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

77

such publication will be donated to any Masonic activity, or
activity of any group requiring Masonic membership as a condition of membership therein.
I 0. The distribution of any such publication shall be made through
United States mail. addressed to the individual for whom it is
intended, except that copies may be forwarded to Lodges upon
their request therefor.

11. All such publications shall be published and distributed at the
same times and during the periods specified by them.
12. No advertising of a partisan political character, or in which
intoxicating liquor is featured, shall be printed in any such
publication.
The owner or owners of any such publication shall apply to the
Grand Secretary for a permit to publish and distribute such publication,
which application shall contain full information as to the title, periodicity
of issue, names and addresses of owners, publishers and editors and the
average number of copies circulated, together with a statement signed
by the owner or owners of such publication that he or they will comply
with the conditions hereinbefore set forth. Upon receipt of such application, the Grand Secretary shall forward to such owner or owners a
permit to publish and distribute such publication, subject to the conditions hereinbefore set forth.
Upon receipt of such a permit, the owner or owners shall print conspicuously in each issue of such publication the following statement:
"This publication is published and distributed pursuant to a
permit issued by the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California, and subject to certain conditions. Such
permit does not constitute this publication an official publication of
or for the Grand Lodge, and does not constitute an approval by the
Grand Lodge of any of the contents herein."

failure to print the foregoing statement in the manner herein provided
shall constitute ~ood cause for the revocation of said permit by the
Grand Master. The printing of said statement in any publication not
having a permit issued as above provided, or after such permit has been
revoked, shall constitute a Masonic offense, and the owner or owners
of such publication shall be proceeded against as provided in the Odinances of Grand Lodge.

ASSISTANC E FOR TEHACHAP I LODGE NO. 313
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, It has been the policy of Grand Lodge when a Lodge has
suffered material damage to its Temple by some unforeseen catastrophe
to assist such Lodge by outright grant in the rebuilding of its Temple,
and,
WHEREAS, By the earthquake on July 21, 1952, Tehachapi Lodge No.
313, suffered the entire destruction of its Temple by earthquake, and,
WHEREAS, The Lodge has on hand approximately $9,000.00 which
it can use towards the building of a new Temple, and,
WHEREAS, Many of the membership of the Lodge have suffered
material damage in the same earthquake and, therefore, little, if any, help
can be expected from its members, and,
WHEREAS, If at this time an appropriation by Grand Lodge is not
made to assist Techachapi Lodge in the building of a new Temple, that
the Lodge will not be able to have a home until a further session of
Grand Lodge.

Now, Therefore, be it Resolved: That Grand Lodge appropriate such
sum as may be found necessary to assist in the rebuilding of the new
Temple for Tehachapi Lodge with the understanding that no part thereof shall be paid to Tehachapi Lodge until the Lodge Financing Committee shall have approved plans and specifications for the new building,
and also until the incoming Grand Master, together with the incoming
Grand Treasurer, and the Chairman of the Finance Committee, shall
have approved the payment to the Lodge of the sum appropriated.
Fraternally submitted,
GEO. W. BENNETT, Master
EARLE. WHITNEY, Senior Warden
L. T. JENKINS, P. M.
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on
Finance.

mittee thus far has been to assemble at noon for lunch and conference
after approximately a half hour general conversation. The sessions have
occupied approximately two and a half hours additional.
In addition to routine recommendations and decisions, Mr. Langan
reported with respect to use of Moody's Service by lodges that forty had
requested Moody's services and that in response to Moody's inquiry,
twenty.-one had submitted portfolios for analysis and that Moody's had
replied with fifteen complete initial reports, the remaining six being in
the process of completion.
Since that time the number of lodges making inquiry has increased
to seventy-two, the number presenting portfolios for analysis to fiftyeight, the num'ber of original reports and analyses prepared to fl.ftyeight, and also number of lodges reporting to Moody's on action taken
were twenty-five, number of reviews subsequenf to initial reports
amounted to forty-two and the total dollar value of portfolios reviewed
·w as $2,105,900.00 approximately.
The mem•bers of the Investment Committee are well pleased with the
services of Moody's represented by Mr. Richard T. Langan, Pacific
Coast Manager, who has been faithful in attendance at meetings and
most cooperative at other times.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Eleventh Annual
Report as your Grand Secretary.
WAYPARER LODGE

u. D.

Wayfarer Lodge U. D., located at Whittier, was instituted on July
1. 1952. only 30 days before the close of the fl.seal year. ~his Lodge did
not collect any dues during the year, and, at my suggestion, the Grand
Master directed that they be not required to pay the per capita tax. It
is respectfully requested that this 'be approved.

No: 659
In making a remittance to Grand Lodge La Habra Lo~ge No. 659
sent in $150.00 on a Masonic Homes Endowment Fund remittance form,
and the amount was credited to that Fund. T~is ~mount s~o~l~ .have
been for the Masonic Homes, representing contributions on six initiates.
The Grand Secretary requests authority to transfer $150.00 from the
Endowment Fund to the Masonic Homes of California to meet the
deficit in the payment due the Homes.
LA HABRA LoDGE

PHOTOSTATIC COPIES OF CHARTERS

We again call the attention of the Lodges to the wisdom of having
the Lodge charter photostated. There are still a great many which have
not availed 'themselves of this service, and we urge these Lodges to
protect.their charters by this method.
CENTENNIAL Boox

The volume commemorating the Centennial Celebration, authorized
by Grand Lodge, has been completed and a copy sent to each Lodge
and to others entitled to receive a copy of it.
MICROFILMING OF RECORDS

As authorized at the last Communication of Grand Lodge, microfilm
equipment was purchased. All· vital membership anq ftnanci~l records,
both of Grand Lodge and of the Masonic Homes, have been microfilmed,
indexed, placed in a steel cabinet and sto.red in the vault specially made
.
for the purpose in the Columbia Masonic Temple. .
Other valuable records will be stored there from time to time.
UNFINISHED BUSINESS

The following matters were continued from the last Annual Communication to the present one:
1. Revision of ceremonies for short form Opening.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OP THE

2. Disposition of proceeds of Estate of Andrew W. Morton, de..
ceased.
3. Special Committee on Ceremonies re installation of Grand Lodge
Officers.
·
4. Report of Investment Committee re constituent Lodges.
5. Recognition of Grand Lodge of Italy.
6. Special committee to study trial procedures.
FIDELITY BoNDS

The Grand Secretary recommends that a blanket Fidelity Bond be
secured covering Officers of Grand Lodge, constituent Lodges, Masonic
Homes, Boards of Relief, Employment Bureaus and Masonic Club..
houses. with a provision for minimum coverage of $5.000.00 and maximum coverage as may be determined, the total premium therefor to be
paid by Grand Lodge. The detail of this proposal is covered in a special
report prepared by the Grand Secretary.
It is recommended that Section 666 be amended to properly provide
for the new program.
COMPENSATION INSURANCE

Every Lodge which has a payroll is required :by state law to have
workmen's compensation insurance. Recent rate changes have added
additional burdens to every policy holder. At the request of the Grand
Secretary a plan has been developed to cover all Lodges with compensation insurance, and, if carried by Grand Lodge, a very favorable rate can
be obtained. It is recommended that this coverage be provided for and
that Grand Lodge carry the expense thereof for the Lodges. The detail
of this proposal is covered in a special report prepared by the Grand
Secretary.
It is recommended that legislation similar to Section 666 be prepared
to authorize such a program.
SALARY OF loDGE ORGANIST

Many Lodges employ an organist and pay a salary for the services
performed. The Uniform Code of By-Laws, as now written, make no
provision for the payment of such a salary and Section 620 is adverse.
This appears to be a necessary expenditure for which there should be
positive authorization.
Ross DIGEST
The sixth edition, 1949, Ross Digest, is exhausted. Authorization is
requested to bring it up to date and print a seventh edition.
MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the membership totals I have made a comparison by
decades beginning with 1912. In the succeeding forty years we have

89

grown from 352 Lodges to 614, and the membership has increased from
48,315 to 207,832.
During the year just closed there were 301 more members initiated
than in the previous years. but there were 198 fewer raised. The net
gain was 5,332 contrasted with 5,700 in 1951.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
Brethren:
Again is becomes my happy privilege to render to this Annual Communication a full and detailed account of the services of your Grand
Lecturer during the Masonic year now drawing to a dose, and to set
forth herein a report of the condition of the Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction, together with a short resume of the activities of the Ritual
Committee.
In preparing this report, I deem it necessary first to acquaint the
brethren with the fact that I have had to rely this year to a large extent
on the co-operation of the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Inspectors
of the Several Masonic Districts. In the early Spring of this year I
suffered a slight heart attack, which kept me more or less inactive for a
period of four months, and was responsible for my absence at four of
the five Spring Conferences. Much of the information contained herein,
therefore has been gleaned from the Annual Reports of the Inspectors,
those fine Masons who give so much of their time and exceptional talents
in the interest of Masonry in California. Each of these Inspectors, now
numbering 145 within our Jurisdiction, has complied with the requirements of Section 53 of Ross Digest, and has given a complete and concise account of the condition of the Lodges in his particular District.
To them I desire to express my grateful appreciation.

Condition of Lodges
With only one exception, the Constituent Lodges within the State
are in a fair to excellent condition. Fewer degrees are being conferred
in most Lodges than has been the case in recent years, and more opporunity is being provided for programs of entertainment and educational
improvement for our members. With but very few exceptions the officers
advancing through the chairs of our Lodges are outstanding in their
respective communities, and are enthusiastically participating in their
Masonic duties. The one exception referred to above is Forest Lodge
No. 66, in the little mining town of Alleghany, where, "due to economic
and other conditions relating to the smaller gold mining communities,
and due primarily to the poor road conditions, the Lodge is not able
to conduct regular meetings for a lack of a quorum." The officers elected
for the year 1952 had not been installed at the writing of this report.
Officers' Coaches
Section 53 (3rd a) of the Ordinances, under the duties of the lnspee. tor, reads, "To appoint in each Lodge within his District an Officers'

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

105

Coach, who shall be a qualified Past Master of the Lodge, and who shall
serve at the pleasure of the Inspector. The Officers' Coach shall assist
in teaching t?e ritual to the Offic~~s of his Lodge, and assist in preparing
them to qualify for advancement. I find that in some cases the Inspector
has overlooked taking full advantage of this law. He has failed to see
the b~nefits both to hi.mself and to the Officers of his Lodges in first
selecti~g the best qualified Past Master available, and then thoroughly
preparing that Past Master for the important duties he has been selected
to discharge. An Officers' Coach, well prepared and zealous in his responsibilities, can be of inestimable assistance to the Inspector and tc
the Lodge Officers.
The Grand Secretary has recently caused to be printed a supply of
"Certificates of Appointment", in handy wallet form, to be issued by the
Inspector when making the appointment of the Officers' Coach. This
certificate is designed not only to make the recipient a little more conscious of his responsibility, but also to impress others with the imP<>rtance of the position. I would urge Inspectors to make full use of these
certificates.

Candidates' Coaches
In recent years I have had ample opportunity to view the work of the
Candidates' Coaches. Those with whom I have come in contact have
exhibited an excellent knowledge of the ritual, and a self-sacri.ftci~g inter~st in th~ newly made Mason. They work long and hard in preparing candidates, and never expect and seldom receive recognition for
their efforts. Let us occasionally reward them with a word of commendation.
District Officers' Associations
In all but twenty-four of our Masonic Districts, Officers' Associations
have been formed and are successfully functioning for the best interests
of our Fraternity. In some of the twenty-four Districts without associations, it is believed to be quite impossible, because of great distances
between Lodges, to successfully organize, and maintain interest in, an
Officers' Association. In other Districts, however, it seems evident that
with a little earnest effort by the Inspector and co-operation from the
Offi~ers of the District, such an association could be organized, and the
requirements of Section 53 (3rd) of the Ordinances complied with.
Degree Teams
It has repeatedly come to the attention of the Grand Lecturer that
the~e are degree teams -0perating in certain parts of the Jurisdiction
which are not c.onf~rming to the ritual prescribed by Grand Lodge, or
are not proceeding in accordance with the restrictions governing degree
teams.

106

. PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

It is generally agreed that degree teams, operating in strict accordance with the laws adopted by the Grand Lodge, have a definite place in
our fraternal life, and that their work, when performed in an exemplary
manner, tends to increase attendance at our meetings and serves to
promote good fellowship among the brethren.
Too often. however, we find that the brothers who temporarily fill the
various places and stations on degree teams disregard our rules an~
regulations (with which I believe most of them to be familiar), and stage
ritualistic travesties for the amusement of the side-lines, with little regard for the impression that we hope to make upon the candidate. This
condition must be corrected or the degree team will be outlawed in the
not too distant future. The regular otHcers and the personnel selected
to illustrate a portion of the ritual in our Lodges are taught by, and are
under the strict surveillance of the Inspector of their respective Districts.
They are required to conform strictly to our prescribed ritual and any
lesser conformity on the part of degree teams only serves to lessen the
dignity and authority of the Inspector. I have occaslonally heard the
remark made by the regular officers of Lodges: "They can get away
with it, why can't we?" The work of the degree team, therefore, should
be more, rather than less; efficient than the regular officers.
The Masters are reminded that they are responsible for conferring
all degrees in their Lodges: that they have the responsibility for inviting
only qualified brothers to participate in the work, and that all of the
degree work "shall be conducted in a dignified manner, consistent with
the high purposes of Masonry and the impression which the degree is
designed to create in the mind of the candidate." Any infractions of
the well established rules regarding degree teams in the future will be
reported to th Grand Master with the recommendation that the appropriate disciplinary action be taken.

A TIME FOR VISION
RALPH C. HINE, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Sir-My Brethren All:
The privilege of serving during this Grand Lodge year has proven
to be, for me, an unique educational experience. While it has been necessary, as required, to do a great deal of talking, it has also afforded
the opportunity to be a good listener. Out of this opportunity comes
the challenge to picture for you the concern of the brethren of all ranks
for the influence, or lack of it, which Masonry in general and individual
Masons in particular have, or will have, during these troubled times.
Two experiences, vivid in my memory, seemed to illustrate that ever
present concern. While these experiences occurred in particular localities,
there can be little, if any, doubt that they could be duplicated under
similar conditions in every community in this Grand Jurisdiction.
Last Memorial Day our Grand Master placed wreaths upon the
graves of two Past Grand Masters. On that occasion the Lodges of the
Community also remembered, in like manner, their deceased Past Masters. As we trod that path of memory, starting with the oldest, brief
accounts were noted of their service to Masonry, the Community, the
State and the Nation. It was a thrilling experience until we reached a
period somewhere in the early thirties when it suddenly became apparent
that, with a few exceptions, little more could be said than that they had
been "good and true.'' Can it be possible that we have reached, even
passed, the point where it is deemed sufficient for a Master Mason,
particularly a Master or Past Master, just to be "good and true1"
On July 25th our Grand Master, after taking immediate steps to
ascertain ·the personal needs of our brethren following the earthquake
of the previous Monday, met with the Officers of our Lodges in Kern
County to survey the material damage suffered by Lodge properties.
The unity of thought, the universal expressions of eagerness to plan
and promote mutual assistance was worthy of our highest traditions.
Can it be possible that we have reached the point where it takes a disaster or a tragic emergency to bring out our latent capabilities1
Thoughtful ly considering these experiences, in the light of the concern so often expressed, these questions posed themselves.
Have we forgotten our heritage7
Have we lost the vision1
Last year the Grand Orator of this Grand Lodge stressed the phrase
"The Master Mason, more so than Other Men," and closed his address
with these thought provoking words"SEE ! THIS OUR FATHERS
DID FOR

us:·

.

109

In the light of all this it seems that this address, devoted to matters
appertaining to the Craft, should consider this our One Hundred Third
Annual Communication, as a TIME FOR VISION.
.
The short period of time, starting this morning and ending Friday
afternoon, should have a special meaning since it might well begin with
the miracle of looking backward into the past and it must end with the
uplift of looking forward to the future. Until now, really, we have lived
our year largely in the present, rarely thinking back beyond yesterday,
rarely farther ahead than tomorrow. Suddenly now, as by a special
blessing, we can see other days in crystal clarity. We see again, how
clearly, the faces that are gone and hear once more the sound of voices
long since stilled. It is aJmost as though the old days were back, and
the old scenes and the old hopes and presences, forming the framework
of our heritage and our vision. As these days pass, our thoughts and
actions ·might well be governed by what we should remember- there are
so many things for us to remember.
Directing our vision backward to the past should we not remind
ourselves, over and over again, that our Forefathers , men with the
Spirit of Masonry in their hearts, brought forth on this continent a new
Nation, "conceived in Liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all
men are created Free and Equal." That these men guided by their memory of the past and their vision for the future builded into the frame• ·
work of the government of this new Nation three great Corner Stones
which are the very essence of the Spirit of Masonry.
These Spirit of Masonry Corner Stones may be stated as folows:
That those who govern should receive their
just powers with the consent of the governed.
That all men have the right to worship God in
accordance with the dictates of their own conscience.
That free public education is a prime necessity
for a people who are to remain free and equal.
We should further remind ourselves that other men with the Spirit
of Masonry in their Hearts, carrying the Torch of this Vision, as pioneers. extended the frontiers of this new Nation westward, ever westward. until they spanned this great continent and were standing on the
shores of the vast Pacific. Some of these pioneers carried Warrants for
Masonic Lodges in their hands as well as the Spirit of Masonry in their
Hearts. They established Lodges wherever they settled, and so as Territorial and State Governmen ts were erected, Grand Lodges came into
being, thus giving assurance that the Spirit of Masonry would continually be impressed upon the minds and hearts of the coming generations
of men, thus ensuring that the Torch of our Forefathers Vision would

111

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

be forever held aloft and that they would guard and maintain the Foundation Walls of these great Corner Stones strong and secure.
.
We need but to look around us to be impressed by the almost miraculous development of this great Nation and this great State anc:t to re~
alize that we must be something more than just "good and true" if we
are to impress the spirit of Masonry upon the minds and hearts of other
men and encourage them to hold aloft and carry forward this Torch
of Vision.
. Our Brother Edwin Markham caught and projected this Vision when
he wrote:
"WE MEN OF EARTH HAVE HERE THE STUFF
OF PARADISE-WE HAVE ENOUGH!
WE NEED NO OTHER THING TO BUILD
THE STAIRS INTO THE UNFULFILLEDNO OTHER IVORY FOR THE DOORSNO OTHER MARBLE FOR THE FLOORSNO OTHER CEDAR FOR THE BEAM
AND DOME OF MAN'S IMMORTAL DREAM.
HERE ON THE PATHS OF EVERY DAYHERE ON THE COMMON HUMAN WAYIS ALL THE BUSY GODS WOULD TAKE
TO BUILD A HEAVEN, TO MOLD AND MAKE
NEW EDENS. OURS THE STUFF SUBLIME
TO BUILD ETERNITY IN . TIME."

"Freedom is that state of being in which a citizen is not conscious
that he is being governed.
"There must be government and there must be laws. Great
masses of men and women cannot live together without organization for the common good.
"That is Government.
"Great communities cannot exist if each individual does exactly
what he wants to do. The whole must be protected against
misconduct on the part of each of its members. Each must surrender to the whole some part of his right to do at all times
whatever he may want to do. This willingness to forego the
right to injure one another must be embodied in a set of
accepted rules of conduct.
"These rules are the law.
"The instant that Government steps over the line and meddles
with any right not ceded to it by the individual, there is an
impairment of Freedom. The instant a rule is enacted and becomes a part of the body of the Law which forbids a citizen
to do a thing which does not harm his neighbor, there is an
impairment of Freedom. The instant a law is enacted which
compels a citizen to do a thing which it is his natural right to
refrain from doing, there is an impairment of Freedom.
"Freedom then, is a state of existence in which a citizen lives
his life and carries on his affairs according to the dictates of
his own conscience, limited only by the necessity that all citizens must be protected against depredations of any one citizen
or group."
This seems deary to express the Vision of our Forefathers when
they builded this Corner Stone into the framework of constitutional
government for the Nation, this State and this Grand Lodge. How well
do we, as Masons, maintain the foundation wall of this Corner Stone?
The mounting complexities of our public, social and fraternal life
has been such through the years that we have, of necessity, delegated
some of our functions to appointed Boards, Commissiorts and Commit~
tees in violation of our traditions that formation of policy shall be dele~
gated only to the hands of elected officials. While theoretically these
committees, or whatever they may be, can only recommend, and their
recommendations have no binding force, still they may strongly influ~
ence opinion, for it seems only natural to assume that they have fairly
considered all of the evidence and reached impartial judgment. Too
often, however, such bodies tend to overstep their prerogatives in their
zeal to do what they consider good.
Since we should set the example, as well as just be "good.and true,"
we can best maintain and strengthen the foundation wall of this Corner
Stone by being very sure, during our deliberations, that this ever in-

110

.

As we carry on our deliberations during the coming days it should
be Vision as well as Reason which tells us that while all this is our heritage from the past, we are the custodians of the present and must be
the builders, who examine, maintain and, as necessary, strengthen the
Foundation Walls of these Spirit of Masonry Comer Stones that they
may be projected into the future bright and vivid with opportunity and
challenge for those who come after us.
While these Corner Stones, like all units of a trinity, are co-equal
in importance and, in the end, must be considered as one, it seems best
to start with the one first mentioned.
0

That those who govern should receive their
just powers with the consent of the governed.
Since we are, first of all, Free-Men and then Free-Masons, it may
be well for us to examine the foundation wall of this Comer Stone in
the light of our understanding of this thing called Freedom. The following. taken from a story by Clarence Buddington Kelland, is chosen as
a basis for our conslderation, and I _q uote:

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

creasing philosophy of government does not inffuence the law making
process by which we, as Masons, govern ourselves.
As we approach consideration of the second of these Comer Stones
we should walk softly, yet proudly, for it is the very stone of foundation
of the Spirit of Masonry.

There are actually three school systems: the public schools, which
carry out the original intention; parochial church schools, which emphasize a particular creed; and private schools, which emphasize economic
or social distinction. As a greater proportion of our youth are encouraged
to attend nonpublic schools, private or parochial, the greater the threat
to our democratic unity and principles.
Therefor, the danger in allowing the ever increasing criticism of
our public school system to go unchallenged. We must, it seem, so
familiarize ourselves with its Officials, its Teachers and their methods,
its courses and their aims, that we can as Citizens, as well as Masons,
challenge at any time and under any conditions hostile critics of our
public school system and make them "show their colors."
Therefore, we should unalterably oppose the diverson of tax funds,
by direct or indirect means, for the support of nonpublic schools, private
or parochial, since their major use would ultimately be to extend their
scope and facilities and thus help them to undermine and eventually
destroy the free public school.
Under the direction of this Grand Lodge we have, ov~r the years,
a proud record of support of our public school system through the observance of public school week. However, the time has come when it
is not enough to pay lip service to this great founding principle one week
a year. We must as individuals stand up and be counted, every day in
the year, especially during the days immediately ahead.
To examine, maintain and strengthen the foundation wall of this
Corner Stone is a vital necessity for, in the final analysis, the Free Public
School and the Masonic Fraternity are dedicated to a common objective.
That of teaching people HOW to think instead of WHAT to think.
Our Vision, turning to the future, must now tell us that these Corner
Stones are in fact the Spirit of Masonry and that they must be considered as one, for should any one of them be allowed to fail, those which
remain could no longer sustain the proud structures which they support.
Our vision might be stimulated by remembering the first" stanza of
an old, old hymn:
ONCE TO EVERY MAN AND NATION,
COMES THE MOMENT TO DECIDE.
IN THE STRIFE OF TRUTH AND FALSEHOOD,
FOR THE GOOD OR EVIL SIDE:
SOME GREAT CAUSE, GOD'S NEW MESSIAH,
OFFERING EACH THE BLOOM OR BLIGHT,
AND THE CHOICE IS GONE FOREVER,
TWIXT THAT DARKNESS AND THAT LIGHT.
Now it should be vision which tells us that when we examine the
foundation walls of these Spirit of Masonry Corner Stones we are ex-

That all men have the right to worship God in accordance with
· the dictates of their own conscience.
When our Forefathers, who were devoutly religious, God fearing
men, builded this Corner Stone into the framework of our constitutional
government, they did so as evidence of their distrust of the organized
religions, occasioned by their bitter experiences in both the new and
the old world. Their basic concept was not only complete separation
of Church and State, that there should be no State Religion, but as
well, that men should, as a matter of right, be allowed to worship, or
not, as they saw flt.
Masonry's concept has always been, always must be, that somewhere in the foundation of all organizations, public or private, which
are worthy to survive, will be found a mythical stone upon which, graven
there by the faith of its mem'bers. will be found the symbol, or the name,
of the Great Architect of the Universe. We need but to review, and
to remember, the ritualistic teachings of this Fraternity to realize that
this Stone of Foundation is present in all Masonic Lodges and through
them all Grand Lodges.
Here too, we must set the example as well as just be "good and
true." We can best do this by demonstrating in our lives and actions
the fact that while Masonry is indeed deeply religious, it is not, and
does not profess to be, a religion. Remembering, at all times and in all
places, that only these indispensable questions, concerning religion, are
ever asked in Masonry.
Do you believe in God and a future existence?
In whom do you put your trust?
To maintain and strengthen the foundation wall of this Comer Stone
should be our never ending aim for which reason, it should 'he, it must
be, our constant effort.
Since it may well be the means by which we are enabled to retain
all three, the last mentioned Corner Stone might be the greatest of all.
That free public education is a prime necessity
for a people who are to remain free and equal.
Are we sufficiently aware of the development of a dual system of
education in this country which is contrary to the founding principle
of this Corner Stone which contemplated a single public school system
which would serve all creeds?

a.mining OURSELVES, for WE are the LIVING STONES .in these
foundation walls which need to be maintained, and, as need be strength- .
ened, if the principles which they represent are to be projected into the
future bright and vivid with opportunity and challenge for those who
come after us.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith present
the Sixtieth Annual Report, for the year ending July 31, 1952, together
with the reports of the Superintendents of our Homes, and the financial
reports of the Treasurer and Secretary.
The Board of Trustees met on October 12, 1951, after the adjournment of Grand Lodge, for the purpose of organization. The election of
Arthur M. Warren, Deputy Grand Master, Frank Harwell, Jr., Senior
Grand Warden and Henry C. Clausen, Junior Grand Warden was formally reported to the Board and on motion duly made, seconded and
carried, they were elected members of the Board.
The Secretary reported the appointment by the Grand ·Master of
L. Harold Anderson and Ralph H. Head to the Board for a term of
three years each and on motion duly made, seconded and carried, they
were elected members of the Board.
In addition to the Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens, the Board is composed of the following Trustees:
Chas. Albert Adams...................... 1952............................ ~.Myron E. Smith
Charles M. Wollenberg ................1953................................Leonard Gross
L. Harold Anderson ......................1954•..••.••..•.•.,.....•.•.......Ralph H. Head
On motion duly made, seconded and carried Charles M. Wollenberg
was elected President of the Board.
On motion duly made, seconded and carried Leonard Gross was
elected Vice-President of the Board.
By virtue of his office as Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge,
F. & A. M. of California, Past Grand Master Francis V. Keesling is
Treasurer of the Masonic Homes of California.
By virtue of his office as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, F. &
A. M. of California, Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson is Secretary
of the Masonic Homes of California.
GENERAL

Superintendent James R. Eubanks of the Home for the Aged at
Decoto and Superintendent Robert M. Henry, of the Home for Children
at Covina have each prepared a detailed report and the Board urges all
members of the Fraternity to carefully read them.
Inflation and mounting costs play no favorites and your Board of
Trustees is faced with the constantly increasing costs of providing proper
care for the old people at Decoto and the children at Covina and in spite
of all reasonable economies which are practiced, the cost of providing
proper and adequate care continues to mount. The Board is of the opinion
that the Fraternity will want these Homes properly conducted, without
extravagances or frills, and ways must be found to meet these costs. The

118

119

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Board recommends to every member of Grand Lodge a study of the
audit which has been prepared.
There are some evidences that there may be a slight increase in the
number of applications for admission to the Home at Covina but the
total population is still far below the capacity of that Home with the
result that the per capita cost is high.
Applications continue to come in at about the usual annual rate.
Some years ago when the State Old Age Pension was increased and
Social Security was in its infancy it was thought that these two factors
might reduce the number of applications to the Home. This has not occurred, however, for the simple reason that mounting living costs make
it impossible for old people to live on the amount secured from these
sources and those fortunate enough to be eligible for the Home at Decato, naturally tum toward the Masonic Fraternity for assistance in
their declining years.

The entire facilities of the Palo Alto Clinic as a diagnostic unit have
been made available to the residents of the Home and the services of the
Palo Alto Clinic staff are available and utilized for any indicated hospitalization or operative procedure. Any patient needing hospital care,
not provided at Decato, uses the facilities of the Palo Alto Hospital.
This plan has worked out very satisfactorily since its inauguration,
January 1, 1952, for a year's trial.
It is hoped that it will !he possible for the plan to be continued ·in the
future as it has brought satisfaction to members of the Home as well
as the operating staff.

BUILDING 0PERATIONS-DECOTO

A number of improvements have been made to the Masonic Homes
property at Decato. ·
A sprinkling system has been approved for the hospital wing of the
Home at a cost of about $10,000.
.
Improvements to the water supply and steam supply have also been
authorized.
A superintendent's residence at Decato was approved early in June
and the work is well underway on this structure. It is located to the north
of the ramp leading to the nurses' residence and commands a dominating
view over the grounds and the valley.
The replacement of the passenger elevator in the south wing is to
he made as well as the modernization of the north and east elevators.
The structures as well as the grounds of both the Covina Home for
Children and the Decato Home for the Aged have been kept in a good
state of repair and are a credit to the Masons of the Jurisdiction.
BUILDING OPERATIONS-COVINA

The employees residence at Covina has been thoroughly modernized
during the year, providing additional apartments, sun porches, and
kitchen facilities. The expense of remodelling has been justified through
happier and more content personnel. A new and better type employee
has hen attracted 'by the improved housing arrangements.
MEDICAL ACTIVITIES FOR RESIDENTS OF THE DECOTO HOME

The Board entered into an agreement with the Palo Alto Clinic for
twenty-four hour medical coverage for any acute or emergency illness
at the Decato Home. In addition, regular office hours are held at the
Masonic Home daily, Monday through Friday, by a physician member
of the Palo Alto Clinic staff.

4-H PROGRAM-COVINA

Of special interest during Lodge visitations to Covina during the
year has been the 4-H farm program instituted by Superintendent Henry.
The benefits of the plan are well enough known to forego detailed description. However, the enthusiasm and interest with which the Covina
boys and girls have entered into the raising and care of domestic animals
have more than justified the relatively small expense. In many instances
the children have profited financialy through their efforts. Entering
animals in fairs and shows has !brought many prize ribbons and commendation to the Home children.
MOTION PICTURE

During the year a Special Committee ·on a motion picture of th~
Masonic Homes has approved a final script and made preliminary arrangements for production. Photographed in color with a background
of Masonic history, the picture promises to be outstanding in its field.
Members of the craft and their families, heretofore unable to visit both
Homes, will soon have an opportunity to become better acquainted with
the facilities. Present schedules provide that copies will be ready for
distribution to lodges during Endowment Month of 1953.
FINANCES

The funds of the Masonic Homes are divided into two categories.
The General Fund which is used for operations, general maintenance
and administration derives its income from per capita tax, the $25.00
Home contribution by initiates and the investment income from the Endowment Fund and Homes securities.
The year end figure as of July 31, 1952 discloses a surplus of $112,999 .95 after paying all expenses. The per capita for this period was
$1.00 per member. This gain added to savings over the past few years
has enabled the Homes to acquire a surplus of $444,356.00 as a rainy
day fund to be used in the event of a major catastrophe or in the event
that the Lodges themselves are unable to continue their per capita c;:ontribution. In the opinion of the Trustees it is deemed prudent to maintain
a reserve of approximately one year's operating costs.

120

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The per capita of 75c, a decrease of 25c over previous years, levied
last October and which has been collected for the coming year's operations, has produced the sum of $153,952.50. After estimating all other
income and providing for an advance of 10% in costs, the Homes will
end the next &seal year with an estimated gain of $5.952.50 for the
period. It is fortunate that the revenue from securities under the new
investment program has increased our income. A review of 8gures will
reveal that the cost of running both homes has increased from $242,884.00 in 1944 to $536,892.00 for the year just closed, an increase of
over 120%.
In the same period our income has advanced from $511,344.00 to
$649,892.00 an increase of about 27%. With a per capita income of only
75c for the coming year, our income will just about meet expenses.
· Relying upon the generosity of the craft to support the Endowment
Fund and with the realization that it may be necessary to ask for an
increase in future years, we recommend the continuation of the 75c per
capita to be collected as of July 31, 1953.
The Special Funds of the Homes are supported by bequests, gifts
and assignments and under our regulations cannot be used for ordinary
maintenance or general operations.
In 1946 the constitutional requirement for a 50c per capita for the
Building Fund was repealed. Since then all bequests not speci8cally
earmarked for the Endowment Fund have been added to our Building
Fund which is now called Reserve for Additions and Replacements. In
addition considera'ble sums have been received with a proviso that the
money be allocated to a specific Home.
We suggest that future contributions or bequests be made to either
the Masonic Homes of California or to the Endowment Fund as the
donor may desire and that no special mention be made of either the
Covina or Decoto Home.
The corporate title of the Homes is Masonic Homes of California
and it is to this corporation that bequests or gifts should be made.
The trustees have reviewed the various special and reserve funds and
have made adjustments which do not appear on the balance sheet as
of July 31. 1952.
·
We have transferred $150,000.00 from Unappropriated Reserves to
Reserve for Additions and Replacements. This will raise our building
reserve to approximately $525,000.00 which we feel is adequate for
our needs in the foreseeable future.
From the same fund we propose to transfer $35,000.00 to the Endowment Fund. Likewise, we plan to transfer $100,000.00 from the
Covina Special Fund and $65,000.00 from the Decoto Special Fund.
This will provide the Endowment Fund with an additional $200,000.00
which will swell its total to close to $5,000,000.00.

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: It is again my duty and my privilege to submit to you this
my 12th annual report of the Masonic Home at Decato for the year ending July 31, 1952.
On August 1, 1951, the beginning of the fiscal year, 116 men and
172 women were enjoying the benefits of the Home, 29 women at an
average age of 75, and 28 men at the average age of 77.5 were admitted
during the year. During the same period 26 women, average 83.2, and
29 men, average age 87.9 passed to the great beyond, and 2 women were
withdrawn. Leaving us at the end of the year with 174 women and 114
men. Included are 9 married couples.

73 or 25% of the population of the Home are being cared for in our
hospital and the east wing. Miss Bess Payne with her staff assistants
·are rendering an excellent service in that department.
For some time we were not entirely satisfied with the medical branch
of the hospital department. In an attempt to improve that service consideration was given many propositions. Finally, the service offered by
the Palo Alto Clinic through Dr. Lee was accepted. The doctors who
visit the Home daily are rendering a very satisfactory service and are
very popular with those whom they are serving. However, the service
is quite expensive.
Mrs. Mildred Harris, who was serving as matron of the Home when
our 1951 report was rendered, terminated her services with the H_ome
on November 1, 1951. Mrs. Esther Esseiva, Past Matron of Riverview
Chapter No. 336 O.E.S., was appointed and took over the responsible
duties of that very important office. During Mrs. Esseivais short tenure
she has proven herself to be capable, consciencious, loyal and a very
willing worker, and· is rapidly becoming very popular with the members
of the Home.
Mr. Paul Shipman, a member of Alameda Lodge No. 167, was ap-pointed Assistant Superintendent of the Masonic Home and entered
upon the duties of that office on February 1, 1952. Brother Shipman
was assigned the responsibilities of the outside work and during his
spare time he is familiarizing himself with the general operations of the
Home. We find him to be extremely interested in his duties, sincere in

his efforts, and kind and considerate of the residents of the Home. Our
Home will be, I am sure, greatly benefitted by his services.
Rev. Henchelwood who had been serving the Home as Chaplain
for some time was forced to resign, due to ill health, on December 1,
1951. The vacancy caused by his resignation was filled on February 1,
1952, by Rev. Howard Steward, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church of
Centerville. He is very understanding and by his counselling is bringing much comfort and happiness to those who call on him each day for
spiritual guidance.

Concrete for the foundation of the superintend ent's cottage was

during the year added greatly to the happiness of the residents.
I do feel, however, that Special mention should be made of two or
three programs which were really outstanding . On August 19th, Mrs.
Bernice Hanson, Chairman of the East Bay Matrons, accompanied with
about 600 members of the association delivered to the Home about
13,000 glasses of jams and jellies. After lunch, which was served in

Matron, Mrs. Louis B. Tamba in our auditorium at which time she and
her Grand Lodge Officers were introduced to the members of the Home.

was prepared for them. Following the festivities they presented a very
excellent program for the pleasure and entertainme nt of the folks at
the Home. Needless to say it was an enjoyable day for every one present.
On the evening of July 11th, the members of the Home held their
annual reception for the Grand Master and his wife. This year it was
a double feature, as the Trustees were holding one of their quarterly
meetings at the Home at the time, therefore, they participated in the
festivities.
·

guests. At the close of the program ice cream and cake were served. A
delightful time was had by all.
Lodges from Sacramento to as far south as Los Angeles have brought
to the Home during the year 34 fine programs, and have exemplified
14 degrees in our Temple. Our visitors' register indicates that of the
2557 visitors who signed our visitors' register 51 were from foreign jurisdictions, the remaining number representing approximate ly 200 lodges
in this jurisdiction.
One or the other of the following Film Distribution companies of
San Francisco provides the Home with a complete program each week
through the year with a special program thrown in on Christmas or
New Years. These programs are appreciated and enjoyed by the Home
Folks. We are very grateful to RKO, Columbia, United Artists, Warner.
Bros., MGM and Twentieth Century Fox, and want to extend to the
members of those fine companies our sincere thankii for their conthn1~d
generosity.

Each Sunday through the year, devotional services are conducted
by a minister appointed by the Chaplain of the Home, reserving one
Sunday for himself.
Our library is well supplied with daily papers, periodicals, and fine
books. These books, magazines, and papers are enjoyed by many of the
members who enjoy good reading material.
To tne Board of Trustees of our Home, without whose timely advice
and willing assistance it would be difficult at times to carry on, we extend

HOME MEMBERSHIP

The population of our Masonic Home Family, as of July 31, 1952,
numbers sixty-two children. Thirty-three boys and twenty-nine girls.
An increase of two children over the preceding year. Nine girls and
eleven boys have left us during the year. Nine by graduation from High
School: ten returning to re-established homes of their parents; and one
boy entering the U. S. Air Force. Eight of our graduates will continue
their education and one boy has selected entering the Armed Services.
The colleges enrolled in by the graduates include: Appointment to the
United States C~ast Guard Academy, New London, Connecticut, Chaffey Junior College, Long Beach City College, and Los Angeles City
College. During the fiscal year of 1951-52 ten boys and thirteen girls
were admitted to the Home, including one boy who was re-admitted.

a Home project. The children engaged in many phases of school activities, such as school social and service clubs, athletic competition, and
scholastic achievement. Sue Burkhalter, '52, graduated with the highest
scholastic honors of the entire graduating class. In addition, Sue and
Patricia Beard were the commencement speakers on this occasion. The
Home was well represented by class and school officers and had many
members in the honorary societies of "Esquire" and "Alcyonians.'' One
of our graduates. Tom Trebell, was installed Master Councillor of
George Washington Chapter, Order of DeMolay and two graduates,
Sue Burkhalter and Patricia Beard held the office of Honored Queen
of Bethel No. 98, Order of Job's Daughters. Swim parties, ·picnics, barbecues, dances, and many other forms of entertainment are encouraged
and afforded our children the opportunity of being host to children of
the community. The children of our Home Family attended Sunday
School and church and take active part in the activities pertaining thereto.
The children's spare time is occupied by participation in our all-round
athletic program: by performing small tasks in their dormitories: chores
on the farm if they are 4-H members: instruction in piano, group singing,
and ceramics; or recreation individually suitable for the various age
groups. It was again our good fortune to retain the Sportsmanship Trophy awarded for displaying the highest qualities in a track and field meet
with eight other homes of similar purpose.
'
IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM:

The renovation and refurnishing of the Employees' Cottage was
completed December 20, 1951. giving to the members of our domestic
and maintenance staff attractive apartments affording a maximum of
comfort and convenience. The parking space adjacent to the Barbecue
Area has been surfaced to provide a clean, convenient parking space for
our picnicing visitors. On our Athletic Field flood lights have been installed, thereby making possible night ball games and affording a wider
use of these facilities. The main kitchen has undergone complete renovation: a terrazzo floor was installed, new stainless steel range, griddle,
oven, toastmaster, and other equipment designed for efficiency and the
healthful preparation of food. A long range plan involving additional
picnic facilities, road resurfacing, farm buildings, and the reclaiming of

128

PROCEEDINGS OF THB

waste lands to permanent pasture, have been approved and should be
completed within the next year.
SUMMER PROGRAM

Five camping periods of two weeks' duration, affording each child a
vacation at Newport Beach under the supervision of a trained and competent staff, is being provided for the children of the Home. The youngsters are given free. play, specialization of interests appealing to their age
group, swimming, hiking, surf and deep sea fishing, overnight "sleepouts", boatrides, and excursion trips to nearby points of interest. For the
girls, additional avenues allowing for self-expression is made possible
by instruction in handicraft. The educational and inspirational inftuence
of such a program is shown by the normal growth and development of
our boys ·and girls-mentally, spiritually and physically. This year a
summer school was organized at the Home for the bene8f of students
who needed coaching in special subjects. This new project met with one
hundred percent cooperation of the children and therefore was an outstanding success.
HEALTH AND WELFARE PROGRAM:

With the exception of childhood diseases, our children have enjoyed ·
especially good health this past year. Under the careful supervision of
Dr. W. P. Magan and his associates, they have been able to participate
to the fullest extent in school. community, and Home Family activities.
Our doctors made a complete physical examination of each child at
regular intervals, thereby making possible the maintaining of accurate
health progress records. This provides each child with an assurance
that everything possible will be done toward their maintaining the physically healthy body that promotes a greater learning capacity. Special
nourishment •. extra rest and a vitamin supplement were given when needed; dietary values were carefully analyzed, and menus planned for the
health and vigor of growing youth. We report eleven cases of measles,
eleven cases of chickenpox and one case of mumps. For surgery we re..
port one appendectomy, four tonsillectomies and one fracture. Dr. Ell..
wood Laine, our visiting dentist, examined each child twice during the
. year and gave one hundred thirty-five treatments in the Home Dental
Clinic. Eleven Children received orthodontia treatments from Dr. Town..
send Paul. Pasadena: one .h undred seven orthodontia treatments are also
recorded. Dr. Wayne D. Kuettel. Covina, continued opthalmic examinations and visual training treatments as part of our health plan. One
hundred fifty-three children were admitted to our Home hospital. with
a total of six hundred ninety-seven hospital days. Five thousand, eight
hundred thirty Home hospital clinic treatments were administered. We
are deeply grateful to our doctors and nurses for their untiring devotion
to the welfare of our boys and girls.

129

FARM AND MASONIC PIONEERS' 4-H CLUB:

During this past fiscal year we have proceeded with our long-range
plan of improvement of farm and grounds. Where declining orange
groves once stood, we now have an excellent pasture for our livestock;
this pasture has been completely fenced. A Fish Pond providing a source
of reserve water for fl.re protection of the wooded section of the Home
property is nearing completion.
The Masonic Pioneers' 4-H Club, composed of our Intermediate
boys and girls, is part of our farm program and has enjoyed a very successful year. The efforts of the children in our 4-H Club were shown in
most gratifying results at the Twenty-first San Gabriel Valley 4-H Fair,
held at Ponoma, in which they received fifteen first premiums, nine
second premiums, and eight third premiums in beef, swine, sheep, and
food preparation classifications. At a Future Farmers of America-4-H
Fair, held in Puente, members of the Masonic Pioneers' 4-H Club were
· awarded one Champion premium, six first premiums, three second premiums, one third premium, and two fifth premiums. We anticipate entering a portion of our swine herd at six fairs throughout the state this
coming year. Our animal husbandry program is also based on a longrange plan and has for the past two years supplied the Home with practi;.
cally all the meat, ham and bacon consumed. The cattle at the Covina
Home are of the beef type and we now have a small registered Hereford
breeding herd. The Hereford breeding projects and some of the breeding
herd are owned by the children. The Home also maintains a small registered Duroc Jersey swine herd, whose production not only meets our
need of fresh pork, but also supplies our table with sugar cured ham,
bacon, and sausage. For this past fiscal year the Covina Home has produced and consumed, in live weight, 16,880 pounds of beef. 8,607 pounds
pork, 1,556 pounds lamb, 272 pounds chicken, I 06 pounds ducks, 589
pounds rabbit.
VISITATIONS:

The visitations of Lodges and affiliated Masonic organizations has
been a source of enjoyment to the children and staff of the Home. A
total of five thousand, two hundred seven guests has been recorded, to
whom we were proud to show our Home and the facilities it offers. This
represents a substantial increase over the previous year. The keen interest of members of the Craft in the welfare of the children is deeply
appreciated and is an inspiration to each one of us to strive for the perfection which is our goal. Donations such as Jams, Jellies, candy, play
and sports equipment, etc., brought to the Home by our visitors have
been greatly appreciated.
ENTERTAINMENT:

Our boys and girls were again special guests at the Annual Barbecue
Picnic, held at Lake Park by Huntington Beach Lodge No. 380, F. &.A.

the new experience of starting out on the highway of life with a spirit
of confidence and faith in ultimately attaining the goals they have set.

THE INVENTORY
Although the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund was created by
Grand Lodge in 1910, it was never considered a very active integral part
of Grand Lodge activities until the establishment of the Endowment
Board in 1933. When the Board started on its program, there was a
very definite educational pattern developed, namely. to enlighten the
Brethren regarding the work and needs of the Homes, and to afford an
opportunity for the Brethren to make special contributions for the support
of the Homes. In short, the purpose of the Board is "to study, devise and
carry out plans for securing an adequate endowment for the Masonic
Homes in California."
The first ten years showed approximately one million and a half
dollars in the Endowment Fund. but the participants were only a small
percentage of the members of the Craft. By the intense educational
program it is most satisfying to see the increase in individual participation. Let us just check the last few years, and we find until very recently

THE PROGRESS
Perhaps no better way to illustrate the progress could be mentioned
than by the increase of Honor Lodges. Your Board suggests an average
of $2.00 per member as being a reasonable contribution for an Honor
Lodge. Let us clarify this statement. Many members would not be
satisfied except by contributing many times this amount, while others in
the same Lodge might find themselves in no position to make any contribution. Thus, the over-all would average $2.0o or more per member.
With this thought in mind, Honor Roll Certificates have been given
to those Lodges obtaining this average amount. A few years ago, a comparatively small number of Lodges reached this goal. The number has·
taken a definite surge forward during the last few years. The past three
years show us the following:
1950
1951
1952
91 Lodges
137 Lodges
178 Lodges
There is only one logical conclusion when we review these figures,
namely. the Craft is becoming Endowment-conscious.
Your Board desires to give proper credit for this progress. The
Masters, and through them the Endowment Chairman and other interested members of the Lodges have made it their personal business to see

13i

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

that their membership was informed. The Inspectors, along with their
other busy schedules have given time and stressed the importance and
opportunity of this work.
In addition to the above, we are most grateful to the Most Worshipful Grand Master, who served for so many years as a valiant member of
the Board and carried throughout the Grand Jurisdiction such a strong
message that there has been a notable result-PROGRESS.
PLANS AND SPECIFICATIONS
Again, we extend our thanks for the wide distribution of pamphlets
which carry the story to the individual member. Never has there been
such a demand, and every effort has been made to meet it.
Our last edition of the Manual of Information was likewise well
received, and used freely by those charged with specific responsibility.
The Redistricting Program of the Board has proven a great benefactor and help to the Masters and Lodges by giving them a contact man
who has aided with their individual programs.
Every member of the Board feels rewarded for his efforts by the fine
response he has received. It is hoped and believed that such work will
yield even better results in another year. Consequently it is expected
that the Board will continue with similar plans and specifications.
We urge your serious and thoughtful consideration of the following
tabulated results. Our present inventory is satisfactory, our progress
encouraging. our plans and hopes for the future a challenge to all.
