REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is the twenty-sixth ( 26) annual report of the Board of Control
to Grand Lodge. In this past quarter of a century, we have seen our
Boards of Relief operating efficiently and economically. Changing conditions of prosperity, depression, peace or war have not permitted them
any deviation from our established practices. A review of the rulings of
this Grand Lodge will show that relief as administered within the jurisdiction of California has kept to the spirit and intent which our ancient
Brethren so wisely and carefully established.
In 1862 the Jurisprudence Committee in refering to a communication
from Vacaville Lodge No. 134, reported to Grand Lodge that sojourning
Masons, their widows and orphans are entitled to relief (Ross Digest
No. 902 ).
In 1877 they reported, "The time when oue of our members needs
and applies for relief is not the time when a Lodge may stop to inquire
whether he has, in something or in many things, offended, and that he
must be presumed to be worthy until his unworthiness has been judicially
determined; and further that it is not the province of the Charity Committee of a lodge at anytime, to canvass or determine the question whether
or not a member of their lodge is worthy of Masonic consideration. Their
only duty is to ascertain if the member is in actual need, and if they find
that he is, they are to relieve him." (Ross Digest No. 896).
Grand Master Angellotti in 1899 decided that the right of relief is
absolute regardless of reimbursement. His decision reads in part, "While
it rests entirely with the Grand Lodge to determine what, if any, assistance shall be given by it to the various Boards of Relief to aid them in
their local work, I cannot believe that the Grand Lodge of California
will ever impose any penalty upon the Board of Relief or subordinate
lodge, simply because it has given necessary assistance to any Mason,
his widow or orphan in distress, within this jurisdiction, wherever he or
she may hail from, and whatever may be the attitude of the jurisdiction
from which he or she may come, as to reimbursement. If so, it will certainly be contrary to what we have hitherto been taught as to our duty
toward our distressed brother, his widow and orphans. The doctrine
that a Mason must, so far as he can relieve a distressed Brother Mason,
is an old as Masonry, and it is one of the foundation stones of the Institution. We cannot disregard it.... There are certain fundamental laws
that are part of 'The Body of Masonry' and that cannot be changed, and
this is one of them .... While we may justly claim that the jurisdiction
to which the distressed brother belongs should reimburse us, if able to
do so, its neglect to perform what we may consider its duty in no degree
lessens our duty to the distressed." (Ross Digest No. 898)

HO

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

..

The Jurisprudence Committee reported to Grand Lodge in 1894,
The duty of a lodge is to its members and to their families, without
regard to their place of residence, and the fact that one of its members
or the widow of a deceased member, has removed to some place beyond
its territorial jurisdiction, does not absolve the lodge from the performance of its well known and necessary duty. When Masons come to us
from abroad or from other States and are in need, we recognize our
duty to give them such assistance as their necessities require, and to
the end that such assistance may be given to those who ought to receive
it, and that our charity may be efficiently and properly bestowed, Boards
of Relief have been organized in our cities and provided with funds for
that purpose. . .. We recognize the duty to give relief whenever a
proper case is presented, and when that duty is performed we think it
only right to report each case to the Lodge of which the recipient is a
member, and to ask, as we should give, reimbursement, that we may have
a fund .w ith which to continue the good work.
"Some of our brethren of other jurisdictions tell us, 'Ttue, you relieved the distress of a member of our family, but you were bound by
your tenure to do that, and to do it without hope or expectation of reward or reimbursement, and to do it so unostentatiously and quietly that
even the left hand should not be advised of the kindly act done by the
right.' That kind of instruction sounds well, but is not, under the circumstances, at all satisfactory, because we have a very distinct belief
that every Masonic family ought to exercise some care over its own members, and make some provision to protect and care for such as need care
and protection.
"We do not think that the whole duty of a lodge consists in making
Masons and using them so long as they are healthy and strong, and
turning them adrift when by sickness or misfortune they are no longer
able to care for themselves .... A Lodge is an organized society, and we
insist that one of the first and most important purposes of its organization is that it shall protect and relieve its own members when they need
protection or relief, and that, except under extraordinary circumstances,
it is false to its trust when it fails to do its duty in that regard, and that
when another Lodge in the same or another Grand Jurisdiction has
furnished such relief. it may properly and of right present its claim for
reimbursement." (Ross Digest No. 892)
The decision of Grand Master Traylor ( 1880) established that the
family of a Mason who had taken his own life, if the Brother was in
good standing at the time of his death, has as much claim on the Lodge
for aid and protection as if his death had not resulted from his own act.
(Ross Digest No. 904).
In 1881 Janesville Lodge No. 232 wrote Grand Master Denson
"In conferring the third degree upon a candidate, and just as he wa~

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Hl

being instructed in the Guard and Sign, he was seized with a sudden
illness and had to be removed from the Lodge room and carried home.
There is little chance of his ever completing the work.'' The Grand
Master's decision was that he is a Master Mason and entitled to be so
considered for certain purposes, but not having been fully instructed,
he is not a member of the Lodge and cannot sit in a Master Mason's
Lodge. He is entitled as a Master Mason for all purposes of charity and
relief and is to be so considered and treated, and in case of his death is
entitled to Masonic burial. (Ross Digest No. 895).
Grand Master Lucas ( 1897) ruled, where there is no evidence of a
legal marriage, a woman claiming to be the widow of a deceased brothe~
Mason should not be recognized as such, and is not an object of a
Lodge's charity. (Ross Digest No. 908 ). He also ruled, after a request
had been made.. to use his power to compel a lodge to render assistance
to the widow of a deceased brother Mason, which he declined to do,
as there was no evidence that the lady was unable to support herself.
He did not consider that the Lodge was under any moral or Masonic
obligation to render her financial assistance. (Ross Digest No. 908).
One of the decisions of Grand Master Preston ( 1896) was "The
widow of a deceased brother Mason who was in good standing at the
time of his death, but whose lodge had subsequently surrendered its
t:harter, becomes a charge, if needy, upon the . charities of the lodge
within whose jurisdiction she resides." (Ross Digest No. 905).
The Jurisprudence Committee of 1897 reported to Grand Lodge "A
worthy distressed Mason who, at the time of his application for aid, is
in good standing in the order, is a just charge on Masonic charity, and
on the lodge within whose jurisdiction he resides, even though his application for membership may have been rejected by said lodge." (Ross
Digest No. 903).
Grand Master Filmer ( 1913) rules, "The son of a Master Mason,
after he has passed the age of majority, or the sister or mother of a
Master Mason is not entitle4 as a matter of right to Masonic charity,
but certain conditions may prevail where such son, sister or mother,
being helpless and incompetent to sustain themselves, and dependent
upon the brother for support, and the brother being unable to extend
relief to them, the lodge may, by extending relief to the son, sister, or
mother relieve the brother himself.'' (Ross Digest No. 900).
The report of the trustees of our Masonic Homes in 1928 called attention to the message of Grand Master Tinnin ( 1886), "When a
Master Mason's daughter marries, she severs her right in the order by
and through her father, and thence can only retain her rights therein by
and through her husband.'' They also noted Grand Master Belcher's
decision (' 1893), "The daughter of a Master Mason, whether of tender
years, or if unmarried, of mature years, is a member of his family and is,
if in need, entitled to ask for and receive assistance from Masons wher-

142

PROCEEDINGS OP THE ·

ever she may be." The report of the Trustees goes on to say that "Our
settled law with regard to widows is that if the widow of a Master
Mason remarries to one who is not a member of our fraternity, she is
not thereafter entitled to Masonic consideration." They conclude their
report with the resolution, "that the word 'orphan' wherever used in
the Constitution or in any regulation, shall hereafter be deemed to mean
the son or daughter under the age oftwenty-one years of a deceased
Master Mason; and no man or woman over twenty-one years shall be
entitled to relief as a matter of right as the son or daughter of a Master
Mason." (Ross Digest No. 901).
A decision of Grand Master Gist ( 1934) was that "A divorced wife
of a Mason is no longer a dependent relative." (Ross Digest No. 910).
The last decision concerning relief recorded in Ross Digest is that of
Grand Master Earl Warren in 1936 wherein he ruled, "The widow of
a Master Mason who was in good standing at the time of his death, is
entitled to all necessary assistance, so long as she remains. a widow."
(Ross Digest No. 907).
·
All of these decisions and reports have ·been adopted by Grand
Lodge.
The Ordinances of Grand Lodge at section 93 says in. part, "The
Board of Control shall make such rules and regulations as it shall deem
necessary for the effective operation of the several Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus within the State ..." These rules and regulations
have been prepared by the Board of Control and are now being used by
our Boards of Relief as the pattern of their everyday operation. Article
XV of the Rules and Regulations includes all of the above decisions and ·
reports.
The Board of Control assures you that relief as admiµistered in this
jurisdiction conforms in every detail to our ancient and honored custom.
We continue to care for those of our needy as their circumstances may
require. Long practice in the administration of relief has permitted us to
develop businesslike methods without detracting from proper considerate understanding, and courteous attitude in the granting of relief. We
still emphasize the importance of placing the responsibility upon the
lodge in which our needy brother holds membership and we look to
them for reimbursement. Our method permits us to break relief problems into two sections, entirely separated from each other. First our
worthy distressed brother, his widow or orphans, are properly cared for
as their needs may require and second the question of reimbursement
is then only a matter to be discussed by the brother's lodge and our
Board of Relief. Thus, in this manner, we can follow the admonition
that the left hand shall not know of the action of the right.

REIMBURSEMENTS
Boards of Relief who are unable to secure reimbursement from the
lodge or Grand Lodge of a distressed brother, may request reimbursement from Grand Lodge by filing with the Board of Control a complete
and detailed record of the case in question, together with the reasons
why reimbursement is necessary.
The following application for reimbursement has been received:
A member of Hang Yang Lodge No. 1048, Seoul, Korea of the
Grand Jurisdiction of Scotland, being destitute applied to the Masonic
Board of Relief of Santa Monica Bay. Investigation established that he
was worthy, and in good standing. He is an experienced engineer, being
well educated and of good habits. Because he is a British subject, employment in his field of engineering was difficult. He had been trying
to support himself by working as a dishwasher and housecleaner. Relief
was granted in the amount of $50. No reimbursement has been received
from hfs lodge. We have recently received word that he is now employed
in the Philippine Islands.

For the past several years, the Board of Control has concentrated
on the problem of developing a Uniform Compact for the use of our
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. In 1951 our proposed
Uniform Compact was presented to the Most Worshipful Arthur Paulsen. Since receiving his approval the Compact has been signed by two
hundred eighty-two ( 282) or 100% of the masters whose lodges make
up our Boards of Relief. The Compact was made effective as of August
l, 1951 and since that date no single question has arisen as to its provisions or interpretation. We therefore attach a copy of the Uniform
Compact as a ~ortion of this report.
Our Boards of Relief now having completed a quarter of a century
under the authority of the Board of Control, we think it a logical time to
have our work, and the legislation affecting it, reviewed by an independent body. We therefore recommend that the Grand Master appoint a
special committee to work with the Board of Control. to study Relief
and Employment legislation, to clarify conflicting or misleading sections,
to prepare new legislation, where necessary, so as to be assured that
their functioning conforms to and reflects the true attitude of this Grand
Lodge; also to analyze all forms, instructions and regulations as prepared by the Board of Control for the use of the Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus such as are contained in the Uniform Compact,
the Standard Practice Bulletin and the Rules and Regulations for Boards
of Relief.
Fratenally submitted,
JACK C . BUTLER, Chairman
JOHN T. MARTIN
Guv A. TOLLE
HARRY F. WHITE
REGINALD M. MILLS, Secretary

The above request for reimbursement together with the recommendation of the Board of Control has been filed with the chairman of the
Finance Committee as required by Section No. 95 of the Ordinances.
BoARD OF CONTROL
The Board of Control has held three meetings during the past year.
In February we met for three days in Bakersfield with all of the Northern
California Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. In May we held a
three day meeting with the Southern California Boards of Relief and
Bureaus in Santa Barbara. We are meeting during this session of Grand
Lodge, having convened on last Saturday and continuing throughout
most of this week.
We are deeply indebted to the representatives of both Bakersfield
and Santa Barbara for their many courtesies. Especially we are indebted

UNIFORM COMPACT
ARTICLE I-ORGANIZATION
Section 1. Pursuant to Section 264 of the Ordinances of the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California, this Uniform Compact is entered into by and between the signatory Lodges for the purpose

of maintaining in this community a Masonic Board of Relief under the
authority and supervision of the Board of Control of Grand Lodge.
Section 2. The Lodges shall indicate assent hereto by causing their
respective Worshipful Masters to sign this instrument in the name of
the Lodge, and after approval by the Board of Control shall be subject
to and governed by this Uniform Compact and the Rules and Regulations of the Board of Control until such time as their withdrawal shall
have been approved by the Board of Control.
Section 3. One original signed copy of this Uniform Compact shall

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON THIRTY-THIRD
ANNUAL OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This Com~ittee's annual report on the Observance of Public Schools
Week endeavors to wrap up in orie package, the inspiring evidence of
increased co-operative effort and results accomplished by local committees in the 33rd Annual Observance.
The added number of splendidly organized reports vividly portray
the co-operative hard work done at community level.
In districbl where unification of lodge efforts has been the practice,
several reports for this year could serve as educational models of professional organization in achieving teamwork, public co-operation and
interest.
Most reports were presented in such a manner that the Grand Lodge
. committee's burdens in reviewing them were greatly alleviated. It is
almost impossible for us to handle loose clippings just dropped into an
envelope. Thanks to the committees who took the time to paste their
clippings to sheets of paper.
We regret to state that all lodges excepting sixty have reported. We
hope that the Masters not reporting realize the necessity of complying
with the Grand Master's Proclamation.
The annual report of this committee. has been printed for the Proceedings of this communication, and advance copies are being distributed. Therefore, we ref er you to the report for details of our activities
rather than take your time to recite its content. Please have your committee review it. Many new ideas are presented.
All reports and materials received from the lodges are on display
in Polk Hall next door. You are invited to visit and study the work of

148

PROCEEDINGS OP THB

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

the many committees. Each report has been reviewed and studied by
our committee.
Many requests have been received to continue with the same type
of material furnished for the last two Observances. This has been
planned. The co.-operation of each lodge is required to see that the
material addressed to the Master is put in his hands and finally given
to his committee.
We are asked to send the material to you early. Our first letter to
the lodges is mailed in January. Information on your reports that "Grand
Lodge material was not received," reveals two major categories of explanation:
The past or present Master; or the Secretary has failed to pass the
material to the incoming Master or Public Schools Week chairman.
Or-the material was received, but not read.
Each year we receive inquiries regarding the date for next year.
Traditionally the Observance starts on the fourth Monday in April.
This avoids conflict with Easter.
•
The date, therefore, would be April 27th through May 2nd in 1953.
Public Schools Week as a statewide Observance originated within
the Masonic Fraternity for the purpose of arousing awareness of the
grave crises that threatened our public schools system at the close of
World War I.
The planning for the Observance was built on a flexible foundation
in order that local programs could be developed to fit community patterns and induce all citizens to make an annual personal appraisal of
their schools.
The program of public schools week, then, was the instrument forged
to implement the objectives. The functional efficiency of that instrument
has been tested by results achieved through its use for over a generation.
Here is a simple "objective" formula with which you may test the
eft'ectiveness of your current planning tools:
1. Will they aid in creating greater community interest in the needs,
the achievements or weakness of your schools?
2. What is the attitude of the school principal and faculty in your
community? Their co-operation is both vital and basic to the success
of the Observance.
3. Have Masonic committee plans been constructed and co-ordinated
to invite active participation by other community organizations and
leaders?
4. Are all brethren in your lodge clearly aware of the mounting and
vital importance of the Observance in relation to the many complex
problems and school shortages faced by most communities throughout
the nation and specifkally in our Jurisdiction?

As virtually every individual lodge report pointed out, without the ·
splendid support, patience and sustained work of all educational authorities-superintenden ts, principals, faculty and individual teachers, the
traditional success and growing importance of the Public Schools Week
Observance would be an impossibility.

149

We owe a debt of gratitude for the unparalleled and unselfish support of this event by individuals and members of the great organizations
which participated in the 33rd Annual Observance of Public Schools
Week.
Once more our thanks to each of you, your committees and all who
worked so hard and faithfully to make our annual Observance the success which your reports indicate it was.
We recommend the continuance of the Public Schools Week Committee and the appropriation of $3,300.00 for the use of the committee
during the coming year.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE D. GAVIN, Chairman

San Franciaco, October 13, 1952
To the M. W. Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
This Committee's annual report on Public Schools Week Observance endeavors to capsule inspiring evidence of increased cooperative
effort and results accomplished by local committees in the 33rd Annual
Observance.
Lodge reports will be displayed during Grand Lodge, and will help
the brethren to understand why this committee's sincere effort fails to do
full justice, in individual credit, to each lodge and district accomplishment.
The care and effort expended in the preparation of so many more
report presentations, reveal justified pride in community Observance results over previous years. The added number of splendidly organized
reports vividly portray the cooperative hard work done at community
level.
Careful study and evaluation of reports from every lodge in the
jurisdiction reveals these signi8cant new trends and developments over
other years:
1. More lodges and even districts united in efforts, with unanimous report of more effective results.
a. In some cases where geographic distance prohibited joint
programs, Masters and Chairmen from several lodges held
meeting to exchange ideas.
b. In districts where unification of lodges has been the practice, several reports for this year could serve as educational
models of professional organization in achieving teamwork, public cooperation and interest.
2. A marked number of lodges reported success in evolving individual programs to meet peculiar or difficult local situations.
(Some cited under "Successful Examples.")
3. More general use of the State slogan and Scroll, though some
lodges used sub-slogans tailored to fit timely community situations.
4. More general recognition that the Grand Lodge objective is
to obtain community-wide participation.
5. Need to correct basic misconceptions revealed in many reports. Your Public Schools Week Committee attempts, in another section of this report to do so in a digest of material previously sent to the lodges.
Specific phases of the 33rd annual Observance of Public Schools
week are reported under captioned topics.

151

"The Public School - An American Heritage"
Most Worshipful Louis C. Drapeau Grand Master proclaimed:
"Education and the enlightenment and understanding that follow
in the path of education is fundamental in its importance to the successful operation of a government 'Of the people, by the people
and for the people.'
"More than three decades ago the Masonic Fraternity in this
jurisdiction, recognizing the importance of free education, founded
and sponsored an annual observance which they designated as PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK. The purpose of the Observance is to afford
a designated time for a periodic stocktaking of what our public
schools are doing and to enable the public to get acquainted with
the teachers and the students, to gain an understanding of their problems. Through the years, Public Schools Week has brought honor
to Masonry for its public service in advancing the interests of the
Public School."
Governor Earl Warren's proclamation emphasized the vital importance to all citizens of the basic objectives recognized and activated by
the Masonic Fraternity when it originated Public Schools Week in California. Governor Warren also said in part:
"One of the great and basic institutions upon which we rely for
the furtherance of our American ideals is our public school system.
It is the.birthright of every American to attend our public schools
and to there acquire the essentials for making ~ honorable living,
as well as an understanding of the reciprocal privileges and responsibilities of American citizenship, the advantages of our way of life,
and the place of our country in the world • • •
"Our school system can meet the objectives expected of it only
when there is widespread public understanding of our schools and
the type of education they provide. This kind of understanding can
best be developed by the intimate knowledge that comes from inspecting the school houses, knowing the teachers and seeing the
work of the pupils."
Our brethren in Hawaii, sparking the Observance in an acute school
facility problem, were instrumental in the issuance of an urgently worded
proclamation by Territorial Governor Oren E. Long.
Proclamations were issued by mayors of cities and towns throughout the state, including a few "firsts" by officials usually reluctant on
the matter of proclamations;
·
The three heads of the York Rite Bodies sent proclamations to the
subordinate bodies requesting no meetings be held during the Week

152

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

that would conBict with the Observance.
Official civic individuals and groups, industries, statewide and local
organizations recognized the Observance by formal resolutions.
Both Houses of the California Legislature formally recognized the
Observance by the following Resolution introduced in the Assembly by
Messrs. Dunn, Caldecott, Lincoln, Rumford, Grunsky and Maloney on
March 18, 1952, and adopted by the Assembly and Senate on March
21, 1952:

Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 5--Relative to the observance of
P°ublic School Week in this the centennial year of the founding of public
schools in this State
WHEREAS, The week of April 28th through May 2d has been
designated as the 33d annual Public Schools Week to be observed
by the public schools throughout California: and
WHEREAS, The Legislature in 1852 made its first appropriation for the support of a state system of free education, thus
making this year's Public Schools Week the centennial observance of the founding of our present fine schools: and
WHEREAS, Some 700 citizen committees in as many communities throughout the State are joining with the school authorities
in arranging an observance of this event in their local schools to
demonstrate the work the schools are doing and their needs of the
present time: and
WHEREAS, Our pioneers in framing the Constitution of California in 1849 recognized that education is the foundation of a
democracy and made provision for our Public School System by
so authorizing it; and
WHEREAS, Today in the growing conflict between free people
everywhere and the slavemasters of the totalitarian states the
need for adequate training and preparation on the part of our
youth is greater than ever today: and
WHEREAS, The proper functioning of all our institutions is the
proper concern of all the people and one of the primary objects
of Public Schools Week is to encourage this concern on the part
of the people; and
WHEREAS, Both the citizen committees in charge and the
school authorities will urge individual visits to one or more local
schools: now, therefore, be it
Resolved by the Assembl11 of the State of California, the
Senate thereof concurring, That all citizens of the State of California be urged to take notice of and participate in the events of

Public Schools Week as a demonstration of the importance of
public education, and the part it has in safeguarding our American ideals and institutions.
The State Depart..nlent of Education, in addition to inclusion of
Public Schools Week in the official Calendar of Educational Meetings
and Events for 1952, in the Fall edition of the monthly Official Publication of the California State Department of Education, Roy E. Simpson,
State Superintendent of Public Instruction addressed the following message, quoted in part, to Californians. (March, 1952 issue.)

"The Public School-An American Heritage."
"The public schools of California will unite in observance of
the thirty-third annual Public Schools Week, April 28 through
May 2, 1952, to disseminate accurate information regarding all
phases of public education. Since public education is dedicated
to respect for the individual as a person and thus to the preservation of our American heritage of freedom for all. this year we
should emphasize the ways in which education preserves and
strengthens American free government.
"Public schools provide a foundation for a unified citizenry
that appreciates American ideals and places a high value upon
the privilege of making them operational. It was in the public
schools that the great body of our adult citizens acquired common
knowledge of the American heritage. And it was in the public
schools that our adult citizens acquired the skills essential to make
the Amedcan heritage a basis for a progressively improved American way of life. The public schools have thus operated as integral
parts of American government . . .
"The growth of population in California creates an ever increasing need for more classrooms and for teachers to conduct
classes in them . . .
"The public schools are your schools. They operate as indispensable parts of American government. You are urged, therefore, to visit them. especially during Public Schools Week and
to continue taking an active part in their development."

TAILORED TO FIT!
( A.l•o •ee "Lodge Report Queriea-Mi•con ceptiona")
A new lodge in the jurisdiction, starting with first Observance this
year, was politely rejected by an able school superintendent who feared
a Masonic committee might interfere with his own well-planned program.
The Masonic committee, with extreme tact knowing local situation:
met again, developed a splendid program supplementing that of the
school superintendent, implemented action to bring in, for the first time,
community-wide participation and interest.
Both school official and our committee are making enthusiastic plans
for 1953 with the hearty endorsement of the once-reluctant superintendent.

"The people of this farming community are taking greater interest
in each Observance. The last few years they have visited schools
throughout the year. Now, (it took several years of missionary work
by our Masonic members) Public Schools Week Observance is really
a climax to a truly great -year-long enterprise."

Another small community where our local community first met resistance, reports:
"Extent of community participation may be Judged by the fact local
fire chief and his staff are on hand to take care of car parking problems
during Public School Open House."

" . . . Our Observances always have been outstandingly successful because our lodge maintains a year-round friendly relationship with
local teachers. Each year we hold a Ladies Night,' when teachers, along
with our families are our honored guests."

A Masonic Officers' Association sparked an entire county's participation by promotion of a "Transportation Fair."
All schools carried on their individual program-as did each lodgebut the unifying gambit commanded national attention.
"All educational groups worked with our fraternity for months in
advance to obtain cooperation, not only of all local organizations,
trained veterans, etc., but all branches of the armed services-several
bases nearby-, transportation industries, civic authorities, etc., in
a score of surrounding communities to make it the 'finest event of its
kind in our school history.' "
Newspaper clippings variously reported from 53,000 to 60,000 attendance at the opening of the "Transportation Fair.''
"This was a big program but well worthwhile and we recommend
it to other communities of similar size and comparable industrial facilities.

The Date
Traditio nal date for the Observan ce of Public Schools Week,
evolved by trial and error through the years as being the best time for
the greatest number of all concerned lodges, school authorities and school
schedules, the avoidance of the moving Easter date, etc.--as reported
in all Grand Lodge Committee Informational material Starts with the fourth Monday. NOT the fourth week in April.

Start Earlier
The following comments may be found in about 50% of the reports:
"Give us date and slogan earlier."
"It is necessary to give school authorities the date earlier so they
can arrange their schedules."
Grand Lodge Committee letter of October 2, 1951, Committee report in 1951 Grand Lodge Proceedings and January, 1952 Letter No. 1 ·
to all masters gave date and slogan of the 1952 Observance.
Immedite effort was made at the close of this year's Observance,
to better the 1951 timing, as note:

1953, 34th Annual Observance:
April 27 through May 2, 1953-'Th e Public School-A n American
Heritage.'

May 20. 1952 Grand Lodge Committee sent such information, quoted

"We have received numerous inquiries about dates of next year's

Grand Lodge Committee /umdiction
1. "Grand Lodge Committee should arrange to appoint local committee chairmen earlier."
2. "Set up local committees of three lodge officers and past Master."
3. "Suggest Grand Lodge Committee contact school authorities
statewide and receive their suggestions of Masonic assitance and
the~ give a directed program. Statewide programs must be controlled to be effective:·
Answers to 1 and 2:
The Grand Lodge Committee's function is to act in an advisory
capacity to local lodges. Committee and Chairman appointments are at
the pleasure of the local Master. Timing for start of program work is
also decided at local level.
The Grand Lodge Committee advises in all material sent out and
stresses in each annual report the benefits of an early start on planning
for the Observance as far in advance, as is consistent with local situations.

Answer to3:
See "Grand Lodge Informational Activities, 1952," of this report
and also "Proclamations."
The Grand Lodge Committee immediately after close of Observance,
starts contact at State level, to obtain and be assured of caoperative
action by State officials. Educational authorities and chairmen of all
Statewide organizations, press, radio and TV networks.
To ask for and accept wholly directed program of school authorities
alone would not be in the tradition, nor would it point to the objective
for which this Masonic project was originated.

"Material Not Received"
Individual study of reports that "Grand Lodge informational material
not received," reveals two major categories of explanation:
1. Past or Presiding Master, or Secretary fails to pass it on to incoming Master or Chairman.
2. Material was received but not read.
The Grand Lodge Committee, throughout the year attempts to correct

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

173

either or both situations through:
1. Sending letters announcing mailing dates of current and future
material, with analyses of such materials, its use or adaptability
to current, local situations.
2. Follow-up letters of inquiry about receipt of material, with suggestion that postcard orders be placed with Grand Lodge Committee if additional copies are desired.

Confl.ictiom and Counter-Attraction•
Some reports this year criticized conftiction of events held -by other
groups.
In one case this occurred due to misunderstanding when another
fraternity had an event on the closing Friday evening of the Week. (It
was assumed that Public Schools Week Observance ended with the close
of the weekend school day.)
The Grand Lodge Committee, prior to February, 1952, had replies
from other groups with formal copies of instructions, edicts, or proclamations asking subordinate groups to cooperate by holding no meetings
or conBicting programs during the Observance.

ACKNOWLEDGEM ENTS!
As virtually every individual lodge report pointed out, without the
splendid support, patience and sustained work of all educational authorities-superintendents, principals, faculty and individual teachers, the
traditional success and growing ~mportance of Public Schools Week
Observance would be an impossibility.
The Grand Lodge of California owes a debt of gratitude for the
unparalleled and unsel8sh support of this event by individuals and members of the great organizations which participated in the 33rd Annual
Observance of Public Schools Week.

·New•papera, Magasinea, Radio, Television
Entire editions, editorial, cartoons, columns and news space were
devoted to the event in papers of every size, from weeklies to great
metropolitan dailies.
Radio and television were generous in time, all the way from spot
announcements to fifteen minute and half hour shows. Both mediums
in some locations broadcasted and televised school programs.
Religious, fraternal, industrial, educational and labor bulletins, magazines and house organs were equally cooperative.
AU lodges were unanimous in reporting this cooperation and in most
cases expressed appreciation to these media in local area.

Grand Lodge was called on at 10:00 A.M .. the Grand Master presid.ing.
The "Grand Chaplain opened the session with the following prayer,
taken from the fly-leaf of the Bible on which George Washington was
obligated when he became a member of Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4.
"O God, Divine Architect of the Universe, we come with
gratiude to Thy Omnipotence. We acknowledge Thee as the
Creator and Preserver of all things. We thank Thee for Thy
daily blessings conferred on us in all our undertakings. More
particularly. 0 God, we crave Thy blessing at this meetiing. Do
Thou preside over us in the spirit of Peace, Love and Charity,
and to Thy Holy Name be Power and Dominion forever."
Amen.

RESEARCH LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge the following
Edict and Resolution was adopted:
"The the Grand Master be and he is hereby authorized and
empowered to issue Special Dispensations to create not to exceed
two Research Lodges under such rules and regulations as he may
·
adopt, and
"That such Dispensation or Dispensations shall terminate in
accord with the provisions of Section 109 of Ordinances on October 1, 1952, and
"That the Jurisprudence Committee shall submit legislation,
to perpetuate and make permanent said Research Lodges and
others which may be created, at the next Annual Com~unication."
Shortly thereafter the Grand Master appointed a special committee
to assist in the preparation of the rules and regulations and to help
organize one research lodge in the San Francisco Bay area and one in
the Los Angeles area. This was done, and .on the evening of May 26,
1952, the two lodges were instituted simultaneously: that in the South
by the Grand Master, and that in the North by the Deputy Grand
Master.
The reports of the Grand.Master, the Jurisprudence Committee and
the Charters Committee will provide practically all the information
needed by the members of this Grand Lodge to pass upon subjects

In the selection of Charter Members it was decided to limit such
initial membership to Past Masters of California lodges and generally
to those living in the San Francisco Bay and Los Angeles ~eas. It
was felt that men with a wide Masonic experience were needed during
the formative period of organization and that demands should not be
made at that time on hard-working officers of constituent lodges or on
those living at a great distance from those areas.
It is hoped that the legislation adopted at this communication will
make it possible for many &ne and talented Masons in all parts of the
state to become members.
The two lodges are engaged in pioneer work at this time as there
are no California precedents to follow; and the experience in other Grand
Jurisdictions, while helpful, does not always apply in a jurisdiction of
this magnitude.
The two lodges are proceeding slowly and with great care to avoid
mistakes. The quality of the present membership assures us of success
if Grand Lodge continues its support of the program. We con8dently
predict that in due time and with proper encouragement these lodges
will make a great contribution to California Masonry.

Pursuant to such resolution, the Grand Master appointed the special
committee which now makes its report.
It has been said that there is no real demand or need for Spanish
speaking lodges, that our foreign language lodges now chartered exist
for historical reasons, and that there is no reason to expand foreign
language lodges in this jurisdiction.
Five foreign language lodges are chartered by our Grand Lodge:
two work in French, two in German and one in Italian. Reviewing the
history of the formation of these lodges, we find that an actual necessity
dictated their creation, that of imparting the principles of Freemasonry
to good men and true in a language with which they were familiar, and
by which they could learn the purposes of the craft without confusion
or obscurity. The earliest of these lodges was chartered in 1852. the
second twenty years later, and the last about forty years ago. Their
continued existence would seem to indicate that they still serve the useful
purpose for which they were instituted, and continue to attract members
within the walls of their lodge rooms. After all, language is only a vehicle
by which ideas are conveyed, and if the conveyance is better made by
the use of one vehicle rather than by another, the form of that vehicle is
relatively unimportant if it serves its purpose efficiently and well.
Your Committee &nds that there is a real demand and need for a
lodge or lodges working in the Spanish language, and that such demand
and need are as legitimate as the existence of the present foreign language lodges. The matter has been discussed with members of the Craft
who are of Spanish ancestry and who are members of California lodges,
and with Spanish speaking Masons who are members of lodges belonging to jurisdictions recognized by us, as well as with other brothers who
are interested in the subject. The reaction has been favorable and enthusiastic, and the reasons advanced for the creation of a lodge or lodges
to work in the Spanish language seem to your Committee to be sound
and logical.
For many years the problem of clandestine or irregular Mexican
lodges operating mainly in Southern California has engaged our attention. The reports of the late Committee on Clandestine Masonry made
to Grand Lodge over the years show that while not numerous, they are .
persistent. The fact that such lodges exist would seem to indicate that
Masonry is attractive to those speaking the Spanish language. Of necessity, those knowing little or no English and being unaware of the irregular character of the lodges will solicit the degrees of Masonry where
they can &nd them, confident that they are affiliating with the great body
of Masonry. Considering the number of men of Spanish ·language
background that reside in California, a mere handful are members of

such men to apply to regular lodges for fear of rejection by reason of
their Mexican or other Spanish derivation, and then again they may be
deterred by the difficulty of language. A lodge working in a language
best understood by them would appeal to them, and would overcome the
diffidence that comes from being in an unfamiliar environment. Opinions
have been expressed to your Committee that the creation of a regular
Spanish speaking lodge would bring to its doors many of the members
of the present clandestine lodges. who would become aware of their
present illegitimate status. and in time the problem of irregular Mexican
lodges would solve itself. It is not to be thought that the membership of
these clandestine lodges is of a low class or character. On the contrary.
it compares favorably with the class and character of our own regular
lodges. The only difference seems to be that we are regular, and they
,are not.
But another reason having nothing to do with legitimacy of membership presents itself. This Grand Lodge recognizes as regular and is
in fraternal relations with twenty-one Grand Lodges that work in the
Spanish language. Seven of them are situated in the Republic of Mexico,
and the remainder are in Central and South America, and in Cuba,
Puerto Rico and the Philippine Islands. We have omitted the nine
Grand Lodges in Brazil, which we understand do their work in Portuguese. The State of California has a Spanish tradition and background
of which it is justifiably proud, and endeavors to retain and perpetuate
the memories of those days of a little over a century ago. before the gold
rush made our state predominantly English speaking. Masons from
Spanish speaking jurisdictions visit California on business and for
pleasure. Yet nowhere in this great state is there a Masonic center to
which they can resort, and partake of Masonic fraternity in a language
they can understand. Many of them who come to make their homes here
undoubtedly would be ready and willing to transfer their Masonic
allegiance to a lodge of their place of residence, but cannot do so because
of their ignorance of English. Such men, generally of high class and
caliber, are lost to Masonry because of their inability to make contact
with a lodge using their native tongue, and California is the poorer on
that account.
A group of Masons in California. we are informed, belonging to
lodges in regular foreign jurisdictions, and speaking the Spanish language. have formed an organization for the purpose of establishing
contact with other regular Masons whose native tongue is Spanish.
for the purpose of maintaining the interest of those brothers in things
Masonic, and to encourage their visitations to California lodges. One
of the main purposes of this organization is to prevent the association
of these brothers with the irregular or clandestine Mexican lodges, and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

181

to keep their Masonic regularity intact. Such a group might well be the
nucleus for a Spanish speaking loqge.
Some of the Spanish speaking members of California lodges have
expressed their willingness to dimit from their present lodges to a Spanish speaking lodge in order to get it started; This would be of great
advantage, and would give a solid California foundation to such a lodge.
No great practical difficulties would be experienced in starting and
continuing such a lodge. The work as done in the German lodges and
the Italian lodge is a literal translation of the work as performed in
English speaking lodges into the German and Italian languages. The
French lodges confer the second and third degrees in a literal translation of the ritual of those degrees from English into French. The translation of the work from English into Spanish would be comparatively
easy. The only difficulty your Committee sees is in connection with an
Inspector to oversee the lodge. Your Committee does not know of any
Past Master familiar with the work in English who could translate it
into Spanish and impart it in that language. and who would be willing
to undertake the task. If no other solution could be found, a lodge could
be dispensated to work in the English language. until a Past Master of
that lodge could be had who would have the ability to handle the work
in Spanish. at which time the lodge could be granted authority to do its
work in that language.
We are taught that Masonry unites men of every country. sect and
opinion. and causes true friendship to exist among those who might
otherwise nave remained at a perpetual distance. Applying this lesson
to the present problem. your Committee sees no reason why this Grand
Lodge should not open still another door into its stronghold, and permit
good men and true to enter into the Craft of ancient Freemasonry, using
a language with which they are most familiar to acquaint themselves
with our ideals and our purposes, our precepts and our examples.
Your Committee therefore recommends:
That Grand Lodge adopt and approve the policy. in proper cas~.
of dispensating and chartering a lodge or lodges to work in the Spanish
language.
ROBERT F. SHIPPEE, Chairman
Because of the fact that the investigation upon which this report is
based was not participated in by us. we feel that we are unable to sign
the report, but we do join in the recommendation.

Re the Resolution of Seaside Lodge No. 504, which has been referred to the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, we beg to report as
follows:
1 ) The question involved has been satisfactorily handled to the
complete satisfaction of Seaside Lodge by action of the Endowment
Board as of October 11, 1952, which action in substance is as follows:
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board agreed that it should be their
policy to give an honor roll certificate, or gold star, to any Lodge that
had raised sufficient sum of money during the fiscal year which entitled
them to the same, providing application for such certificate, or gold star,
be made accompanied by a certified statement signed by the Master, or
Secretary, stating that sufficient money had been raised during the fiscal
year, and giving the definite amount of such money.
2) It is understood that the issuing of such honor roll certificate, or
gold star, is entirely an action of the Endowment Board, and in no way
suggests the changing of the official records, or the designated amount
raised by the official auditor's report.
3) Any Lodge receiving such an honor roll certificate, or gold star,
would not be entitled to the same during the next fiscal year, unless
sufficient monies had been raised to place them on the preferred list.
4) This action by the Endowment Board was not to be interpreted
as to set a p1ecedent, or be binding for subsequent years.
ERNEST G. BASHOR
Chairman

GEORGE WASHINGTON AND MASONRY

take over the superintendence and education of five children. She must
have done a wonderful job! The schools in those days did not have the
variety of subjects nor the educational facilities of today and Washington's schooling was sporadic. Washington educated himself, evidenced
a great interest in surveying and became a recognized surveyor July 20,
1749. at the age of 17. After several years of frontier fighting against
the French and Indians. in which he displayed great courage and resourcefulness, he was placed in command of the troops of Virginia at the
age of 23.
He was elected to the Colonial Assembly of Virginia in 1758, and
the following year was married to a widow named Martha Custis, who
had two children. Washington never had any children of his own and
it is clear from his writings that his stepchildren were treated with all
the love and consideration that his own children would have received.
The Lodges may not have been as strict about age in the early days
as they are now and probably with good reason. In those days men
matured and accepted the responsibilities of life at a much earlier age
than we do now. I find that Washington applied for membership in
Fredericksburg Lodge in 1752, was initiated November 4th of that year,
passed to the Degree of Fellowcraft March 3, 1753. and was made a
Master Mason August 4, 1753. You will note that Brother Washington
was actually only 20 years of age when he was initiated but legally he
was 21. When the new calendar was adopted in England the British
Parliament ordained that any man whose birthday fell within certain
weeks of 1732 could legally consider himself a year older than he might
otherwise have been.
The records of Lodges in those days are meager and of course his
Lodge had no reason to particularly note the activities of its young
member. We must accordingly wait until the later years to flnd records
of the Masonic activities of George Washington.
Those of us who have studied American history will recall the
gradual deterioration of the relationship between the Colonies and
England during the period from 1758 to 1776. We find that during this
period there was considerable growth in the membership of Masonic
Lodges. During the French and Indian War warrants had been granted
by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts for the formation of Lodges in
the army and it ·became a custom to establish Masonic Lodges in the
army camps. The Lodge in Washington's army was called American
Union Lodge and available records show that Washington visited this
Lodge on frequent occasions.
When the Revolutionary War started in 1776 all of the Grand
Lodges in the Colonies were under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of England but commencing in the spring of 1777 the various Colonial
Grand Lodges began to declare their independence and set themselves
up as Colonial Grand Lodges. The Masons of Virgina offered George

An Address Delivered by

w ...LEO E. ANDERSON

Past Master, Hollywood Lodge No. 355
George Washington. first President of these United States, flrst
Master of Alexandria Lodge No. 22 under the Grand Lodge of Virginia,
flrst in war, flrst in peace and first in the hearts of his countrymen.
We all know that George Washington was a Mason. Many of us
have, hanging on the wall of our lodge room, that famous picture of
Brother Washington presiding over his Lodge. But how many of us
know anything about the Masonic history of Brother George Washington?
This coming November 4th will be the 200th anniversary of the initiation of George Washington in Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4 at Fredericksburg, Virginia. During that month Masons all over the world will
join in celebrating that event. The Grand Master has proclaimed the
week of November 3rd to November 8th as George Washington Bicentennial Week in the jurisdiction of California. I hope that what I have
to say will increase your interest in the program outlined in the Grand
Master's proclamation and assist you in carrying it out.
There have been many great men in history but George Washington
is the man of destiny in modern civilization. Listen to the words of Joseph
Fort Newton: "A great and simple man-modest, quiet, gentle, wisein whom patriotism was a passion and a prophecy: Freemasonry a fragrance. a fellowship and a philosophy: great enough to refuse a crown
and live a life of private nobility and public service: picking his way
where no path was, amid wild passions and perils: leading his people to
victory, peace and ordered honor: leaving his labor as a legacy of inspiration to mankind, and his character as a consecration to his country."
To talk about George Washington and Masonry is to talk about
the early history of Masonry and Masonic Lodges in these United
States. Washington was born about the same time that lodges were
formed in the Colonies with authority to act. His date of birth was
February 22, 1732. According to the old calendar, which was then in
use, Washington was born on February 11, but when the new calendar
was adopted and the dates adjusted. his birth date becomes February 22.
Little is known of his early life. Washington's father died when he was
eleven years old but prior to that time must have instilled in young
George some of the characteristics which have made him famous. The
cherry tree story, with which you are all familiar, was supposed to have
happened when George was about six years old and even though it may
only be a story, is an indication of his early training and a tribute to
his character. Washington's mother, at her husband's death, had to

188

PROCEEDINGS OF THB

Washington the position of Grand Master, but he declined because he
had held no official position in Masonry up to that time and felt that
without such background he should not accept this high office. He also
felt that his army duties would require his entire time.
We should recall, first, that a span of 126 years covered the founding
of the 13 Colonies-from the Virginia Colony in 1607 to the founding
of the Colony of Georgia under General Oglethorpe in 1733. The
nationality, motives and aims of the people who landed on the eastern
shore of North America during that century and a quarter were just
about as widely separated as the years which intervened between the
first and the last.
Without attempting to labor the point, it is sufficient to say that,
with all the divergent interests which made up their climatic, economic,
social and political environments, Washington faced a tremendous task
when he took command of the Continental Army at Cambridge, Mass.,
on July 3, 1775.
Most of the men who joined his army were raw, colonial militia,
poorly armed, jealous of sectional rights, partial to their local officers
and reluctant to leave their farms and firesides apparently unguarded.
They enlisted for short and limited terms, often leaving to return home
to plant and harvest food crops, receiving little, if any, pay and that
in a paper currency which had no metallic base or stable purchasing
power.
The story of the war for independence is filled with stories of
Masonic activities. About 52 of Washington's generals were Masons.
Masons played most important parts in the Boston Tea Party, the
signing of the Declaration of Independence, the writing and adoption of
the Constitution and the other great events of those days. Brother
George Washington is well known to all of us as the presiding officer
at the constitutional convention.
We find that the Lodges of those days celebrated the Festival of
St. John the Evangelist in December and also celebrated the Festival
of St. John the Baptist in June, as many of our Lodges do today. It was
quite common for Lodges to adjourn their meetings and proceed in a
body to a church for services and our records show that W a~hington
often joined in these occasions. An interesting record of such an occasion
relates to a meeting in December 1778 in Philadelphia. The Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania was celebrating the Festival of St. John the
Evangelist and Washington was present. Following the lodge meeting
more than 300 brethren proceeded to Christ Church in procession where
ia sermon for the benefit of the poor was preached by the Reverend
William Smith, the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania. At the close of the service more than four hundred pounds-a
large sum in those days--were collected for the relief of the poor and
distressed. Records show that Brother Washington attended Lodges

GRAND LODGB OF CALIFORNIA

189

at various places during his travels and often attended the celebrations in honor of St. John the Baptist and St. Jcihn the Evangelist.
In 1780 a meeting was called in Philadelphia to consider the propriety
of appointing a General Grand Master over all the Grand Lodges in
the United States. You will recall that there is one Grand Master for
all Lodges of England. This meeting was under the auspices of the
Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania and at the close of the session a communication was addressed to other Grand Lodges recommending such
an office and also recommending that George Washington be the General Grand Master. The various Grand Lodges were not well acquainted
with each other and records were not available in the several jurisdictions to permit quick action on this proposal and it apparently died
through inaction and due to the fact that there was no occasion whereby
the various Grand Lodges could get together and determine the powers
and duties of such an office. This recommendation was again made in
1780 but failed for similar reasons.
.
There are numerous records in the writings of Washington and
others of Lodges in both the English and American armies. There are
records of ten Lodges in the American army and there are also records
of the existence of Lodges in the English army since the records and
property of such Lodges were captured by American troops on various
occasions, but Washington always insisted upon these records and
properties being segregated and returned to their rightful owne~s. Th~re
is one record of a chest containing masonic records and clothmg being
captured and returned to the British under a £.lag of truce with a. guard
of honor at the direct order of General Washington. The masonic sash
and apron 'thus returned were the property of Serg.eant Kelly who p~e­
sented them to Montgomery Lodge in New York wtth an accompanying
letter covering the occasion.
At the close of the war the army established a general headquarters
and General Washington caused a building to be constructed in such a
manner that it would serve as a Lodge Hall as well as a meeting place
for various groups and to this hall the members of the Army Lodges
repaired after their exacting duties.
.
Following the end of hostilities, things gradually quieted down and
on December 23, 1783, Washington resigned his commission and returned to Mt. Vernon.
Alexandria Lodge had been established at Alexandria, Virg~nia, a
short time before Washington returned to Mt. Vernon and Washmgton
was immediately invited to join with this group. He accepted the invitation and visited with this Lodge on several occasions. In 1784 General
Lafayette returned to America and visited Washin~ton at Mt. Ve~non.
you students of history will recall his great part m the war for. independence and the close friendship which developed between W ashmgton
and Lafayette. While I have found no records to substantiate the fact,
it has 'been generally assumed that Lafayette was a member of the fra-

ternity. Of one thing we are certain. Preceding this visit to Mt. Vernon,
Madam Lafayette with her own hands made a beautiful masonic apron
of white satin with the emblems of masonry delicately delineated with
needlework of colored silk. This apron, with some other masonic ornaments, was placed in a highly finished rosewood box. also covered with
masonic emblems, and given to George Washington in August 1784.
This apron was later presented to the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania.
In April of 1788 Alexandria Lodge Number 39, under dispensation
from the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, was changed to Alexandria
Lodge Number 22 under the Grand Lodge of Virginia and George
Washington was the first Master of the Lodge under this new jurisdiction. He was unanimously re-elected Master December 20, 1788. That
same year he was elected President of the United States by the unanimous vote of the representatives of the Colonies.
In those days the Capitol of the United States was in New York
and the inauguration of Brother Washington, as the ftrst President,
was set for April 30, J789. Masonry played a very prominent part in
this ceremony. General Jacob Morton, Master of St. John's Lodge in
New York and Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of New York,
was the Marshal of the day, and Robert Livingston, Chancellor of the
State of New York and Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of New York,
administered the oath of office to George Washing ton on a Bible which
was brought from St John's Lodge for the purpose. This Bible is indeed
a treasured possession of St. John's Lodge. Brother Washington continued as Master of his Lodge until December J789.
It is not my purpose to cover the events of the two terms of Brother
Washington as President of these United States. The problems were
many and this nation was fortunate in having a man of Washington's
character and ability at its head during this formative period. He never
made any attempt to hide his connection with the fraternity but, on
the contrary, continued his masonic activities and was generally regarded in Europe as the head of Masons in the United States.
All four members of his cabinet were Masons. Thomas Jefferson
was Secretary of State. General Henry Know was Secretary of War.
Alexander Hamilton was Secretary of Treasury and Edmond Randolph,
who had been Grand Master of Virginia when Alexandria Lodge No. 22
was chartered with brother Washington as its first Master, was Attorney
General.
But let Washington himself testify in his own words to the Masonic
in8uence in his life: "If it has pleased the Supreme Architect of the
universe to make me an humble instrument to promote the welfare and
happiness of my fellow man, my exertions have been abundently recompensed by the kind partiality with which they have been received;
and the assurance you give me of your belief that I have acted upon
the Square in my public capacity, will be among my principal enjoyments
in this Terrestrial Lodge." And again, in these words from his pen:

"Being persuaded that a just application of the principles on which the
Masonic Fraternity is founded must be promotive of private virtue and
public prosperity, I shall be happy to advance the interest of the society,
and to be considered :b y them as a deserving brother."
One of the great ceremonies of those days took place on September
J8, 1793, when the cornerstone of the Capitol of the United States was
laid. The cornerstone was placed at the Southeast corner of the building as was then the custom. The records of the day show that the cere. mony was conducted by the Grand Lodge of Maryland with Washington' s Lodge. Alexandria Number 22, participating. A tremendous procession formed the morning of September J8th and marched to the location of the building. In this procession were the officers and members
of several Lodges, public officials. companies of artillery, workmen, and
others. George Washington marched with the Grand Master pro tem
of the Grand Lodge of Maryland and the Master of Alexandria Lodge
Number 22 and these three distinguished brethren performed the ceremony of laying the cornerstone, Brother Washington acting as Grand
Master. Differing from these ceremonies of today, the artillery discharged volleys every few minutes during the address given by the
Grand Master pro tem of Maryland and this seems to have been the plan
of the day. The ceremony seems to have been almost identical with our
present day ceremony, including the pouring of corn, wine and oil ·upon
the cornerstone. You may be interested in a portion of the published
account of that ceremony. It reads as follows:
"The procession marched two abreast, in the greatest solemn dignity,
with music playing, drums beating, colors flying, and spectators rejoicing, from the President's Square to the Capitol of the City of Washington, where the Grand Marshal ordered a halt, and directed each file in
the procession to incline two steps. one to the right and one to the left,
and face each other, which formed a hollow oblong square, through
which the Grand Sword-Bearer led the van, followed by the Grand
Master P. T. on the left, the President of the United States in the centre,
and the Worshipful Master of .No. 22 Virginia on the right; All the
other orders that composed the procession advanced in the reverse of
their order of march from the President's Square to the Southeast corner
of the Capitol, and the artillery filed off to a destined ground to display
their manoeuvres and discharge their cannon; the President of the
United States, the Grand Master P. T .• and the Worshipful Master of
No. 22 taking their stand to the East of a large stone. and all the craft
forming a circle westward, stood a short time in awful order. (This
means beautiful order).
"The artillery discharged a volley. The Grand Marshal delivered
the commissioners a large silver plate with an inscription thereon, which
the commissioners ordered to be read. and was as follows:
" 'This southeast ·comer-stone of the Capitol of the United
States of America, in the City of Washington, was laid on the J8th

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

day of September, 1793, in the thirteenth year of American independence, in the first year of the second term of the Presidency of
George Washington, whose virtues in the civil administration of his
country have been as conspicuous and beneficial as his military valor
and prudence have been useful in establishing her liberties, and in
the year of Masonry, 5793, by the President of the United States,
in concert with the Grand Lodge of Maryland several Lodges under
its jurisdiction, and Lodge No. 22 from Alexandria, Virginia.
"'Thomas Johnson, David Steuart, and Daniel Carroll, commissioners; Joseph Clarke, R.W.G.M., P.T.; James Hoban and Stephen
Hallate, Architects; Collin Williamson, M. Mason.'
"The artillery discharged a volley. The plate was then delivered to
the President, who. attended by the Grand Master P.T., and three most
Worshipful Masters, descended to the Cavazion Trench and deposed
the plate, and laid it on the corner-stone of the Capitol of the United
States of America, on which was deposed corn, wine, and oil. when the
whole congregation joined in reverential prayer, which was succeeded
by Masonic chanting honors, and a volley from the artillery.
"The President of the United States and his attendant Brethren
ascended from the Cavazion to the East of the corner-stone; and there
the Grand Master P.T .. elevated on a triple rostrum, delivered an oration fitting the occasion, which was received with brotherly love and
commendation. At intervals, during the delivery of the oration, several
volleys were discharged by the artillery. The ceremony ended in prayer,
Masonic chanting honors, and a 15-volley from the artillery.
"The whole company retired to an extensive booth, where an ox of
500 lbs. weight was barbecued, of which the company generally partook,
with every abundance of other recreation. The festival concluded with
fifteen successive volleys from the artillery, whose military discipline
and manoeuvres merit every commendation. Before dark the whole
company departed with joyful hopes of the production of their labor.''
At the conclusion of his second term. Washington determined to
retire to private life and delivered his farewell address, which is recognized as one of the American Masterpieces. He returned to Mt. Vernon
and again assumed the duties of managing his estate, frequently visiting
his Lodge at Alexandria. Friends and acquaintances were always welcome and it was seldom that the Washington family sat down to dinner
alone. Many are the stories of hospitality, kindness and consideration for
others which come from those days.
In these days when old standards of conduct, honesty and reverence
for God seem to have been laid aside by such a large proportion of our
'people, it is essential that emphasis be placed on the life of George
Washington and the part his home life, church and fraternity had in
making him the great man he was. Washington's home life showed
him a lpver of the fireside, a domestic-minded householder, a man care-

193

ful of his property, but generous with his servants, a devoted husband·
a father whose loving kindness was no less in view of the fact that th '
relationship was not of blood; a man who loved the outdoors the earthe
the growing grain, the wild game; a hospitable man who ~ffered th~
best he had in the happiness that there were many who enjoyed breaking bread with him; a man to whom church and divine worship were a
part of life.

In December, 1799, Washington became suddenly ill with a very
bad cold and, in spite of all that could be done, he died December 14,
1!99 at the age of 68. Alexandria Lodge handled the arrangements for
his funeral and conducted the Masonic service as part of the occasion.
. Thus ended a great and glorious life, to which Lord Byron paid this
tribute:
"Where may the wearied eyes repose
When gazing on the great
Where neither guilty glory glows
Nor despicable state?
Y es--<>ne, the first, the best,
The Cincinnatus of the West
Whom envy dared not hate
Bequeathed the name of Washington
To make men blush there was but one.''
Thus passed from active participation in the affairs of this country
a man who has been well described as the Father of his Country, but who
m~y also be described as the Masonic leader of his day-first in the
hearts of his t:ountrymen and first and always in the hearts of his
brethren.

At the last Annual Communication, Grand Lodge enacted new law,
which is now a part of Section 127 of Ross Digest, reading as follows:
"No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction of Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print
advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which
purports to be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body, order or organization requiring
Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership."
Your committee prepared an application form, a copy of which is
attached, under which individual Masons might meet the requirements
of the Grand Master respecting the solicitation and publishing of advertising in pursuance of the law above quc:>ted. This form was approved
by the Grand Master on November 30, 1951. in language as follows:
"The report of the Special Committee on Publications, submitted to me under date of November 21, 1951, is approved in full,
and it is directed that all applicants seeking the express sanction
of Grand Lodge, required under the new law, shall make the
application therein recommended and comply with all rules therein
suggested.
"Before any sanction is granted to any publication, it is directed that all applications therefor shall be forwarded to the Grand
Secretary, Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, 25 Van Ness
Avenue, San Francisco 2, and shall be by him transmitted to the
Special Committee on Publications which Committee shall submit
it to the Grand Master, together with its recommendation as to
approval or disapproval."
Applications on the form provided, which required the applicant,
under oath, to agree to abide by certain conditions therein, were submitted by the publications indicated below and approved by this committee. In addition to the conditions embodied in the application, this
committee, in view of the directive of the Grand Master dated November 30, 1951. with the consent and approval of the Grand Master, impressed other conditions, to which the applicant agreed, reading as
follows :
"1. That no part of any trestle board of any Lodge or District
Officers Association, including list of Lodge officers, calendar of
Lodge meetings, or official statements by Lodge officers. be carried
in the publication.
"2. That no use be made of any Lodge roster or official membership list.

II.
On November 30, 1951, the Grand Master issued a directive which
was sent to all Lodges, reading in part as follows:

"1. All solicitation, acceptance or publication of advertising
in Lodge publications (bulletins, etc.) shall cease.

201

·:2. No Lodge shall permit its trestle board to be published in
any publication other than its own Lodge bulletin.
"3. No advertising in ·notices, programs, circulars, rosters,
dodgers, napkins, place cards, gifts, gadgets, and other similar
miscellaneous media shall be permitted."
The foregoing directive of the Grand Master merely emphasized
and brought to attention long-standing Masonic law (Sec. 127 Ross
Digest) forbidding commercial ventures, which law had been long
ignored.
On December 5, 1951, the Grand Master held that the foregoing
directive applied to all Bodies requiring affiliation as a condition to
membership. Applications were received from numerous Bodies and
some Lodges seeking sanction; but none was processed, because the
directive of the Grand Master quoted above forbade advertising by
Bodies and Lodges in their own publications. It is pleasing to report
that most all Lodges and most Bodies requiring Masonic affiliation as
a condition to membership have strictly complied with the Grand
Master's directive.
As evidence of compliance with the Grand Master's directive by
some Lodges, it must be reported that the Masters of Naval, Solano,
and Vallejo Lodges, by their joint efforts, have created the Vallejo
Masonic Bulletin, which serves the three Lodges by carrying their
respective trestle boards and the necessary information to their members, without advertising of any kind or chartcter. This bulletin is a
credit to the Masters, their Lodges and this Grand Lodge. The whole
structure of Masonry was founded upon a self-supporting basis. It
was never the purpose of Masonry to make money through commercial
ventures. This Vallejo Masonic Bulletin is a monument to true Masonic
purposes, for it is self-sustained by the three Lodges.
Most of the state heads of other Bodies have issued directives or
bulletins commanding their subordinate Bodies to cooperate with the
Grand Lodge and comply with all ·Grand Lodge law and edicts of the
Grand Master.
In January of this year, a bulletin directing compliance with the
Grand Master's directive was sent by the Supreme Scribe by order of
George R. Wishart, Pharaoh of the Supreme Pyramid of Sciots, to all
constituent Bodies. On June 11, 1952, the Grand High Priest of Royal
Arch Masons, the Grand Master of the Council of Royal and Select
Masters, and the Grand Commander of Knights Templar sent a joint
bulletin to their constituent Bodies directing strict compliance with the
edict of the Grand Master.
On February 3, 1952, the Grand Matron of Eastern Star sent a
letter to all chapters quoting the Grand Master's directive and directing
compliance therewith.

IV
It should be definitely understood and remembered that freedom of
the press or expression is not on trial here. No effort has been made to
limit either in any fashion. Our great problem requiring solution is advertising or commercialism in the name of Masonry or under the color
of Masonry. This problem should be resolved in favor of the many and
not the few who seek personal gain.
Your committee desires to commend Past Grand Master Paulsen for
accenting the subject of commercialism in Masonry and to applaud our
present Grand Master, the Honorable Louis C. Drapeau, who has so
faithfully, forthrightly. and fraternally fostered the solution. Progress
has been made during the year in reducing advertising in the name of
Masonry and eradication is hoped for in the near future.
This Masonic year may be called the year of education, for the
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary, and this committee have striven
