Questions and Answers About Publications
Many questions have been addressed to the Special Committee on
Masonic Publications. The following answers give an explanation to
many of the questions propounded:
Question No. 1: Why is a Lodge not permitted to sell advertising in its
monthly bulletin?
Answer: Because every Lodge in California is prohibited from going
into business in any way, nor can a Lodge solicit pecuniary
assistance. (Ross Digest 126 and 127) In accord with our
long standing law the Grand Master on November 30, 1951,
issued an edict reading as follows:
" ( 1 ) All solicitation, acceptance or publication of advertising
in Lodge publications ( bulletins, etc.) shall cease.
"(2) No Lodge shall permit its trestle board to be published
in any publication other than its own Lodge bulletin.
" ( 3) No advertising in notices, programs, circulars, rosters,
dodgers, napkins, place cards, gifts, gadgets and other similar
miscellaneous media shall be permitted."
On December 5, 1951, the Grand Master held that this edict applied
to all Bodies requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership.
Question No. 2: Why do these restrictions apply to Bodies requiring
Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership?
Answer: Because a group of Masons cannot organize to do what their
Lodge is forbidden to do. Under the American system of jurisdiction, all collateral Masonic Bodies recognize the supremacy
of their respective Grand Lodges, and other organizations
which require Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership-although in no way recognized by Grand Lodge-must
obey the Masonic law of the jurisdiction in which they operate.
Question No. 3: Was this prohibition against advertising in Lodge publications changed in any way by the legislation concerning pub-

205

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

lications adopted at the annual communication of Grand Lodge
in 1951?
Answer: No. This violation of Masonic law had grown gradually (and
had been tolerated) until the edict by the Grand Master on
November 30, 1951.
Question No. 4: What was the extent of the legislation adopted at the
annual communication of Grand Lodge in 1951?
Answer: The legislation adopted reads as follows:
"No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction of Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or
print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be Masonic in name or character, or
which is published by or for any body, order or organization
requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership."
Question No. 5: .Who may apply for sanction of Grand Lodge to solidt,
print or publish advertising in a publication which purports
to be Masonic in name or character?
•
·
Answer: An individual Mason or several Masons acting as individuals
but who are not acting as the representative of any Lodge or
other Body.
Question No. 6: Why cannot Lodges, Bodies or organizations such as
Officers' Associations. etc .• apply for such sanction?
Answer: For the reason stated in the answers to Questions 1 and 2.
While the wording of the 1951 legislation on publications
would seem to imply the possibility of giving Grand Lodge
sanction to publications issued by Lodges, etc., the Grand
Master has ruled that the other well-established Masonic law,
against commercial enterprises and soliciting donations, prevents granting Lodges or Bodies such a sanction.
Question No. 7: How can qualified persons obtain the sanction of Grand
Lodge to print advertising. etc.?
Answer: By the vote of Grand Lodge when it is in session, and when it
is not in session its powers are exercised by the Grand Master.
Question No. 8: Will the Grand Master grant such a sanction? .
Answer: No. But when a qualified person files an application (in duplicate) on the form provided by the Grand Secretary, requesting
permission to carry advertising in a so-called Masonic publication, the Grand Master may, in his best judgment issue a
statement, attested by the Grand Secretary, in words as
follows:

Lodge. However, a strict compliance with the requisite specifications, on the part of this publication, will m'e et the requirements
of the Grand Master respecting the solicitation and publishing of
advertising in this publication. The Grand Master reserves the
right to revoke this statement at any time.

before such a statement will be issued?
Answer: Among other things, the applicant must certify and agree in
writing as follows:
1. That no part of any trestle board of any Lodge or District
Officers Association, including list of Lodge Officers, calendar
of Lodge meetings, or official statements by Lodge officers, will
be carried in the publication.
2. That no use will be made of any Lodge roster or official mem~rship list.
3. That no money will be accepted from any Lodge for subscriptions or any other purpose whatsoever.
The applicant also must under oath agree to abide by and strictly
comply with the following conditions and specifications:
a. Advertising will not be solicited or accepted upon a commission basis by agents, employees, or otherwise.
b. No person except a member in good standing of a Lodge in
this jurisdiction will be permitted to solicit or accept advertising for this publication.
c. No advertisements of beer, wines or liquors will be solicited,
accepted or printed.

or printed.

Question No. 10: What protection does this statement by the Grand
Master afford those who solicit, spansor, insert. place or print
advertising in the so-called Masonic publication to which the
statement has been issued?
Answer: The statement says. "a strict compliance with the requisite
specifications, on the part of this publication. will meet the requirements of the Grand Master respecting the solicitation
and publishing of advertising in this publication." This would
appear to provide immunity from discipline, provided of course
the publication strictly complies with all of said specifications

207

and conditions. It must be understood that the Grand Master
can at any time impress additional restrictions.

Question No. 11: How long will the sanction implied by the Grand Master's statement continue?
Answer: Until revoked by the Grand Master or Grand Lodge.
Question No. 12: Can a Lodge or Body requiring Masonic affiliation as
a condition to membership receive, permit or accept rosters
provided by a party or organization which prints its advertisements in or on the cover of the roster? _
Answer: No. This is forbidden by the answer under Question No. 1
above.

Question No. 13: Why is a Lodge forbidden to publish its trestle board
in any publication other than its own publication?
Answer: Because the material in a trestle board is for the use of its own
members and for such other individual members as the Lodge
may permit to receive it. The trestle board's contents should
not be exposed to the general public. The trestle board of a
Lodge includes a full or partial list of its officers with their
addresses, a calendar of Lodge events and a list of the projected meetings with commentaries thereon.

Question No. 14: Would it be improper for a Lodge to permit a news
item concerning one of its officers or one of its meetings. which
is to be held, to be published in a so-called Masonic Publication?
Answer: Apparently this would not be a trestle board, and if the information would not violate some other Masonic rule, such a
n~ws item would not be improper.

Question No. 15: Would it be proper for a Lodge to insert in a nonMasonic newspaper a publicity item announcing a meeting?
Answer: This would in no way contravene the legislation re publications
adopted at the last session of Grand Lodge, for that legislation
applied only to advertisements in publications "which purport
to be Masonic in name or 1;:haracter." Thus, if it were otherwise
proper, a Lodge could even place a paid advertisement in a
newspaper of general circulation which was in no way Masonic in character. While a Lodge may insert in such a newspaper a publicity item announcing one meeting, it may not
insert a list of meetings for the entire month, because this
would take on the aspect of a trestle board.

Question No. 16: May a Lodge pay money to assist a so-called Masonic publication?
Answer: No. This would be an unlawful use of Lodge funds. This is a
subject which the Lodge would have to consider in connection

208

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
with placing a paid advertisement in a non-Masonic newspaper.

Question No. 17: Why are certain parties permitted to violate the legislation concerning advertising in so-called Masonic publications?
Answer: No such violations are permitted. The party who violates,
directly or indirectly, assumes the burdens. Masonic law clearly specifies the method for dealing with Masonic offenses.
Most Masons are anxious to obey Masonic regulations. A few
through ignorance, misinformation or subterfuge, have continued to publish advertising in so-called Masonic publications
which have not been approved or for which no application has
has even been filed. Some through ignorance, misinformation
or subterfuge have not complied with the Grand Master's
edicts. The heads of ·most other bodies and organizations have
directed compliance with the Grand Lodge legislation and the
Grand Master's edict. Their cooperation is praiseworthy.

Trial Record No. 330
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred the petition of C. F. 0. for
restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry begs leave to report
as follows:
The accused was expelled by San Pasqual Lodge in 1922 on the
charge that he had committeed grand larceny and had been sentenced to
State Prison. He now filed his petition for restoration and has given the
required notice thereof to San Pasqual Lodge.
The petitioner states that the State Prison Board set his sentence at
five years. He served about one year and seven months in the prison and
at an honor camp in Northern California. He was paroled in December
of 1923 and went to Boston, Mass. where he finished his parole and
worked until 1927. At that time he returned to California and has been
continuously employed with one company in various capacities for over
21 years.
His reasons for seeking restoration are so well stated that we are
taking the liberty of quoting them verbatim:

We feel that the petitioner has sustained the burden of showing that
he has made a complete atonement for his error and therefore deserves _
favorable consideration. In recommending restoration, however, we feel
it encumbent to point out to Grand Lodge a matter of policy. In 1875
Grand Lodge established the rule as set forth in Section 875 of Ross
Digest; that a petition for degrees could not be received from one who
had served it term in state prison. In 1918 a resolution to put this rule
into statutory language by amending Section 208 of the Ordinances
failed to pass, which could be construed as a decision of Grand Lodge
that this policy should not be a part of our law, at least in statutory form.
The matter was thoroughly reviewed in 1951 on the recommendation of
the Grand Master that Section 875 be set aside and disapprQved. The
matter was presented to Grand Lodge in majority and minority reports
of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. Grand Lodge adopted
the majority report which disapproved the Grand Masters suggestion
and thus the principle of Section 875 was re-~ffirmed and a Lodge cannot accept the petition of a former felon. In other words, under the
present law a former inmate of state prison is forever disqualified from
petitioning a Masonic Lodge. Does that same disqualification attach to
a member who is expelled for conviction of a felony and imprisoned in
pursuance thereof so as to bar his restoration? Section 875 does not
apply because it specifically refers to petitions for degrees and not to
restoration. Section 314 of the Ordinances provides that Grand Lodge
may, if good cause therefor be shown and proof of notice is given, restore to the rights and privileges of Masonry any Mason who has been
suspended or expelled within its jurisdiction. In 1951 and at almost
every previous annual communication, restoration has been granted to

GRAND LODGE OP CALiPORNIA

216

217

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

expelled Masons who have been guilty of unmasonic conduct consisting
of the commission of a felony and for which they have served a term in
state prison. Because of the emphasis placed upon the question of imprisonment for a felony given last year, we have dwelt upon the matter
here at length. We want Grand Lo4ge to realize that if you adopt the
resolution ·to be offered in this case you determine as a matter of policy
that imprisonment for a felony for which a member is expelled does not
in and of itself bar him from seeking restoration.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That the petition of C. F. D. for restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry be and the same is hereby granted.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 840
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred-the petition of E. M. R. for
restoration to the rights and privileges to Masonry, begs leave to report
as follows:
The petitioner, E. M. R. was expelled on September 6, 1934, for unmasonic conduct based upon two specifications: First that he had deserted, neglected and wilfully failed for a period of two years to provide
for his four minor daughters, then of the ages of 16, 14, 13 and 5, all of

whom were dependent upon him for support, and second, that he was a
fugitive from justice, a warrant for his arrest having been issued under
Section 270 of the Penal Code of the State of California charging failure
to provide for his minor children.
It appeared at the trial that a reasonable effort to locate the accused
had been made and the trial proceeded even though there was no evidence that the accused had really received a copy of the summons and
charges. The evidence at the trial showed that the wife of the accused
had obtained a divorce from the accused and had custody of the minor
children. She testified that he had failed to support them and that she
.
was living upon relief provided by the county.
In 1949 the accused filed a petition for restoration. That petition was
denied without prejudice because of the fact that there was no evidence
as to what effort the petitioner had made to support his children since
he was expelled. The report denying the petition suggested "that the
petitioner be advised to present evidence as to his support of his minor
children since 1934 or his reason for not doing so".
The petitioner has flled under date of July 5, 1952, a further petition
covering in detail his occupation, activities and earnings since 1930. As
set forth in the petition, he was working as a salesman on a commission
basis and his earnings were insufficient to meet the payments as ordered
by the court. Finally in 1940 he went on active duty with the Army as a
1st lieutenant and has been with the Army ever since. At the present
time he is a Master Sergeant and is stationed in Europe. Since the time
he went on active duty with the Army he has made payments on account
of the payment ordered by the court. He has submitted cancelled checks
for the sum pf approximately $800.00 to evidence these payments. His
original petition for restoration is supported by good letters of recom.
mendation and proper notice has been given to the Lodge.
We feel that the petitioner has established that he is entitled to
favorable consideration on his petition. We therefore offer the following
resolution:
Resolved: That the petition of E. M. R. for restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry be and the same is hereby granted.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1256
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances is divided as to the disposition which
should be made in the matter presented by Trial Record No. 1256 from
Palos Verdes Lodge No. '389. A basic question of Masonic policy is
involved.
The facts are these: T. M. C. is a member of Palos Verdes Lodge
No. 389. He resides at Scottsbluff, Nebraska, and is president of T. C.,
Inc., a corporation. This corporation, under his management, operates
a liquor store pursuant to a properly issued license by the State of
Nebraska. Tpe license is of the so-called "off-sale" variety: liquor is
not consumed on the prel'.!lises.
The Grand Jurisdiction of Nebraska has made it a Masonic offense
for a Mason to engage in the sale of intoxicating liquor. The actions
of T. M. C. are therefore a violation of the Masonic law of Nebraska.
By proceedings duly and regularly done and had before a Nebraska
Trial Commission the accused was ordered expelled from Palos Verdes
Lodge No. 389. No appeal was _taken and this action has now become
final in the Grand Lodge of Nebraska. Such action was beyond the
jurisdiction of Nebraska Masonry. It had no authority to expel a California Mason from a California Lodge. Only a California Lodge by
and with the approval of this Grand Lodge may properly take such
action. However, the Grand Lodge of Nebraska could expel a Mason
resident there from all the rights and privileges of Masonry in Nebraska.
We regard the action of the Grand Lodge of Nebraska as doing this and
nothing more.
The record of the Nebraska proceedings was filed with this Grand
Lodge and received its attention in 1951. At that time your Committee
on Grievances recommended by a divided vote of five to two that no
action be taken on the matter here, basing such recommendation upon the

222

223

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

fact that conducting a liquor store is not a Masonic ~ffense in California. Grand Lodge declined to approve this recommendation and
ordered the matter referred to Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389, pursuant
to the provisions of Section 331 of our Ordinances which reads as
follows:

"Every Freemason is amenable to the laws and regulations of the
Masonic Jurisdiction in which he resides."
The majority of our Committee answers that a Mason should only
be expelled in his home Lodge and Grand Lodge for offenses which are
there declared to be the basis for expulsion: that, in this case, the accused
has been rendered amenable to the "laws and regulations" of Nebraska
by being expelled from the rights and privileges of Masonry in that
Grand Jurisdiction; that more should not be taken from him; and that
to forfeit his California Lodge membership for an act which is not
punishable in California is obviously unfair. ·
You have the question, my brethren. If you agree with the minority,
your action should be to reverse the action of the Trial Commission in
finding the accused not guilty of unmasonic conduct and in acquitting
the accused and by finding the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct and
&xing the penalty at expulsion.
If, on the other hand, you agree with the majority of the Committee,
you should adopt the following Resolution which I now offer and move
its adoption:
Be It Resolved that the action of the Trial Commission of
Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389 in finding the accused not guilty of
Unmasonic conduct and in acquitting the accused be, and the
same hereby is, ratified, affirmed and approved.
Adopted.
On reconsideration, the accused was found guilty of unmasonic conduct, and tlte penalty fixed at expulsion.
See report of Committee on Jurisprudence for action.

"Whenever it shall appear by the record of conviction from
another Masonic jurisdiction, recognized by us, that a member
of one of our Lodges. resident in such jurisdiction, has been suspended or expelled for unmasonic conduct in such jurisdiction
while a resident thereof. it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden
of the Lodge in this jurisdiction of which he is a member to prefer
charges against him for the acts and conduct alleged in the
charges preferred in the foreign jurisdiction and of which he was
there convicted, and the same proceedings shall thereupon be had
as in ordinary cases; provided that the record of conviction of the
foreign jurisdiction shall be received on the trial as prima facie
evidence of the guilt of the brother of such acts and conduct."
Pursuant to this action of Grand Lodge, charges were flied in Palos
Verdes Lodge charging T. M. C. with unmasonic conduct based on a
specification setting forth that the accused had engaged in the sale of
intoxicating liquor in Nebraska. A trial was had in due and proper
order. The _accused was found guilty of the speci.6cation but not guilty
of unmasomc conduct and was, therefore, acquitted. The matter is now
before you for final disposition.
Section 210 of our Ordinances prohibits a Mason in California from
engaging in the saloon business or as a barkeeper except in connection
with, and as a part of. the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant.
It is not a Masonic offense in California for a Mason to operate a liquor
store where liquor is not consumed on the premises. It will be observed
that, in this respect, our Masonic law differs from that of Nebraska.
The question is, therefore, squarely presented: Should the Grand Lodge
of California expel a Mason from a California Lodge when such Mason
has been expelled in a foreign jurisdiction for conduct which is unmasonic in such foreign jurisdiction but is not unmasonic in California?
A majority, four of this Committee, recommend that the action of
the Trial Commission of Palos Verdes Lodge acquitting the accused
be affirmed. Three members of the Committee feel the accused should
be expelled.
The minority argues that a sojourning Mason should conform to the
Masonic regulations of the jurisdiction in which he resides and for a
violation thereof should forfeit his rights and privileges of Masonry
everywhere, including in his own Lodge.· They assert the matter is covered by Landmark Seventeenth (p. 567 Ross Digest) which reads:

your committee concurs, but we are of the opinion that Grand Lodge

Trial Record No. 1269
The charge~ against accused, A. M. H., a member of James Madison
Lodge No. 572, are very loosely drawn. The first speciftcation alleges
that the accused falsely stated in his application for the degrees that he
knew of no legal or moral reason why he should not become a Mason
when. as a matter of fact, he had several past criminal convictions against
him, one being a felony case which resulted in a prison term. The
second specification lumps together the arrest and conviction of accused
for assault with a deadly weapon in Superior Court of Los Angeles
County in 1951 and a subsequent arrest and conviction for disturbing
the peace in Beverly Hills City Court.
As we have pointed out year after year, the arrest and conviction
for crime does not constitute a Masonic offense, but it is the law violation
itself which is the Masonic offense, and it should be so pleaded in the
charges. Upon the Masonic trial, the judgments of conviction in the
state courts are prima facie evidence of guilt of the offense charged.
Grand Lodge in 1951 adopted the policy that "the failure to disclose
prior criminal convictions in response to Question 12 of the Application",
standing alone, does not constitute a Masonic offense. However, in
this case, the a<!cused did falsly answer the questions as to. occupation

226

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Trial Record No. 1273
and residence during the preceding ten years by omitting reference to his
prison term. His application is dated in 1947 and his prison term was
from 1932 to 1939.
Accused was found guilty of both specifications and of unmasonic
conduct and expelled.
However, it appears t~at the summons and charges were mailed to
accused in Los Angeles just ten days before the trail. A person residing
within the jurisdiction of the lodge must be served personally by the
tiler· or some other person designated by the Master. If residing elsewhere in the state service may be made by mail but must be at least
thirty days before the trial. There is nothing in this record to show that
accused ever received the charges and he did not appear at the trial. For
this reason, the expulsion must be reversed, and the matter returned to
the lodge for retrial. Amended charges should be prepared alleging the
falsity of the application for degrees as to occupation and residence, and
alleging the commission of the felony and misdemeanor covered by the
second specification in the present charges.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved: That the action of James Madison Lodge No. 572, in expelling A. M. H., be and the same is vacated and set aside and_ the matter
returned to the lodge for filing amended charges, and for trial thereon
after proper service on the accused.
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1273 reports as follows:
Accused R. P. R. was charged with unmasonic conduct in two specifications: First, that he had been convicted of conspiracy to defraud the
United States Government in violation of Section 80, Title 18, of the
United States Code; Second, that the violation of this Statute is a felony
with a maximum penalty of ten years or $10,000.00 fine.
The Commissioners found the Accused "guilty" of the first specifica·
tion and "not guilty of unmasonic conduct."
While the specifications are not well drawn, from ·the evidence it
appears that the gist of the charge was that the Accused conspired to
defraud the Government by using a veteran's preference to purchase
war surplus property when, in fact, the property was not being purchased
for the veteran. The property consisted of a crane which the Government sold to the veteran for $4,520.25. Accused furnished the money
for the cashier's check which the veteran presented to the Government
for the crane and, in addition, paid the veteran $220.50. Accused admitted that the crane was not bought for the veteran but wa!> bought
for Accused's partner in the purchase and sale of war surplus materials.
The evidence clearly indicates a deliberate, intentional fraud practiced
upon the United States Government.
Under these circumstances your Committee is of the opinion that the
finding of "not guilty of unmasonic conduct" is unwarranted and should
be set aside, 'and that Grand Lodge should supply a findl.ng of "guilty
of unmasonic conduct" and that the penalty should be fixed at expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved: That the Trial Commission's finding in Trial Record No.
1273 that R. P.R. is guilty of the specification be approved and affirmed;
that the finding that he is not guilty of unmasonic conduct be disapproved
and supplied; and that said R. P. R. be and he is hereby expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

Ing that the accused was on November 26th, 1951 adjudicated guilty

the Norwalk State Hospital.
The trial commissioners found the accused guilty of each of the ten
specifications and guilty of unmasonic conduct: but upon the question
of the penalty to be imposed voted two for expulsion and seven against,
and voted unanimously to fix the penalty at suspension: this despite
the fact that there is no evidence in the record of any circumstances in
mitigation of the ten offenses.
Your Committee is in an agreement with the findings of guilt in this
case, and believe that such findings should be affirmed: but we cannot
agree that the penalty of suspension is an appropriate one. Each of the
ten separate offenses specified charges conduct involving moral turpitude. If the penalty for these acts be only suspension, the Lodge would
be in a position to restore the accused to membership at any time, and
Grand Lodge would, by approving that penalty, be in effect abdicating
its right to review the question as to whether one convicted of an act
or acts involving moral turpitude has become rehabilitated before restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry. This right is one that Grand
Lodge has reserved to itself in cases where the wrongdoer has been expelled. and we think with good reason.
(See Sec. 343, Constitution and Ordinances)
(Trial Record No. 1157, 1949 Proceedings. p. 254)
(Trial Record No. 1045. 1946 Proceedings, p. 140)
(Trial Record No. 1048, 1946 Proceedings, p. 142)

Resolved: That the findings of guilt of the specifications and the
charge in Trial Record No. 1286, be and the same are affirmed: and that
the penalty therein be and the same hereby is. by action of this Grand
Lodge fixed at expulsion.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1301
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1301, reports as follows:
Accused, J. S. A., a member of Oxnard Lodge No. 341, was charged
with unmasonic conduct based upon his conviction in the Los Angeles
Superior Court of one count of abortion and one count of conspiracy to
commit abortions for which he was placed on ten years probation.
The Commissioners found Accused guilty of the specification and of
unmasonic conduct and fixed the penalty at suspension.
The findings of guilty of the specification and of unmasonic conduct
are amply supported by the evidence and your committee concurs in these
findings. Your committee, however, is of the opinion that the penalty of
suspension is inappropriate in a case such as this which involves a
serious felony, and that the penalty should he raised to expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved: That the Trial Commission's finding in Trial Record No.
1301 that J. S. A. is guilty of the specification and of unmasonic conduct
he and it is hereby affirmed and approved: that the sentence imposed by
the Trial Commission suspending J. S. A. from the rights and privileges
of Masonry he and the same is hereby set aside and disapproved; and
that, by action of Grand Lodge, the said J. S. A. he and he is hereby
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

In concluding his portion of the report of the Committee on Grievances, Chairman Frank B. Belcher pointed out that this terminated 23
years of service by him on the Committee; he also announced that he
had advised the Deputy Grand Master of his desire not to be reappointed
on the Committee.

Pursuant to Section 333 of our Ordinances, the Grand Secretary
duly and regularly gave notice to the accused advising him of his conviction, and that unless he elected within sixty days to have a trial by a
Masonic Lodge within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, he would stand expelled from all rights and privileges of
Masonry. The accused did not elect to have such a trial. As a result,
he stood automatically expelled sixty days following July 8, 1952, the
date of the notice by the Grand ~ecretary.
Your Committee on Grievances offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
Be It Resolved that the expulsion of J. M. P. from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry be, and the same hereby is,
ratified, affirmed and approved.
Be It Further Resolved that the Grand Secretary be, and he
hereby is, authorized, empowered and instructed to transmit a
copy of this report to the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted
Masons of Michigan, together with a report of the action taken
by Grand Lodge on this resolution.
Adopted.

One of the importan t duties of your Committee on lodge financing
is to see to it that no Masonic lodge embarks upon a building program
so ambitious as to hazard the organiza tion and its members. There are
too many examples of misguided optimism and enthusia sm in the form
of monumental temples in Californ ia which have been built and lost,
with a conseque nt reflection on our cherishe d fraternity . It is pleasing
to report that your Committee on lodge financing has enjoyed the fullest
cooperation from all the constitue nt lodges involved, in carrying out
this policy.
This report would not be complete if it did not pay tribute to the
builders of nearly forty new Masonic temples in our golden state during
the past six or seven years. Theirs has been an outstand ing contribu tion
to Masonry , not only in their own communities, but in Californ ia and
througho ut the world as well.
Masonic temples are built today only by overcoming superior odds
and every possible obstacle. It requires vision and faith-fa ith not
without works-a s well as intelligence and courage. One may never
know what practical Masonry is until he labors in the vineyard s, either
in the building of a new temple or serving on a committee, such as your
committee on lodge financing. Few ever realize just how much men will
sacrifice for this great ideal which we call Masonry . And one's profound
belief in the Divine Creator is strength ened every time he observes his
brethren building these temples with their own hands, and as he contemplates the handiwo rk of the Great Architec t of the Universe as He
guides, protects, and sustains the workmen. As evidence of this protection, it may be interestin g for the members of Grand Lodge to learn
that, although most of the voluntee r labor employed on these temples is
inexperi enced-m any wielding a hammer and saw for the first timenot one single serious accident has occurred to mar their glorious accomplishments.
Masons generally and those in Californ ia particularly, owe a nreat
deal to these workers on the temples. They are to be commended and
congratu lated by all of us.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws have carefuUy examined the 111
Amendments to By-Laws submitted for approval during the past year.
This number indicates that Masters have given careful attention to the
Lodge By-Laws.
·
One of the strong foundations of Masonry is its continuous endeavor
to have uniformity of procedure. In keeping with this thought, we have
our Uniform Code of By-Laws in California. Ross Digest, page 54, tells
us it was made obligatory in October 1898, and as amended to October
1939, and reaffirmed in 1948. Legislation enacted by Grand Lodge is
binding, of course, on all constituent Lodges. Some of it may require
changes in the Lodge By-Laws, the same as Lodge action that changes
the amount of your fees for degrees, yearly dues, etc. Other matters do
not need to be included in the Lodge By-Laws. If the Lodge desires to
use the alternative meeting date provision for stated meetings that fau on
a holiday, the By-Laws should be amended to so provide. If the Lodge

241

245

PROCBBDINGS OP THE.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

desires to apply the legislation passed in 1951 as to the applicant who
does not complete his second and third degree, the Lodge may do so
and it is not necessary to include it in the Lodge By-Laws. That legislation is an Ordinance of Grand Lodge. When in doubt as to the necessity
of including something in the Lodge By-Laws, write the Grand Secretary's Office and the matter will be properly considered or referred and
in due time a complete answer will. be sent you. Amendment forms and
form for certifying of the amendment by the Lodge Secretary are available and you will find our Grand Secretary one hundred per cent cooperative in advising and guiding you through the proper procedure.
Some difficulty has been experienced in filling out the portion of the
By-Laws section regarding the affiliation fee. We urge that no blanks
be left unfilled. If no affiliation fee is charged, use the word "no" or
"nil." and strike out unnecessary words. Some Lodges have well covered
it with these words "and for affiliation the sum of $5.00," or "and for
affiliation there shall be no charge." As to the provision for an alternative
meeting date if the stated meeting falls on a holiday and the Lodge does
not desire to use that portion of the section, simply so state, and strike
out extra words. One Lodge stated as follows: "except in any month
when the regular meeting date shall fall on no exceptions or......................
legal holidays. the stated meeting shall be holden the............................of
·-·-----····-·······-·-··-··month at................m. ••
This is not necessary: the two words "no exceptions" would have
been sufficient. Where the intent is clear, we have raised no question,
even though the surplus words have made it cumbersome.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Death, the great leveler of mankind, is never idle. He strikes with
the tedious monotony of the tick of a metronome. He considers neither
age, position. wealth or need. He will take the most learned and brilliant
mind with the same reckless abandon that he will call the most ignorant
savage. He will beckon the babe cooing at its mother's breast as quickly
as he will call the one who has passed three score years and ten. His
workings are an eternal mystery to mankind, for at times he can be
exceedingly cruel and at others he can be exceedingly kind. In his cruel
nature he demands the youth, the young man who has established a
family and has every expectancy f!)r a long and happy life. He will take
the bread-winner and leave a family helpless. He will call the young
mother. thus depriving the children oi one of life's greatest blessings.
In his more considerate moments he will lay his soothing hand upon
the brow of the incurable. the aged. the infirm and the helpless.
While we do not understand the dual nature of death we accept it
as part of God's perfect plan. and agree with the poet Norton, who said:
"For death and life, in ceaseless strife
Beat wild on this world's shore,
And all our calm is in that balm.
Not lost, but gone before."
Since the 1951 Communication of the Grand Lodge of California 319
Masters and Past Masters of this jurisdiction have answered the final
call. Of this number 31 had been members of the Fraternity for half
a century or more: 201 were members for more than 25 years, 38 were
affiliate Past Masters. having occupied the Oriental Chair in other
jurisdictions. We have lost three Past Grand Masters: Gilbert C.

Brother Logsdon's Masonic career was his true life's history. His
devotion to Masonry formed the pattern of his life. He received his
third degree in San Bernardino Lodge No. 348 on May 22, 1919, and
served as Master during 1927. His devotion and ability were rewarded
by the Grand Lodge by his appointment to the office of Inspector of the
then 104th Masonic district in 1937, which office he held until his retirement in 1950.
His enthusiasm for Masonry took him into many of its dependent
organizations. He became a life member of the Consistory at Los
Angeles, a member of the Order of Eastern Star where he served as
the Worthy Patron of Gate City Chapter in the year 1921, and he was
a charter member of the order of Sciots at San Bernardino, being chosen
as its Toparch in 1924. He served as captain of the Sciots' drill team
for several years and carried them to many successful competitions.

RALPH H. LOGSDON
(By William T. Hunter, Jr., Past Master No. 348.)
In seeking a descriptive passage that might in some way portray the
principles and character of our beloved Ralph H. Logsdon we might
recall these lines:
Be strong!
It matters not how deep entrenched the wrong,
How hard the battle goes, the day how long:
Faint not-fight on! Tomorrow comes the song. (Babcock)
Ralph H. Logsdon was born at Tustin, California, October 12, 1888,
the ~on of William and Gertrude Logsdon, early settlers of that beautiful
inland valley near the sun-bathed shores of Southern California.
The following year the Logsdon family•moved to San Bernardino.
There Ralph grew to manhood and acquired those admirable traits of
character which endeared him to the hearts of his many friends.
He was a man of great capacity, of wide experience and practical
knowledge. "He was the warrior that came forth when all other champions held back." He was respected, and his advice and comfort were
sought by men in all stations of life. His was a great moral strength,
founded on the principle that truth and right are the only considerations.
After graduating from San Bernardino High School he completed a
course in the Sturgis Business College, where he became interested in
advertising, and in 1910 he moved to San Francisco and entered the
advertising field.
Opportunity required Ralph Logsdon, in 1911, to travel south to San
Diego. Here, nearer to his former home he became associated with the
Spreckels Theater Company, and it was here that he met Ruby Pierson
who was to become the constant companion and inspiration of his life.
They were married September 17, 1913. In 1915 Ralph and Ruby moved
to San Bernardino. There they suffered the loss of their infant son,
·
William Frank Logsdon.
Ralph purchased the C. G. Peck Paint Store in 1920, where he had
been employed since his arrival in San Bernardino, and which he operated until ill health forced his retirement in 1949. The Logsdons then
took up their residence in an apartment of their court at Santa Barbara,
California. There Ralph found the rest and contentment that he felt
would restore his tired body. The Great Architect summoned Brother
Logsdon on September 13, 1951 while the sun was still in its greatest

251

Notable among the Masonic accomplishments of Past Master Ralph
Logsdon was his planning and directing of -the laying of the cornerstone of the High School at Barstow, California. This job brought to
Ralph special praise from the Grand Master and resulted in their mutual
cooperation in the chartering of Barstow Lodge in 1940, and in a lifelong friendship.
Even as his first official duty as Inspector had been the cornerstone
laying at Barstow, so his final official act was the planning and direction
of the layins of the corner-stone of the Hall of Justice at San Bernardino
in 1949.
It is known that Ralph Logsdon attended each Grand Session from
1925 until his ill health required that 1949 be the final year. During his
time as Inspector Rim O' the World Lodge No. 711 was instituted and
Ralph devoted much time to the original formation of this Lodge. San
Bernardino and Barstow Lodges will long remember that Ralph Logsdon
so capably conducted their installation ceremonies year after year as
long as he was physically able. It was with great reluctance that he
gave up the tradition of installing Barstow Lodge officers, which custom
he and the then Grand Master Wm. B. Ogden had instituted. Ralph H.
Logsdon gave much to Masonry. He gave of himself, all that he had.
This thought must have been a great satisfaction to him as he approached
the Anal hour and surely there were no regrets, but with this thought 'he
faced the Supreme Grand Master:
Yes, I have had, dear Lord, the day:
When at Thy call I have the night,
Brief be the twilight as I pass
From light to dark, from dark to light. (Mitchell)

JAMES LEO WARD

Masonic Board of Relief in 1927, where he served with honor and
distinction until his death.
Initiated in University Lodge No. 394 of Los Angeles October 21,
1912, Passed November 4, and Raised November 25 the same year.
Earl immediately became an earnest and enthusiastic member of the
Fraternity. November 24, 1920 he affiliated with Garvanza Lodge No.
492 of Los Angeles, and was elected Master for the year 1925. He was
secretary of the Lodge in 1926-1927. He was elected treasurer in 1929
and filled that office for 22 years. He held the 32nd Degree in the Ancient
and Accepted Scottish Rite, being a member of the class graduating
September 13, 1913. He was also a member of the Eastern Star and of
Al Malaikah Temple Ancient Arabic Order Nobles of the Mystic Shrine.
The year 1925 was an unusual and exceptional one in Masonic circles in Los Angeles. The Masters of the various lodges recognizing
that changes and improvements could and should be made, organized
themselves into a group with the title of "Quarter Century Club." The
services of the Club cannot be over-estimated. Earl Thaxter was its
secretary. The ravages of time have decimated its ranks, and while
the club does not now function, its accomplishments are easily recognized by those who were familiar with the situation that existed more
than a quarter of a century ago.
Brother Thaxter was especially endowed by the Great Architect of
the Universe for his position on the Board of Relief. He had a sympathy and understanding for those in distress which inspired immediate
hope and confidence. His help and advice led many to a safe haven in
a troubled world. He restored self confidence in many to whom the
burden of existence seemed too heavy to bear. At the same time he was
quick to discern the imposter, the lazy and the deadbeat. He was anathema to those who would defraud the Order.
Earl was devoted to his religion, and was a founding member of the
Highland Park Christian Church, and for many years was an elder and
treasurer.
Brother Thaxter was married December 24, 1914, to Miss Martha
May Corn. Of this union one son was born, Norman Thaxter, now a
resident of Alhambra, California.
The funeral services were held in his beloved Church amid a profusion of floral offerings. Past Grand Master Ellsworth Meyer officiated,
assisted by Fred L. Norh, Past Master of Garvanza Lodge as Chaplain.
Earl's deep-seated ideals came alive through his personality, and his
spirit and influence will be with us for years to come.

In 1950 Grand Master Arthur .Paulsen appointed James Leo Ward
of Crescent City a member of the Committee on Pay of Members.
Brother Ward served faithfully and was reappointed by the present
Grand Master. Death overtook him at Ashland, Oregon, thus cutting
short a splendid Masonic career.
Leo was born March 9, 1892 in Gualala, Mendocino County, California. When six years of age the family moved to Crescent City, and
he spent the balance of his life in that community. Leo was educated
in the public schools of Del Norte County, and shortly after graduation
from high school he married Katheryn Maris. Three children were
born of this union-Maris, Chester and Margaret.
His business career began as an employee of the Hobbs-Wall Lumber Co. of Crescent City. He later becam.e a distributor of automobiles,
and upon the sale of the agency became agent and distributor of the
products of the General Petroleum Corporation. At the time of his death
he was associated with his son, Maris, in Ward's Propane and Gas
Service.
For many years Brother Ward took an active interest in civic and
community affairs. His especial interest was the public school, and as
trustee of the Del Norte County High School his efficient work will
long be remembered. He was Past Commander of the American Legion
Post No. 175, a member of its affiliate, the Past Commander Club, and
a member of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks. As Past
Master of Crescent Lodge No. 45, two months before his passing, he
installed his son Maris as Master.
He was buried in the Mason.ic Cemetery according to th~ ritualistic
ceremony, mourned not only by his brethren but by the host of friends
which so good and kind a man had made over a long life of right, just,
and helpful living.
Leo is survived by his wife, his three children, two sisters, a brother,
five grandchildren,· and a number of nephews and nieces.

Born in Los Angeles May 19, 1889, Earl lived his life in this State.

El Centro office where he worked until 1915, when he became auditor
for the Vessey Produce Co. · The latter firm in 1918 promoted him to
the main office at the Terminal Market in Los Angeles. He co~tinued in
this office until he became Executive Secretary of the Los Angeles

FRANK GRAVES FALLOON

For 22 years Frank Falloon occupied the important office of Inspector
of the 75th District. He was appointed by Grand Master Albert Boynton
October.21, 1925 and served until ill health forced his resignation December 31, 1947.

254

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Frank began the ascent of the Masonic ladder by being initiated
March 1i. 1916 in Sunset Lodge No. 352 in Los Angeles. He was so
proficient in memorizing the monitorial and esoteric work that one week
later he received the Second Degree, and two weeks after his initiation
was made a Master Mason. September 8, 1916 he was elected to receive
the degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Los Angeles,
and graduated with the Spring Class June 1, 1917.
Born November 28, 1887, at Hiawatha, Kansas. Brother Falloon
received his early education in that city. He later attended the University of Kansas at Lawrence. and graduated as an engineer. Coming
to Los Angeles his ambition changed and he began the study of law.
Successfully passing the bar examination he was admitted to practice
May 15, 191 7.
April 6. 1917. the United States entered the First World War, and
the following August 24th Frank enlisted in the Signal Corps, U. S.
Army. He soon achieved the rank of First Sergeant. His knowledge of
engineering stood him in good stead and he was recommended for the
Signal Officers' Training School. being commissioned a Second Lieutenant April 28, 1918. Five months later he was promoted to First
Lieutenant. Shortly after the termination of hostilities Frank was mustered out of the service, but the call of the Army was strong in his blood,
and on April 20, 1920 he entered the Signal Corps Reserve with the
rank of Captain.
' Veterans' affairs were of especial interest to him, and on June 15
1920, he was elected Commander Los Angeles City Inter-Post Council.
American Legion. September 22, 1922 he was elected State Executive
Committeeman, American Legion. December 7, 1927 he became Commander Sunshine Post No. 251, American Legion.
Frank's military career interrupted his Masonic work, and upon
entering the Army he resigned as Senior Deacon of Sunset Lodge. In
1920 a dispensation was issued to a group of Veterans of World War I
who had organized a lodge. naming it Clarence F. Smith in honor of a
Captain of that name who was a member of the Ninety-First Division
of the American Expeditionary Forces lost his life in the battle of the
Argonne Forest. Frank was a charter member of this lodge: conferred
the first degree in the new lodge. and became its Master in 1922. He
was a member of Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine, and for 19 years
was Secretary of the Southern California Past Masters Association.
Frank Falloon died September 19. 1952. The services were conducted by Clarence F. Smith Lodge, P. H. Montgomery, Past Master
and Secretary, officiating. Interment was in beautiful Inglewood Park
Cemetery
He is survived by a nephew, Donald Falloon.
Frank took an active, serious and able interest in everything that
pertained to Freemasonry. He gave much to the Masonic Homes. Until
we meet again in our Father's House we bid him farewell.

JAY A. POWERS

The passing of any member of the Grand Lodge is a shock to all of
us. but when Death points her icy finger at a member of our official
family the hurt strikes doubly deep. Such a wound came to us September 24, 1952 when Jay A. Powers, Grand Pursuivant, died at his home
at 1803 Wellington Road, Los Angeles.
Born in Tacoma, Washington, May 22, 1893, he was five years of
age when his family moved to California. He spent the balance of his
life in the Los Angeles area, devoting much of his time to civic affairs.
Among other activities he was President of the Los Angeles Chamber
of Commerce, Building and Safety Committee, President of the local
chapter of the Masons and Contractors Exchange, a member of the
City Board of Building and Safety Commissioners. and President of
the seventh annual Construction Industries Exposition and Home Show.
Jay. an ardent and enthusiastic Mason, was raised in San Pedro
Lodge No. 332. As soon as the statutes permitted he joined all bodies
of the York Rite at San Pedro.
The unprecedented increase in population in the southern section of
Los Angeles in the nineteen-twenties impressed upon him the necessity
for another lodge in that area. In 1926 he, with others of like mind,
held several meetings to discuss the matter.. The result of these meetings
was the foundation of Jordan Lodge No. 654, of which Brother Powers
was a charter member, and was its Master in 1930. He was the architect and builder of Jordan Temple, donating his time. knowledge, experience and labor to the completion of that splendid edifice.
At the One Hundred Second Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California Jay Powers was appointed Grand Pursuivant. The
Most Worshipful Louis C. Drapeau, who made the appointment, officiated at the last rites, a~ly assisted by the Reverend Thomas Grice,
Grand Chaplain. Interment was in Inglewood Park Cemetery.
Jay Powers was in ill health for some time and was not unmindful
that the end might come at any time, and he frequently expressed a
thought that was concisely put by the poet Edward Young, who over
two centuries ago wrote:
"We see time's furrows on another's brow,
And death entrench' d, preparing his assault:
How few themselves in that just mirror see."

*

*

*

*

The philosophers through the ages have told us that all pleasure
is tinged with pain, and it is on such occasions as this Memorial Service
that this truth is thrust deep into our consciousness.
Our departed brethren have been of divergent religious and political
beliefs, but they have shared with us the knowledge of the ancient mysteries: they have given us of their time, their experience, their substance,
and their friendship. They have shared with us the fundamental truths

256

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of existence. They have believed with us in the fatherhood of God and
its corollary, the brotherhood of man. They have believed with us in
the immortality of the soul. the nature of the immortality being known
only to God.
The pleasure of their association is now a happy memory, their
passing leaves the tinge of pain. We question not our Father's right to
call them, neither will we question His wisdom when He calls us, for we
believe that all things are for the best for him who trusteth in the Lord.
The omnipresence of God was their comfort, and it is ours. The poet
Cartwright has said:
"The Lord, the high and holy One,
Is present everywhere;
Go to the regions of the sun,
And thou Wilt find him there.
"Go to the hidden ocean caves,
Where man hath never trod,
And there beneath the flashing waves
Will be thy maker, God.
"Fly swiftly on the morning's wing,
To distant realms of earth;
Wher'er young birds with sweetness sing,
And warble forth their mirth.
"Wher'er the lion makes his lair,
Or reindeer bound unseen;
Thou'lt find His ready presence there,
And know where God has been.
"All nature speaks of Him who made
The earth and air and sky;
The fruit that falls, the leaves that fade,
The flowers that bloom and die.
"The lofty mountain's lonely vale,
And mighty forest trees,
The rocks that battle with the gale,
The ever-rolling seas.
"All tell the omnipresent Lord,
The God of boundless might,
By angels loved, by saints adored,

EULOGY
GILBERT

c. DEFOREST

By ARTHUR PAULSEN, Past Grand Master
No sadder task can be allotted to any man than that of paying the
final tribute to a great friend and great Mason. But when that man is a
friend whose record speaks eloquently of his character and achievements,
it is a privilege to pay that tribute.
Gilbert C. DeForest, the 78th Grand Master of Masons in California, was born in New Lancaster, Miami County, Kansas, September 18,
1889. In his early youth he moved to Redding, California. He first
attended the schools of that city and later completed his education at the
College of Commerce in Stockton, California.
After his return to Redding he engaged actively in business and in
due time became the owner-manager of Redding Laundries, Inc., and
was so engaged until the time of his passing in January of this year.
~ng before the commencement of his Masonic career, he became an
outstanding leader in civic affairs,-<>ne distinguished by his wise counsel. his courage and his high ideals. For many years he served as a trustee
of Shasta Union High School and later of Shasta College and it may
truly be said that his zeal in support of the public schools of his county
equalled his devotion to Masonry.
'In 1911 he was united in marriage to Miss Meda Everhardt. This
marriage was blessed with the birth of two sons, Stanley and Russell
DeForest, who, with seven grandchildren survive him.
"Gil." as he was affectionately known among his many friends, was
raised in Reading Lodge No. 254 on January 17, 1922; was appointed
Senior Deacon the following year and served as Master of his lodge
during the fourth year of his Masonic career. He was a member of the
York Rite Bodies of Redding and the Scottish Rite Bodies and the Shrine
in Sacramento. At the meeting of the Supreme Council of the Thirty..
third Degree, held in Washington, D. C. in October, 1945, he was
elected to the rank and dignity of Knight Commander of the Court of
Honor.
Brother DeForest was a natural ritualist. While serving as Senior
Warden of his lodge and at a time when he had been a Master Mason
for only three years, the then Grand Lecturer commenced to prepare
him for the office of Inspector and shortly after he became a Past Master
that appointment was made. He served in that capacity until August
1936, at which time he was appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer. He held
that office until he was elected Junior Grand Warden in October, 1941.
After proceeding thru the intermediate offices he was installed as Grand
Master in October, 1944.
While he was widely and favorably known as a Ritualist among the
leaders of Craft Masonry circumstances later prevented him from becom-

258

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

ing equally well known as a Grand Master. He toiled unceasingly during
most of his Masonic life to bring ritualistic perfection to the lodges and
brethren within his district and elsewhere. For years he was a valued
member of the Ritual Committee of Grand Lodge and even among the
most proficient members of that group he spoke with the voice of
authority.
During his year as Grand Master he had the privilege of installing
his son, Stanley, as Master of his lodge and later on conferring the three
degrees upon his younger son, Russell.
But if he enjoyed those privileges while Grand Master he was denied
most others. He entered upon his duties in that high office during the
darkest hours of the Second World War. Gasoline was rationed, travel
restricted, hotel accommodations denied and all but the smallest m.eetings
prohibited. For Gil DeForest there was no trip to a ~rand Ma~ter s Conference in Washington; no journey to the Islands. Little remamed but to
stay at home and attend to the burdens of administration that beset all
Grand Masters. The Annual Communication was limited to one day.a day of work.
•
And here begins the story of an enforced slackening of Masonic
effort and the substitution of another great and increased service of love
and devotion to an invalid wife. No amount of public or fraternal work
had ever caused Gil DeForest to neglect his obligations to home or family.
He had always been a loving and considerate father, a devoted husband.
About this time Mrs. DeForest suffered a stroke and for the next &ve
years became increasingly dependent upon her husband's care and
attention. During that long and trying ordeal every resource and every
moment at his command were devoted to her need and comfort. Reluctantly, but willingly, he resigned from his office as Assistant Grand
Lecturer, which he had resumed after retiring as Grand Master, so that
he might devote his time unstintingly to her. Her passing on October 8,
1950 left him a lonesome and sorrowing man with little desire to go on
alone. For a short time subsequent to her death, he wa·s induced to
resume his duties as Assistant Grand Lecturer but he soon asked to be
relieved. His heart had crossed the great divide with the companion he
had chosen for all time.
On the evening of January 24, 1952 he installed the officers of Mount
Shasta Lodge No. 281 and appeared to be in good health and of cheerful
spirit. Early the next morning he was found sitting beside the window of
his bedroom where death had overtaken him.
Past Grand Master DeForest will long be remembered as a great
ritualist. Those of us who knew him best will remember him as a &ne
citizen; as a sympathetic, kind and loyal friend; as a fearless, practical
exponent and practitioner of the principles of Masonry--a steadfast
believer in the doctrine that Masonry must be lived as well as taught.
We shall miss his sage advice and skilled direction but we need not

mourn because he feared to go. So &rmly did he believe in the teachings
of Masonry that when the summons came he was prepared and eager to
join the devoted loved one already gone to take up her abode in that
mansion not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
The lonely vigils at the bedroom window have ceased and our brother
is now happy in his Father's house.

EULOGY
RANDOLPH VIRGINIUS WHITING

By FRANCIS V. KEESLING, Past Grand Master, Grand Treasurer
It was my privilege to have shared the very deep friendship of Randolph Whiting, and a personal tribute in a measure may be reflected in
this memorial.
The poets, Whittier, Markham and Foss sang of mountains and the
man, contemplating, we may well imagine the magnificence of mountains,
their ruggedness, tbeir natural resources including sustenance of life,
their influence on climate, and their impact on humanity. Foss appealed" Bring me men to match my mountains." Such a man was Randolph
Virginius Whiting, a grand man. Reared and living through early youth
in the region of the most wonderful mountains, verily he was a rugged
youth and ruggedness characterized his manhood.
His early education in the public schools at Quincy was followed by
studies preparatory to admission to the University of California. While
so occupied bis early initiative and determination were manifested as he
completed courses essential to admission which were in addition to those
available at the academy he attended, where he also taught at the time.
In due course he was admitted to the University and, again devoting part
time to teaching as well as participating in athletics, he was graduated
with the Bachelor's degree. Thereafter, having matriculated at Hastings
College of the Law, he graduated with the degree of L.L.B. in 1895. He
immediately engaged in the practice of law in San Francisco where he
continued with great success until his final illness. He was indeed a lawyer. The post of Reporter of California law reports is a distinguished
one. From 1897 and several years thereafter, he was Editor of California
Decisions and California Appellate Decisions, being advance sheets of
California Reports. Thereafter in 1915 he was appointed Assistant
Reporter and in 1918 Reporter, which he held until 1940.
Instinctively he was interested in public affairs. His early affiliations resulted in his being appointed Assistant District Attorney by the
Hon. Lewis F. Byington, which office under such excellent administration
was noted for its conduct. He remained until 1906, meanwhile engaged
in some investigati~n of flagrant corruption in the existing municipal
government.

261

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

During World War I he devotedly served on Draft Board No. 12
in San Francisco. He was President of the Bar Association of San Francisco, 1930-:32 and· it was he who proposed and inaugurated the permanent quarters of the Association. Early in 1930 the San Francisco
Committee on Charter Revision came into being and, at the organization
meeting, he was elected Chairman of that very representative committee
of public spirited citizens. This committee in the midst of its activities
was frustrated by opposition of some of the groups which sponsored it.
However, the need for a new charter had been impressed on the public
and there followed an election of freeholders who drafted the existing
charter. These are but a few specific instances of his public activities.
He was always to be found aligned in the cause of better government, and
was recognized as one of San Francisco's outstanding citizens.
He demonstrates his wise concept of sound government as he speaks
again from his address as Grand Master-"The spirit and genius of
America, which were developed by our revolutionary fathers, insuring
religious liberty: free speech, free press and freedom of individual action
as far as is consistent with the rights of others, have been embodied in
our Constitution, and we should cherish and jealously guard it. It has
survived the stress and strain of civil and foreign wars, internal disturbances and the attacks of foes within and without our gates. The statesmen of the world have proclaimed our instrument of government to be
the greatest that the mind of man has yet conceived, and that those who
conceived and framed it were the greatest group of statesmen that ever
gathered together at one time." * * * "Our Constitution provides a
method for orderly and deliberate change when circumstances require
it," ·a s he excoriates Communism based upon the record developed by
Congressional investigation (in 1931 ) amply quoted. He manifested
perspicacity as he warns in those days far away-"There is reason to
believe this organization has insidiously infiltrated our higher educational
institutions, public schools, civic organizations, public offices, and even
to some extent churches, the Army and Navy and other government
departments." He demands that "As Masonry has had such an initial
part in giving to us our great government,. so should it stand guard to see
that its rich gift shall not be impaired by the subversive influence of
enemies within or without the borders of our country."
He practiced out of the Lodge those great moral duties inculcated in
it. He also naturally and to the extent of human ability set a guard over
his thoughts, thereby preventing the approach of every unworthy
thought. He worshipped as an Episcopalian, and for a while was a
member of the Chapter of Grace Cathedral.
He enjoyed golfing at San Francisco Golf Club and his membership
in the Bohemian Club, with its congenial fellowship, entertaining programs at the club and ceremonials and festivities amidst the beautiful
redwoods at the Club's wonderful grove.

. His mason!c career is an extensive and distinguished one-Master,
King Solomons Lodge 260, 1909, and membership California Chapter
No. ~ R.A.'M" California Commandery No. 1 K.T., Islam Temple,
Mystic Shrine, San Francisco Bodies Scottish Rite, in which he served
as Orator during the years 1936-37, K.C.C.H., October 19, 1937. He
served on the Grand Lodge Committee on Appeals and Grievances for
many years and as chairman of the Committee on By-Laws, 1929-32,
when he was elected Junior Grand Warden, and was elevated successively until elected Grand Master, October 1934. He served from
February 1935 for one year as Chairman, Conference of Grand Masters
of Masons of the United States, Washington, D. C.
He came by his Masonic leaning very naturally. His uncle, Hon.
George C. Whiting, who had been Acting Secretary of the Interior, was
Grand Master of Masons in the District of Columbia at the time of his
death in 1867, having served in that capacity for almost eight years.
George C. Whiting Lodge No. 22, F.A.A.M. of Washington is named
for him.
His name signifies his Virginia antecedents, and he was ever a
splendid gentleman and truly upheld the traditions of the "F.F.V."
Though rugged he was most gentle. He and his delightful wife enjoyed
the society of a host of estimable and genteel friends.
Crowning the foregoing illustrious record, his greatest achievement
was when, as a student at Bowen Academy, he met the charming Mary
~oslet, daughter of the headmaster and founder, which was the beginrung of a great romance. They were married soon thereafter, and fortunately the qappy companionship extended almost through their lives, as
he survived his beloved by only a few years. He never recovered from
the great shock and the great loss. This may be understood when one
would describe the love and affection that existed as Byron described it_:_

260

"She was his life,
The ocean to the river of his thoughts
Which terminated all."

EULOGY
JoHN STEWART Ross

By JoHN R. MOORE, Past Grand Master
John Stewart Ross dwelt among the creatures of earth from May 21,
1879, to August 31, 1952. His birth occurred ~t Osceola, Nebraska,
whence he departed for California at the age of ten with his father, John
Ross, and his mother, Isabella (Stewart) Ross. He attended the free
public schools at Pomona, San Diego, and Los Angeles in the days when
it was popular to urge the minds of children toward respect for home
and country-which perhaps in later years influenced him to adopt the

262

263

PROCEEDINGS OP THE.

GRAND LODGE. OP CALIFORNIA

rigid attitude that our concern for our public school system and our
country should be coextensive and that an attack from whatever source
upon our public school system is an attack upon the foundation stones
of our country. Concerning our public schools, he said in his message as
Grand Master, " ... destructive forces work the more effectively when
other forces are asleep."

In the unstinting expenditure of his time, John S~wart Ross erected
his own Masonic monuments which will live in· the hearts and minds of
his brethren from generation to generation. He fathered and made
functional our Officers' Associations and perfected our Inspectoral
Corps. Others have talked much about Masonic education. John Ross did
not waste the English language, but by his work on the Officers' Associations with the Inspectors, he created a Masonic educational facility
which has become a keystone.

His education on the college level was obtained at the University of
California at Berkeley, where he received his A.B. degree in 1902, and
at Harvard Law School. from which he took his degree of LL.B. in 1905.
At Cal.• the charming Dora Bramlet of Fresno was his schoolmate.
who, on May 5, 1906, became his lifelong, devoted helpmate, to whom
were born four children-Isabella, Jean, Neil, and Gordon.
John Stewart Ross was a distinguished lawyer. He engaged in the
practice of his profession in Los Angeles from 1906 to 191 O; in El Centro
from 1910 to 1927; and again in Los Angeles, where he resided from
1927 to date of his passing. The legal tomes of lmperiai County, California, and other records of Imperial Valley Irrigation District; El Centro
Club of Rotary (of which he was the first president): Central Union
High School District (of which he was a member for fifteen years ) ; and
Imperial Valley Bar Association (of which he was several times president) all bear witness to the good work and deeds of our brother.
The outstanding Masonic career of John Stewart Ross spanned two
score and two years. He became a Master Mason on June 9, 1910, in
Highland Park Lodge No. 382; dimitted to El Centro Lodge No. 384 on
February 6, 1911. and served as Master in 1912-13; was Inspector of
Imperial County District 1914-27; member of Committee on Grievances
1922-26; elected Junior Grand Warden in 1927: and presided over this
Grand Lodge as Grand Master in 1930-31. He was a member of our
Committee on Jurisprudence from 1935 and served as chairman from
1946.
He served as Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of
Knights Templar of California in 1947-48 and was a member of all York
Rite Bodies-Past High Priest of El Centro Chapter No. 109 of Royal
Arch Masons; Los Angeles Council of Royal and Select Masters No. 11;
Past Commander of Saint Gabriel Conclave No. 14. Order of the Red
Cross of Constantine.
He held membership in all Scottish Rite Bodies in the Valley of Los
Angeles, earned the rank and decoration of Knight Commander of the
Court of Honor in 1919, and was coronetted a 33° Mason in 1927.
He was Past Potentative of Al Bahr Temple, Ancient Arabic Order,
Nobles of the Mystic Shrine. and received the Honorary Legion of Honor
from the Order of De Molay in 1937.

Of course, his outstanding monument is our Ross Digest, now in its
sixth edition, which is an annotated compilation of our Landmarks,
Ancient Laws, Constitution and Regulations. This arduous task was
begun by our Master Craftsman in 1928, and the first edition was presented to Grand Lodge in 1930. It is pleasing to recall a cruise in the
autumn of 1928 by a group of brothers as guests of our late Past Grand
Master, Dana Weller, on his yacht which anchored in Cherry Cove at
the island of Santa Catalina. In the late afternoon all were swimming,
diving or fishing except John Ross, who was laboring on his Digest on the
afterdeck. I went to him and said, "Come on John and have fun." He
looked at me for a while and replied, "What do you think I am having?"
Concerning the first edition presented to Grand Lodge, our then Grand
Secretary, John Whicher, recorded the following:
"The compilation has been no inconsiderable task, involving
painstaking research and intelligent labor, and is donated by the
compiler, who asks no reward. He feels that he is amply paid by
the encouragement given by his brethren of the Grand Lodge."

•

While Grand Master, Brother Ross dedicated the Masonic Memorial Monument in Forest Lawn Memorial Park at Glendale. His
earthly remains now rest at the brow of a hill near this monument.
Perhaps the most personal Masonic pleasure came to Brother Ross in
1947, when he installed his son Neil as Master of Pentalpha Lodge No.
202. At the time, a speaker quoted the appropriate question of Sophocles:
"What greater ornament to a son than a father's glory, or to a father
than a son's honorable conduct?"
John Stewart Ross was a tender, responsive husband and father and
a noble citizen. He was a faithful. zealous Mason who earned the endless
gratitude of his brothers. On the fields of honor, verity, fidelity and
justice he sought no quarter and gave none. He attracted all who were
worthy of his friendship and regard. Time will declare him among the
Masonic immortals.
Our departed brother, who walked humbly " beneath the benignant
bend of the all-seeing Eye," now dwells in speechless silence in the unseen land. In our fraternal meditation we whisper, "Soft and safe to
thee."

Grand Lodge was called on at 10:00 A.M .. the Grand Master
presiding. The Very Reverend Grand Chaplain offered the morning
prayer. The minutes of Wednesday morning, October 15th, were read
and approved.
Those committee reports which had been referred to, and reported
on by, the Committee on Segregation are here printed in full for convenience of reference.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
·. In addition to advice given to Grand Lodge officers and to committees and the subordinate bodies, the Committee on Taxation has also
aided the Grand Secretary's office in advising the subordinate lodges
with reference to the change in postal rates for Third Class postal material. Permission was obtained from the postal authorities for Grand
Lodge to flle the necessary copy of the Constitution and By-Laws in a
master flle, leaving it to the individual lodges to Ale with the local Postmaster the Petition for Exemption from the Amended Rates that went
into effect on July 1, 1952.
We again call to the attention of the lodges that a report must be
made of all employees, except ritualistic officers, wh0se wages are more
than $50.00 per calendar quarter for both the State Employment Act
and the Federal Social Security Act and to pay the taxes assessed
thereon.
During the year there have been no appreciable changes in the
rulings and interpretations relative to the Social Security Act. The
important thing is that each lodge should have its report flied and if any
objection is made, it will be promptly communicated directly to the lodge
by the governing authority.
We should state further, with particular reference to those lodges
that contemplate the creation of a non-proflt building corporation, that,
generally speaking, the Department places such a corporatiQn in the
same preferential group as is the lodge, providing the lodge owns the
stock of the corporation.
Respectfully submitted,
R. P. WISECARVER
