REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE
MASONIC CLUB HOUSE, LOS ANGELES

We set a maximum budget of $21 ,000.00 for the work and our
decorator has managed to meet it. You will be pleased, we believe, to
learn that we do not request a single cent of this cost by additional
appropriation from the grand lodge-and further, that it has been paid
without dipping into our securities, except for one five thousand dollar
bond which had been called.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the academic year which closed in June the social and
philanthropic activities of the masonically affiliated students who use
the large and beautiful club house you maintain adjacent to the campus
of U.C.L.A. were substantially the same as those outlined in our reports
to the annual communications in 1950 and 1951 . The new academic year
opened with the beginning of classes on September 22, three weeks ago.
In our reports to the 1950 and 1951 communications. we indicated
the approach of the day when major redecorating of the club house
interior would be necessary. In fact in 1951 we had moved in that
direction by the tentative selection of new carpeting for the main lounge
and foyer when information was received that carpet prices would
probably decline. We deferred action for a year during which· carpet
prices declined four times, for a total of 25%. Our information indicated
a stabilization of prices and the possibility of a rise, hence in June of
this year we resumed our task with a probable saving of three thousand
dollars on the carpets selected.
We employed a free lance decorator formerly with orie of our largest department stores and began the rather long task of selecting colors
and patterns for drapes, carpets and upholstery materials. The board
delegated the selection to a committee consisting of Directors Wilson,
Cooper, Crane and the chairman. Directors Klarquist and Smith also
attended some of the committee sessions.
The committee was fortunate in being able to call upon Bro. Russell
Northrop, Inspector, and head of the drapery department of one of the
large motion picture studios, and Bro. Lucius Croxton, also a Past
Master of Mt. Olive Lodge No. 506, and art director of another studio,
for expert advice as to colors and materials. We wish to acknowledge
our appreciation for the several midnight sessions in which they participated and so materially assisted.
The club house was built in 1929 and despite the fact that the
average yearly use exceeds 7,000 student visits, the original drapes,
furniture and carpets were still in use and presentable. This long life is
eloquent testimony as to the quality of materials originally used.
During the redecoration we replaced all drapes and carpets in the
entire building and had all the furniture redone and reupholstered. All
woodwork was repainted and seven rooms were repainted. Numerous
new items of desks, lamps, shades and wiring were also added. The
result has been most pleasing. We can best describe it by a paradox,
the visitor will find the interior completely changed and yet the club
house is the same.

Two new members of the board were nominated and elected during
the year, Bro. Charles Listenwalter, a Past Master of Westlake Lodge
No. 392, and Bros. Frank H. Reinsch, a Past Master of Liberal Arts
Lodge No. 677. The former is a retired business man with extensive
Masonic and temple experience. The latter is a member of the faculty
of the University.
We were saddened by and suffered a distinct loss in the passing of
Bro. John Stewart Ross, P.G.M., who had been a faithful member of
the board for twenty years. Suitable notice of his long service to the
craft will be made by the Committee on Necrology and we join in their
expressions.
For the ensuing year we propose the following budget and recommend that the same be referred to the Committee on Finance:

At the June meeting' of the Board of Directors, a get-togethe r conference was held with some of the present and the new officers of the
Student club at which matters of mutual interest were discussed, and
which proved helpful to both the Board and the managemen t. President
Keldgord pointed out some of the problems faced by the Club and similar collegiate organization s. Due to the expiration in the Spring of 1951
of Public Law 346, and GI Bill, many veterans were effected, and there
was a noticeable decrease in enrollment. In addition to the loss of the
veteran students, the University enrollment was further lessened by the
Federal Selective Service. Enrollment on the Berkeley campus dropped
from a peak of 24,000 to the present 16,000. This has made a marked
decrease in all campus organization s. It also resulted in a drop of the
average age of the university student. The average age estimate for
1948-49 was 23.6 years. It is now 19.6 years.
Still another factor affecting enrollment in college organization s has
been a serious drop in the financial status of students. This seriously
affected the social events at the Clubhouse which demanded considerable
individual expense. However, in other social events which involved no
particular extra individual expense, the attendance was surprisingly
large.
A committee was appointed to examine the possibility of lowering
membership fees. The result of the study was a recommenda tion that
the dues be unaltered-a dding that, whereas, the student sometimes felt
financially 0.nable to attend social functions involving individual expense, he did not feel that the membership fees are prohibitive. C?n the
contrary. he frequently voiced amazement at the low cost of membership.

Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Wofshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Berkeley, California respectfully submits its report covering the managemen t of the Club for the year 1951-1952.
The Board is pleased to report that the physical properties are in
excellent condition. The improvements and repairs planned in the budget
have been carried out satisfactoril y, and well within the budget. Your
Directors have met regularly and have worked co-operative ly to promote
the purposes for which the Club is operated.
As a part of this report, we respectfully submit the annual budget
prepared for the year 1952-53. In addition to the general operating
expenses, a number of items are included to cover upkeep and improvement~ at the Clubhouse. Because of careful managemen t by the Board
of Direc!ors, a ~ood part of these items can be cared for by savings
effected m carrying out the projects of the current budget. This is all
carefully set forth in the budget prepared for the year ending August
31, 1953, and attached hereto as Exhibit "A".

year by the student group, and wish to highly compliment President

There are a· number of problems, organizati onal in nature, to whom the
Masonic Club bas played host for a number of years. I shaH restrict .
my comments to observatio ns made during this past school year.

It appears that the Masonic Club is suffering from a malady common
to most collegiate organizati ons in 1952. Due to the fact that Public
Law 346 (commonly known as the "GI BiJJ") expired for most veterans
in the Spring of 1951, the enrollment at the University decreased noticeably. This decrease became evident in the months of Septembe r and
October of 1951.
In addition to the loss of the veteran-st udent, the enrollment of the
University has been further lessened by the Federal Selective Service:
The decreased enroHment of the University has been represente d
proportion ately by decreased membership in campus organizati ons. The
peak enroHment of the University was reached some four years ago, at
which time the Registrar' s records showed an enrollment of approximately 24,000 students on the Berkeley campus. During this past school
year, the Registrar' s .flies recorded an enrollment of approxima tely
16,000 students.

280

281

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Along with the decrease in the number of University students there
has been an accompanying alteration in the collective characteristics of
the University student. Whereas, the average age of the University
student in 1948-1949 was estimated at 23.6 years, the average age of
the student today is estimated at 19.6 years. The· sense of responsibility
and the spirit of co-operation which are developed via maturity are no
longer evident either in the classroom on campus or within the internal
structure of off-campus organizations such as the Masonic Club.
Despite the increased immaturity of the college student who supports
the campus organization, the mechanics of administration within the
organizations have become more complex. Although its appearance may
be deceiving, the administration of the University Masonic Club is not
unlike the administration of a small business concern.
Another factor which has hindered the effectiveness of campus activities has been the lack of finances among college students. As most of
you are undoubtedly aware, this factor has presented a perpetual problem to the scholar. During the past few years, however, the University
and University organizations have prospered. This prosperity, which
undoubtedly· was a result of the so-called "war boom" and "post-war
boom," ceased to exist with the beginning of the 1951-52 school year.
This factor is well-recognized in the campus community. As a result of
my campus radio program, I have had frequent opportunity to discuss
this topic with Telegraph Avenue merchants, all of whom have noticed
the decline in the student's spending power.
The student's financial problems have been manifested in the attendance at some of our social events. Events which· have drawn capacity
crowds in past years were poorly attended this year. On the other hand,
events which in past years have attracted little or no attention were
surprisingly well-attended. It is noteworthy that the affairs which demanded considerable individual expense (i.e. rental of tuxedos, corsages,
etc.) were the same events at which our attendance figures were low.
I would say that our variety show, our initiation dinner-dances, our
parent's night, and our Club picnic were given the greatest support by
the mem~ship. Our reception for the Grand Master, Most Worshipful
Louis C. Drapeau, was poorly-attended for two ( 2 ) reasons: first of
all, the reception for the Grand Master is an event which requires considerable expense on the part of the student: also, our reception for the
Grand Master was held during the same evening that the University
presented the Junior Prom. The date for our Grand Master's Reception
was chosen by the Grand Master in mid-November.
. ·
Although the attendance was not exceptionally large for our Grand
Master's Recepti?n, we felt that the Grand Master's performance, his
personal charm and his excellent choice of topics were sufficient compensation for the effort and expense connected with the reception.

.During the fall semester, I appointed a committee to examine the
possibility of lowering membership fees; the committee was chairmanned
by Robert Asnard, one of our most capable and most experienced members. After investigation and questioning among the membership, the
committee recommended that the dues rate be unaltered. Whereas, the
student sometimes felt financially unable to attend social functions, he
did not feel that the membership fees were prohibitive; on the contrary,
he frequently voiced amazement at the low cost of membership.
Whereas, our social functions have not always been well-attended,
the everyday use of the Clubhouse has continued at a high rate. A high
percentage of our members utilize the Clubhouse facilities four-to-five
times during the school week. It is interesting to note that the Clubhouse
is used 'Very little during the weekday evenings or on Sundays, excepting
the Sundays during which activities are scheduled. After six o'clock in
the evening, the Clubhouse ceases to serve as any kind of a studentcenter. The same situation, only to a lesser degree, is true on Sundays.
From the standpoint of economy, the use of the Masonic Club
facilities during Sundays and evenings does not warrant the operation
of the Clubhouse at those times, nor does it compensate for the cost of
utilities consumed during the evenings and on Sundays.
I

Attached hereto you will find the Report of the President of the
University Masonic Club: this report covers the school year 1951-52.
I have written this letter of introduction in the hope that it will clarify
any questions which may arise with the perusal of the attached report.
In preparing the aforementioned report, I have tried to submit unbiased
material-there has been no attempted "whitewash."
In closing, I should like to express my gratitude to each of you, the
members of the Board of Trustees, for the sincere interest that you have
shown in the Club. Your e.fforts have been appreciated greatly: it has
been a pleasure to work with you during my term as President of the
University Masonic Club.

* In addition to the items enumerated above, monthly business meetings.
as described elsewhere within this report. were held. Council meetings.
meetings of the pledge classes. and variety show rehearsals rounded
out a very full social calendar for the year.
I. New Equipment:
Various items of equipment were obtained for use in the Clubhouse throughout the year. New Sling cabinets and a new tablemodel radio were purchased by the membership, in addition to the
purchase of new equipment for the ping-pong and billiard facilities.

284

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Perhaps the most important addition to the equipment of the
Clubhouse was the erection of the long-needed outside bulletin
board. This board, complete with its fluorescent lighting. was made
possible largely through the efforts of C. Melvin Davis and Marvin Martin, our representatives from Henry Morse Stephens
Lodge.
·
II. Organization:
In accordance with the provisions of the Club Constitution, the
Executive Council was elected during the regularly-appointed
elections. The appointive officers were named soon after the elections. Because of ever-changing conditions and new demands, the
tasks of the Excutive Council were numerous.
Heretofore established office hours for Council members were
maintained throughout the year. During his office hour, the Council member acted as receptionist for the Club.
III. Membership:
According to the files maintained by our membership secretaries, our total membership for the year was 385 members . .This
figure does not include a number of life-members who also used
the Club.
As a part of the membership drive, the previously-established
"pledge classes" were continued. For the first time in a number
of years, the Club succeeded in locating a booth at the end of
registration line at the University. For many years this booth was
made impossible by administrative "red tape" at the University.
IV. Snack Bar:
The downstairs lunch counter. commonly referred to as the
"Snack Bar," has operated during the year with a minimum of
difficulty. Of all the Club activities, perhaps the Snack Bar enjoys
the most constant patronage by the members.
V. Activities, Recreational and Social:
For the first time in two years, a ping-pong tournament was
held among the Club members. The billiard facilities and other
recreational equipment were utilized a great deal during the year.
The social program was varied and well-rounded. ( For information not found in the social activities listed below, please refer
to the attached social calendar for the year 1951-52..)
1. Open Houses:
For a two-week period at the beginning of each semester,
the Masonic Club held open house . festivities. The entire
campus public was invited to attend these functions. Approximately seven-hundred students visited the Masonic Club during the open houses.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

285

2; Other Visitors:
During the year, approximately thirteen-hundred individuals, excluding the aforem~ntioned students who attended
open house functions. visited the Clubhouse. Many of these
visitors were parents of members, visiting brethren, and other
interested individuals.
3. General Business Meetings:
As is required by the Club Constitution, general business
meetings were held once monthly during the entire school year.
The membership was invited and encouraged to attend these
meetings and the meetings were held in conjunction with either
a dinner or a coffee hour.
4. Movies:
.
Because of our recent acquisition of a new Bell and Howell
16 m.m. projector, we inaugurated a program of showing motion pictures on Sunday evenings: The pictures were shown for
a nominal charge and the films were obtained through a com·
mercial film distributor in San Francisco.
5. Philanthropic Projects:
In keeping with the Club's heretofore established policy,
the Masonic Club spent a certain amount of time in philanthropic endeavor. During the Fall semester, a party for spastic
children was held at Christmastime. The party was a huge
success and everyone, including guests and hosts, had an enjoyaJ>le time.
During the Spring semester, a number of Club members.
armed with appropriate stage props and a questionable degree
of Thespian talent, journeyed out to the Masonic Home at
Decoto, where a variety show was presented.
In addition to the above-mentioned activities, a number of
the Club members, under the supervision of the Upper Division
Women's Representative, donated blood for use in Korea. The
blood donations were arranged through the cooperation of the
Berkeley Chapter of the American Red Cross.
VI. Publicity:
It is felt by a number of interested persons, including the retiring Council and the retiring President, that the Club's greatest
problem is found in the realm of publicity activities. Despite the
very fine efforts of the publicity director and a costly publicity
program, it is felt that the Club does not receive sufficient pub...
licity. Any publicity which the Club has received through the
efforts of the Grand Master, the Board of Trustees, the Masters
of various Blue Lodges, and. other sources has been appreciated
immensely.

286

As a part of our publicity program for the year 1951-52, the
members of the Club utilized the University newspaper, announcements on a campus radio show, bulletins of the several Blue
Lodges, the newly-erect ed outside bulletin board, book matches,
pamphlets, and an always-effective program based on word-ofmouth publicity.

VII. Constitutional Changes:
Two years ago, in the belief that it would facilitate the management of the Club, the organization was put on a yearly basis.
This year, after a trial of two year's duration, the yearly basis was
abandoned in favor of a return to managemen t via a semester plan.
In keeping with the demands being made by the Selective
Service Act, certain other provisions regarding qualifications for
office were adopted by the membership at the mid-year elections.

.
.
Correspond ence with the Masters of the resp~tive lodg.es urging

Brother Arthur S. Crites, a member of the committee, resides at
Bakersfield and is personally well acquainted with the territory involv~d.

local brethren, and bas also kept informed as to the Masonic Temple
at Bakersfield.
The Temple at Tehachapi and all of its furnishings were destroyed
by the shock of July 21, 1952. At the same time the Temple at Maricopa
was seriously damaged, and after-:;hocks have rendered it so unsafe as
to require its demolition.
The Temple at Bakersfield suffered somewhat from the shock of
July 21, 1952: these injuries were seriously aggravated by the shock of
August 22, 1952. It is our understandi ng, however-~nd we p~ayerfu~ly
hope that it is correct-tha t the injuries can and will be satis~a~tonly

out the stricken area with inspiring courage and fortitude. Ever since

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SOJOURNERS
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Your Committee which was appointed a year ago and known as the
"Sojourners Committee of Grand Lodge," wishes to report as follows:
The work of this new Committee, in a new field of endeavor, has
been most interesting and we trust, beneficial to the local Lodges. and
an asset to this Grand J uridiction.
For many years, Masons from other jurisdictions were gradually
coming to California, here to make their homes, a few joined our Lodges,
others attended our meetings, and many became lost to the fraternity.
In recent years, the influx has not been gradual. thousands have been
pouring into our metropolitan areas, others into our tourist centers and
rural districts, some to find employment, others to enjoy retirement. Our
Grand Masters have felt for many years that these Masons who have
come to live with us, with no intentions of returning to their former
homes. should be encouraged to join our Lodges near which they live and
become a part of this Grand Jurisdiction. And so local committees were
formed in every Lodge "at the request of our present Grand Master",
whose duties were to see that all sojourning Masons were invited to
attend Lodge, and when they attended were made to feel welcome.
This committee has held several meetings, with Lodge committees,
and at the open forums many interesting suggestions were brought to
light.
The members of the committee were assigned Lodges within a certain
radius of their homes, and have been a great help in arranging programs,
and speakers.
Many of our Lodges have set aside special nights where the sojourners have been given a special invitation to be their guest with free
meals and entertainment. If the sojourners are made to feel at home,
they will want to join our Lodges, and if our Lodges are friendly and
courteous the thousands of sojourners in our midst will become paying
members.
The work of the Committee can only be to assist and suggest; the
work must be done by the individual Lodge. Masters must appoint their
sojourners committees and see that they function. The Lodges that
have reported to us are only a few of the many who have cooperated in
this work, but have failed to report.
They all indicate that their efforts have been well repaid. Interesting
breakfast meetings have been held, to which many of the lodge committees responded and were present, and according to all reports much good
was accomplished.
·

293

It is impossible for your committee to measure the returns in one
short year; time and Grand Lodge reports will show whether the effort
was worthwhile, but the Lodges that have worked are the Lodges which
have benefited.
No appropriation was made for the work of this Committee and so
its efforts have been limited; Lodges must be contacted, and it is impossible for the members of your Committee to do this in person. Letters
with suggestions and advice should be sent periodically; for this reason,
your Committee recommends that if this Committee is to be continued,
the sum of one hundred dollars ( $100.00.) be appropriated to this
work, and that a sojourners committee be established in each Masonic
Lodge as a standing committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DeMOLAY

It is further recommended that the sum of $750. be appropriated to
cover its necessary expenses for the coming year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
.
During this masonic year, your special committee on DeMolay has
again endeavored to carry out in a careful manner the original purpose
of the committee as set forth by the most worshipful Grand Lodge of
1946.
The over all results have been most gratifying.
The program as developed in the San Diego area is of particular
interest at this time.
Through the efforts of the Grand Lodge committeeman, Kay V.
Smith and the inspectors of that area, there was passed last year a resolution by the San Diego County Masonic Officers Association. The
resolution stated that the third week of February of each year be set
aside to be known as "DeMolay Week". That all Blue Lodges in the
area be urged to remain dark during this week. That all Masters urge
their members to attend at least one DeMolay meeting during this week.
Due to lack of time necessary to prepare for this week, the first
DeMolay week met with only moderate success. However, the second
annual DeMolay week which was observed in February 1952, was an
outstanding success. Each Masonic lodge in the county visited a
DeMolay chapter where one of the DeMolay degrees .was exemplified.
A summary of the week showed 583 Masons attended one or more
meetings, 237 of whom were witnessing DeMolay work for the first time.
The Committee notes with interest the continuance of the outstanding work in Southern California and particularly that area in and around
Los Angeles under the guidance of Honorable Judge William R. McKay
of the Grand Council of the Order of DeMolay.
A greater interest is now being shown by the Blue Lodges of the
East Bay area, under the guidance of committeeman Edwin R. Brooks
and the Masters and Wardens' Association of that area.
Notice also should be made of the increase in the DeMolay membership and a stronger programming in and around the Sacramento district.
This, in a large part, is due to the zeal of committeeman Alvin E. Clark.
Nevertheless, in view of the satisfactory progress as reported, DeMolay is losing many of its members and potential members to the
Armed Services.
In addition to committee members mentioned so far in this report,
Brothers Moyers of Fresno, Butterfield of Riverside, Honaker of Compton, Flierl of Hayward, and Peters of Los Angeles have been of assistance in informing the Blue Lodges of the DeMolay activities in their
respective areas and desire to be of assistance in carrying out the plan
as originally adopted.
It is recommended that the committee be continued, and its numbers
be determined by the most worshipful Grand Master.

Fraternally submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Information reports as follows:
Your Committee reports that the four booklets distributed to the
candidates during their initiatory period continue to stimulate interest,
and that this portion of its program seems soundly established.
At the f 950 Communication your Committee presented with its report
the manuscript of "707 Questions and Answers about Freemasonry"
with the recommendation that this manuscript be referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and to the Committee on Ritual
for their examination and recommendations, and it was so referred.
As this was our Centennial Communication, your Committee realized
that there would be insufficient time for these Committees to consider
the manuscript and to report back at that session of Grand Lodge.
The report of your Committee to Grand Lodge at its 1951 Communication referred to the submission of the manuscript the year preceding, but no report was presented by the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes or by the Committee on Ritual on the subject. Your
Committee realizes that it is no small task to consider carefully a manuscript of approximately one hundred pages. However, your Committee
has several other projects in prospect, including an Essay on Freemasonry to which reference was made in the Committee's report of last
year, but it is felt that nothing further should be submitted until the
work now presented has been approved or disapproved.
No doubt the efforts of your Committee in .behalf of Masonic in-

296

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

formation of necessity must be slow, and that the time of busy men to
review critically its work is limited, but your Committee is in duty bound
to point out that a program of education must be kept moving in order
to sustain interest. and that too long a delay in its operations is likely to
breed indifference and to cause a loss of momentum. Therefore, the
pending manuscript should be disposed of in order that ·y our Committee
can proceed with its work.
Your Committee recommends:
1. That subject to approval by Grand Lodge of the "707 Questions
and Answers about Freemasonry," the sum of $5000 be appropriated or added to the Grand Secretary's printing appropriation
for the publication of this book; that copies thereof be distributed
free to each lodge in number approximately 1% of the membership of such lodge, with a minimum of 3 copies to each lodge,
and that additional copies be sold to lodges or members at approximately the cost to be estimated by the Grand Secretary.

ensuing Masonic year the sum of $500.00.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON MEMORIAL
TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
·In rendering the report of this special committee, it seems in order to
review briefly at this point what has transpired to date since the committee was first appointed in 1948. The Grand Lodge is on record that:
1 ) The facilities at 25 Van Ness Avenue are totally inadequate
to hold an Annual Communication.
2) The Grand Lodge is continuing to grow; hence, the need for
more adequate facilities.
3) The Civic Auditorium in which we are now meeting is also
inadequate because it is a general purpose building, and does
not lend itself to the peculiar requirements of this great fraternity; hence, is not the solution to our permanent housing
problem.
4) The Grand Lodge has made available to this committee the
balance of the War Relief Fund, raised during World War II
in the amount of $158,507.H.
5) The Grand Lodge approved a 50c per capita tax at its last
Annual Communication.
6) The committee was authorized to expend moneys for investigition and study purposes, subject to prior approval of the
Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, and Chairman of
the Committee on Finance.
Your committee has continued its efforts and while one of our valued
members, Brother Henry J. Brunnier, engineer, has not been able to
attend meetings since last June, he has been a most valued consultant.
At this point, I think it well to record that while his inability to serve
is a distinct loss to the committee and to this Grand Lodge, he is bringing great credit and honor to this Grand Lodge. and the State of California, for he has been honored by his election to the high office Qf
President of Rotary International.
While this committee officially consists of Brothers Henry J. Brunnier. James Hurst and the Chairman, we have sought counsel from many
Brethren, particularly those possessing special abilities in connection
with our assignment. Since our last Annual Communication, we have
held eleven special meetings and have held numerous unscheduled meetings.
We are greatly indebted to Past Grand Master Francis V. Keesling
for his wise counsel and advise, and for the use of his office as a meeting
place. Other outstanding men of Grand Lodge invited to attend some
of our meetings when available were the Grand Master, the elected
officers of Grand Lodge, the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
Brother Albert Roller, Architect, and others.

As was indicated in our 1951 report to this Grand Lodge, the committee has come to the conclusion that pethaps the best interests of this
Grand Lodge could be served by purchasing a building already in
existence and converting it to our use. This, we have concluded, is
sound, and have located such a structure. In order to come to this
Grand Lodge with a specific recommendation, we employed the services
of Mr. Albert F. Roller, architect, to make a study for the committee.
In this regard, he utilized the engineering offices of Mr. Henty J. Brunnier.
Our agreement with Mr. Roller is that he will bill us for work done,
at cost, and if the building is purchased and he is employed as the architect, his preliminary expense will become a part of regular architect's fees.
Your committee has progressed sufficiently with our sturdy to submit to you for consideration and approval the purchase of ......................
...................................., a property already in existence.

It is intended that the foyer shall be executed in colorful marbles and
terrazzo. Flanking the lobby are lounges for smoking, off of which will
be located the public toilet rooms; two committee rooms and two check
and coat rooms are available from the lobby, as are credential and registration spaces.
Thought has been given to providing facilities that would make the
auditorium attractive for limited conventions or public lectures, requiring
approximately 2,500 seats, and for which there is considerable demand.
From this source revenue could be secured in the interim between Grand
Lodge Sessions.
The auditorium will be designed with every thought directed toward
the achievement of perfection in acoustics and lighting.
The work area - particularly the Grand Master's station and the
Altar - has an unobstructed view from any seat in the building.
The work area indicated on the plans is flanked by two draped processional entrances leading from a spacious robing room. This is one
of eleven large committee or display rooms intended to be provided at
least in part with movable partitions so that two or three of the areas
can be combined if the need requires.
Two of these rooms are intended to serve as the offices of the Grand
Master and Deputy Grand Master, and one as an office for the Grand
Secretary and his staff.
This area can be reached from the main office building lobby without
passing through the auditorium. Separate toilet facilities are provided
for this area. •
The preparation of the plans and the work of remodeling the building
will take about twenty months, so that the first possible session of Grand
Lodge in this location would be in 1954.
The land area can be easily adapted to our use in that it has streets
on three sides. The plot contains 21 ,656.25 sq. ft. The value of the land
is conservatively appraised at $1,000,000.00. The estimated reproduction cost of the buildings in a recent appraisement made for insurance
purposes was $3,368,970.00.
The buildings are now 100% occupied and it has been estimated by
experts that the office building can be operated to show a net return of ·
$75,000.00 per annum after allowing for 10% vacancy. It is hoped that
we can purchase the property, make the necessary alterations, furnish
and equip it for approximately $3,000,000.00.

The site of the proposed Memorial Temple of the Grand Lodge of
California, Free and Accepted Masons, is situated in the downtown
business area. The property has two buildings located on it, one a onestory auditorium type building with a contiguous twelve-story office
building. These lend themselves admirably well for the proposed purpose.
The real estate on which the two buildings are situated is one of the
few remaining large parcels of downtown financial district property on
which a future increment of value is a real potential.
The following is a description of what is contemplated in the plans
for the Memorial Temple.
The exterior facades executed in gray and black polished granite
will present an imposing modern building. The landscaped areas on
the east and west will further complement the character of the structure.
Upon entering from ............................ Street, one will find himself in
a spacious foyer on street level with an imposing grand staircase centering in the lobby and leading to the lower concourse, which is in two tiers
and provides 1,250 seats.
The balcony is reached by four staircases and seats 1,220 people.
The total seating in opera-type chairs is 2,470.

Recognition of Grand Lodges
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes begs leave to
report as follows:
Your committee has made diligent inquiry regarding the merits of
the foreign jurisdictions that have applied for the recognition of this
Grand Lodge, and finds that several of said jurisdictions are entitled to
our recognition and amity.
This Grand Lodge, in 1923, established the following rules for
recognition of foreign Grand Lodges:
1. That the foreign Grand Lodge in question represents a substantial unity of the Freemasons of the territory over which it
assumes jurisdiction; i.e., the Country, Province, or State.

300B

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

2. That it has been lawfully organized by three or more regular Lodges.
3. That it is independent, having entire dogmatic and administrative authority over resident Masons and the symbolic Degrees within its territorial jurisdiction.
4. That its ritual is fundamentally in accord with the ancient
landmarks, customs, and usages of the Craft. This involves:
A. Monotheism;
B. The Volume of the Sacred Law a part of the furniture of
the Lodge;
C. Secrecy;
D. The symbolism of the operative art;
E. The division of symbolic Masonry into the three degrees
of Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft, and Master Mason.
legend of the Third Degree.
The
F.
5. That it makes Masons of men only.
6. That it is non-sectarian and non-political; i.e., that its
dominant purposes are charitable, benevolent, educational.
and religious.

THE GRAND LoDGE OP ARGENTINA

This Grand Lodge was founded in September, 1858, and its jurisdiction consists of the whole of the Argentine Republic. It is independent of
all other bodies and confines itself to the symbolic grades. It fulfills all the
requirements of the Code of Rules of this Grand Lodge. It has 45 Lodges
and 2,700 members. It is sovereign and independent of any other body
in its jurisdiction, except in the case of the District Grand Lodge of the
United Kingdom of Great Britain, which has 40 Lodges and works in
English and has had a treaty with the Grand Lodge of Argentina since
the year 1860, that is to say, 93 years. The two bodies work in perfect
_
amity and concord.
Your Committee finds the Grand Lodge of Argentina to be entitled
to recognition and, therefore, moves that it be recognized.

THE UNITED GRAND LoDGE OP GERMANY

All the Lodges recognized by us in Germany prior to the World War
went out of existence, and now, after a lapse of 12 years, Masonry is
re-established in Germany and the Provincial Lodges of Bavaria, the
Hanseatic Provinces, Lower Saxony, the Provincial Lodge of Nordrhein,
and the Provincial Lodge of Wurtt-Baden have united in forming the
United Grand Lodge of Germany. They have 10,105 members and 205
Lodges, and are on a firm basis and conform to all the requirements for
recognition set by California.
The United Grand Lodge of Germany has been recognized by 50
foreign Grand Lodges, including Missouri, Utah, Louisiana, Connecticut, New Jersey, South Carolina, Michigan and Rhode Island, as well
as several other American Grand Lodges.
We. therefore, recommend that the Grand Lodge of California
recognize the United Grand Lodge of Germany.

Should We Have a Judge Advocate?
Your Committee, to which was referred the Recommendation .and
Ruling No. 2 of the Grand Master's message, reports as follows:
The Grand Master reported to us that our Junior Grand Warden,
Henry C. Clausen, had done an outstanding job in handling the legal
work during this year. He recommended that a special committee be
appointed by the incoming Grand Master to study the desirability of
establishing an office to carry on this legal work and to report its findings and recommendations to the next communication of this Grand
Lodge.
The calls upon the Grand Master for rulings and decisions are becoming more numerous and burdensome and this suggestion may lead
to a solution to the problem.
We. therefore, move that the Grand Master's recommendation be
adopted.

Revision of Section 5 3
Your Committee to which was referred the resolution to amend subdivision 9 of Section 53 of Ross Digest reports as follows:
The proposal would eliminate from the duties of an Inspector the
requirement that he inspect the books of his Lodges and report the result to the Grand Master.
The proponents of the legislation were under the impression that
the requirement for inspection included something in the nature of an
audit. Your Committee feels that the Inspectors should, at least once
a year, inspect the books of their Lodges to see that proper up-to-date
records are being kept and the results of the inspection should be reported to the Grand Master through the Grand Lecturer. or otherwise.
Such an inspection does not require an audit of the books. unless such
an audit appears desirable from the inspection.
We, accordingly. recommend that the resolution be not adopted,
and move the adoption of this report.
Adopted.

Adopted.
Repeal of Section 501
Your Committee, to which was referred the resolution to repeal Section 501 of Ross Digest. reports as follows:
Sections 50, 51 and 52 of Ross Digest require the Grand Lecturer
and the Assistant Grand Lecturers to see that the ritual is strictly conformed to and Section 248 of Ross Digest gives to Grand Lodge the sole
power to change the ritual.
Section 501 of Ross Digest implies that the Master of a Ladge may
omit a portion of the opening and closing ceremonies. These words
were not necessary to the decision and they have caused some confusion.
Since uniformity and clarity in our laws and decisions is most de..
sirable and for many years, our Ritual Committee has held that no part of
the esoteric work in the opening and closing ceremonies can be omitted,
we move that Section 501 be deleted from Ross Digest.
Adopted by 5/6 vote.
Dedication of Public School Buildings
Your Committee to which was referred the resolution relating to a
ceremony for dedicating Public School Buildings reports as follows:
The resolution proposes that a Committee be appointed to write a
form of ceremony especially designed for the dedication of Public School
Buildings. Masons are particularly interested in our public schools and
it seems proper that we should have available for our use a dedication
ceremony directly relating to Public School Buildings.
We. therefore, recommend the resolution to you and move its adoption.
Adopted.

305

Revision of Section 25 5
Your Committee, to which was referred the proposal of the Grand
Secretary to revise Section 255 of Ross Digest to clarify and revise the
statement as to those members of Lodges whose dues may be remitted,
reports as follows:
The proposed legislation clarifies the section to eliminate some misunderstandings. permits the remission of the dues of a brother who has
been in good standing for 40 years regardless of need and raises the age
from 70 to 75 for the remission of dues for special service to the Lodge.
The revised section reads as follows:
A Lodge may annually remit the accrued dues of those of its members
who are unable to pay them.
A Lodge may remit in advance the dues of those of its members who
have been members in good standing in a Lodge or Lodges of this Judisdiction for a period of 40 years or more.
A Lodge may remit in advance the dues of those of its members over
the age of 75 years who have rendered special service to the Lodge and
who merit such remission.
Remission of dues in advance as herein provided must be by special
resolution. applicable only to the particular member, or members, whose
dues are to be remitted.
A Lodge shall not remit the dues of its members, or any of them, for
any stated period, nor in advance, except as herein provided.
We move the adoption of the revised section.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence in the
above recommendations.
Report adopted by 5/6 vote.

Brother Claude Lenz, Past Master of Ionic Lodge No. 520 has presented a lengthy resolution, which we had best summarize.

body, a constituent lodge, temple association, are lawful deductions on

expeditiously and possibly with better results by that committee than
by adoption of the resolution. We, therefore, offer the following motion:

Committee on Taxation for exploration and a report to our annual communication in 1953.
Adopted.

Increasing Membership of Committee on Lodge Financing
The Grand Master under the heading of Recommendation No. 3,
has recommended increasing the membership of the Committee on Lodge
Financing.
The name of this committee is the source of much confusion as to
its duties and it is frequently confused with our Committee on Finance.
It is not a committee on paternalism, it does not finance lodges and is
not concerned with the finance of any lodge except that portion which
has to do with building and improving temples.
The work of the committee is very extensive, it requires numerous
conferences with lodge members and building committees. It must cover
the entire state and is involved in every temple building project, acquisition and improvement.
We heartily agree that its membership should be increased from the
present seven, including a Master and Warden, to nine including the
Master and Warden members and recommend that you adopt legislation
to that effect when it is presented.
Adopted.

In his annual message last year, the then Grand Master, Brother
Arthur Paulsen, recommended that provision be made in our jurisdiction
for research lodges. which would resemble a conventional lodge, but
would do no degree work. They were to study Freemasonry, prepare
papers and addresses and do research work. Complete proposed legislation was offered.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes approved the
policy inherent in the recommendation. The matter was the subject of
spirited discussion and the proponents acquiesced in a modified proposal
that the matter be deferred to this Communication, and that in the interim, the Grand Master be authorized to grant not more than two dispensations for research lodges under such terms and conditions as he
might prescribe. The Grand Master promulgated regulations which were
substantially the legislation which had been proposed and issued two
dispensations, one lodge to be located in northern California, and one
in southern California.
The two lodges were instituted on the same evening in May. Under
the regulations, these lodges meet once a month and hold a stated meeting four times a year.
The lodge in northern California has prepared material on the Constitution of the United States and this material has been presented to a
number of lodges during September. The lodge in southern California
has developed a panel on Masonic symbolism. It was given in the lodge,
repeated in the wilds of Ventura and in Inglewood Lodge. It has also
developed a panel on the pros and cons of discussions of political ques-

Disaster Assistance
- Nine officers and past officers of four constituent Lodges offer a
resolution which in substance proposes:
A levy of $1 upon each applicant for degrees and each affiliating
brother from another jurisdiction, for the purpose of assisting a certain
class ?f lod~es in ~aintaining their lodge buildings and for lending
financial assistance m cases of financial misfortune.
The resolution pro~ides that 40% of the accumulated fund may be
loaned on a deferred interest-bearing repayment basis, ana that 60%
of the fund shall be invested and the income therefrom expended by gift
to lodges in financial distress.
. Your ~ommittee feels that these special levies are generally un~esirable. It is very easy to explain to a candidate a levy of a special
item of $1 for the George Washington Memorial Endowment Fund, but
a levy of $1 toward a fund to maintain or rehabilitate poverty striken
lodges of our own jurisdiction is, to say the least, not very good public
relations and is apt to cause some wonderment on the part of the applicant.
Grand Lodge has always been generous to its historic lodges when

Relief for Tehachapi Lodge No. 313

We have before us a resolution offered by Brother Laurence B. Ruppers, Worshipful Master of Vermont Square Lodge No. 515, which in
substance proposes that Tehachapi Lodge No. 313 be authorized to solicit
lodges and individual brethren for subscriptions to assist them in rebuilding their temple and also to manufacture and sell gavels and ornaments made from the timbers of their destroyed building.
The earthquake of July 21, 1952, and the subsequent tremors completely destroyed the Masonic Temple at Tehachapi. California.
With one or two exceptions. it has been the policy of this Grand
Lodge not to permit such solicitations, and it has always been our policy
that lodges should not engage in business enterprises. Tragic as has been
the destruction. we believe that this particular resolution should not be
.
passed.
Tehachapi Lodge No. 313 should be continued in existence as an
active lodge. It has been a healthy lodge: its members are good active
and enthusiastic Masons. ·The community itself is an appropriate place
for a Masonic Lodge and a proper Lodge Hall is essential to the welfare of the Lodge. However, with all this, Tehachapi Lodge needs and
deserves assistance. This is not a case of destruction by fire, with the
brethren of the Lodge being culpably negligent in not carrying adequate
insurance. It appears to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that here is a clear case where the Lodge deserves the assistance of
Grand Lodge on a cooperative basis.
We, therefore, recommend that the particular resolution be not
adopted, but that the problem of the relief of Tehachapi Lodge No. 313,

312

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

under these circumstances, be referred to our Committee on Lodge Finances and our Finance Committee, with the request that these co·mmittees present a plan of cooperative assistance in the construction of a
new Masonic Tem;>le at Tehachapi.
It is our thought in this respect that, with a building plan approved
by the Committee on Lodge Finances, the Grand Lodge should contribute
an appropriate limited sum on a cash-matching basis with the funds
otherwise available to the Lodge, without a solicitation, and that the
brethren of the Lodge, in addition to their cash contributions, also by
personal services contribute as much work toward reconstruction as may
be reasonably possible.
Referred to Committees on Finance and on Lodge Financing.

Oversize Lodges
The Grand Master in his annual message, under the heading of
recommendation No. 1, calls attention to his opinion that there comes
a time when lodges become too large and he points out some of the
losses which such lodges suffer. He states that he should like to have
consideration given to restrictive legislatio~ upon the number of candidates which larger lodges might receive in a year and the duty to sponsor
and foster new lodges. However, he recommends for the present, the
appointment of a special committee to study the problem and report at
the next annual communication.
Several Grand Masters have called this situation to the attention of
the craft, but the number of groups petitioning to form new lodges has
not been in proportion to the increase in membership. The last printing
of membership totals of all our lodges is as of July 31, 1951, more than
a year ago, but it discloses surprising conditions. Of course the figures
about to be given will be larger when the proceedings of this communication are printed, but as of July 31, 1951, 128 lodges had a membership in
excess of 500: 18 had a membership in excess of 800: 14 had more than
900 members: 10 had more than 1,000 members: 4 had more than 1100:
1 had more than 1200. The new compilation for this year will probably
show that 4 lodges now have more than 1200 members.
San Diego is probably the most crowded. The nine lodges in that
community in the order of their age had memberships of 977, 1189, 1204,
710, 559, 498, 601, 611 and the baby, 157. The growth has been recent,
but there has been only one new lodge formed there since 1927, a period
of 25 years. In Los Angeles and other communities, the average membership of all lodges is in excess of 500.
In keeping with the recommendations of the Grand Master, we offer
the following resolution:
·
Be it resolved, that the incoming Grand Master be requested
to appoint a special committee to study the problem of large
memberships in our lodges and report its 8ndings and recommendations at our next annual communication.
Adopted.

Plural Membership
A resolution to amend secti_on 163 of our ordinances has been presented by Brothers John H. Ferguson, P;M., Long Beach Lodge No. 327,
and Arthur J. Sissons, P . M .. Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674.
The purpose of this resolution appears to be two-fold: first, to clarify
existing provisions which permit a member of a California lodge to be

317

a member of a lodge in another jurisdiction, if the other jurisdiction permits dual membership, and secondly, to permit a member of a California
lodge to belong to more than one lodge in this jurisdiction at the same
time. The first purpose does not modify our present policy: the second
does.
The number of jurisdictions which permit a member to belong to more
than one lodge in the same jurisdiction has steadily increased over recent
years. As of January 1, 1952, the following jurisdictions permit a Mason
to belong to more than one lodge in their jurisdiction: Alabama, Arizona,
Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida. Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts,
Michigan, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New York, North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, a total of twenty-two.
In Canada of the nine grand jurisdictions eight permit their members
to belong to more than one lodge.
We know that in England membership may be held in as many
lodges as one desires. We are not advised what is the rule in other
countries.
Of the eight jurisdictions in Canada which have been mentioned,
six place no limitation on the number of memberships held at one time;
two jurisdictions limit the member to two memberships.
In the United States thirteen jurisdictions place no limitation on the
number of lodges in the same jurisdiction to which a Mason may belong.
These are: Alabama, Arizona, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts.
Michigan, North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South
Dakota, Virginia and Wisconsin.
Some years ago we of California adopted legislation permitting dual
membership, one of which must be in another jurisdiction. Last year
we permitted a dual membership in this jurisdiction of a limited nature
in connection with the two research lodges.
We can appreciate that there might be one or more .reasons why a
given brother might wish to belong to more than one lodge in this jurisdiction. The most obvious is that he desires to, for reasons of friendship,
interest or close associations. We all know that some of our brethren
are transferred as to their places of employment from one part of the
state to another. Family situations or health reasons may be the cause
of moving from one place to another.
Sentiment, family traditions or service as an officer may be suffiicient reasons for not demiting from the lodge at the former residence,
but there may be a strong and commendable desire to become a member
of a lodge in the new place of residence. It is indeed difficult to see
wherein Freemasonry would suffer one iota from permitting the additional affiliation in any of these instances. It would seem that there
might be benefits to be gained from the interest and activity in the new
community.

318

319

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

There is yet a further situatioo in which benefit might accrue from
a change of our policy. When a group seeks to form a new Lodge, it
and this grand body will benefit if the first Master and even other officers are experienced Past Masters. At present, it is difficult for such
a group to find such qualified leaders because many are loathe to sever
their memberships in the lodge they served as Master. This legislation
might make them available.
While no member of this committee feels a present desire to acquire
membership in any additional lodge it does not see that it should say
to a brother who is willing and desires to pay dues in more than one
lodge and assume the responsibilities and duties of additional membership: No, you can't do it.
We have examined all the privisions in the proposed legislation and
approve the policy thereof. We recommend its adoption.

The proponents of the amendments moved their adoption in the form

Method of Voting
A resolution has been introduced ·by Brother Ralph C. Hine, our
Grand Orator. It recites in its preamble that our law presently requires
that when a matter is referred to committee or more than one committee that the committee or committees must report before a vote is
taken on the questions. It points out that sometimes a vote is taken on
the committee report rather than upon the matter under consideration
and if .the report of a committee is against the matter proposed those who
favor the measure must vote in the negative on the motion made by the
committeeman in order to express their approval of the measure, thus
leading to confusion on frequent occasions.
We might add that on occasions, the report of one committee has
been favorable and that of another unfavorable. In such a case the
confusion incident to the vote on the second report has been compounded.
·
The resolution proposes an amendment to section 26 of the Con~
stitution and section 69 of our ordinances to provide that when the vote
is taken, it shall be on the amendment or item of business; hence, those
who favor the measure will vote "aye.. , and those who do not, will vote
"no" regardless of the favorable or unfavorable nature of the committee
report or reports.
We approve the policy involved in the resolution and recommend
the adoption of the amendments proposed.
The Jurisprudence Committee reported their agreement with the
form submitted, but that they did not believe the legislation to be
required.

Publications
Several resolutions relative to the amendment of section 127 of Ordinances adopted at our last annual communication, and the Grand Master's recommendation and ruling No. 44, have been referred to this
committee. We have examined and considered questions of policy implicit in them. To discuss them individually would consume much time
due to their number and the length of some, and would serve no useful
purpose as several are similar in effect and merely vary in expression.
At our last annual communication a report was received from the
Special Committee on Masonic Publications which recommended the
adoption of an amendment to section 127. After considerable debate the
amendment was adopted. It reads as follows:
"No lodge or member of a lodge, without the express sanction
of Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication which purports to be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by
or for any body, order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership."
It will be observed that the prohibition prescribed by the section
operates on two classes, lodges and members of lodges, and on three
types of publications, those put out by lodges, those put out "by or for
any body, order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership" and those which, for clarity, we shall call private
publications.
Under date of November 30, 1951, a letter addressed to our lodges
and all other interested parties was sent out. The text thereof is set out
in the appendix to the annual message of the Grand Master. Except for
the quotation of the amendment it makes no reference to publications by
or for other bodies, orders or organizations requiring Masonic affiliation
as a condition to membership. The text of recommendation and ruling
No. 44 states that based upon the original section 127 and the amendment thereto, concordant bodies were refused approval for publications
containing advertising.

It is not the province of this committee to express a legal opinion
whether the original section, which makes no reference whatever to any
other body, order or organization and which has been the law of this
jurisdiction for many years, prohibits concordant bodies from publishing
a periodical containing advertising: it is not the province of this committee to express an opinion upon the question whether this grand body
possesses the power to tell another body. order or organization that it
may not put out a publication which contains advertising matter. It is
the province of this committee, however, to express to you our considered
opinion as to the wisdom and policy of attempting to exercise such
power if it is possessed: therefore, as a committee on policy and not as
individuals, we shall assume for the sake of this report only, that the
power is possessed and may be exercised.

320

We are of the opinion that it should not be the policy of this grand
body to attempt to say to the Royal Arch, Knights Templar, Scottish
Rite, Shrine, Eastern Star, Amaranth, White Shrine, Sciots, Grotto, De
Malay, Job's Daughters, Rainbow Girls or any other order or organization, that it may or it may not put out a publication containing advertising or that it must first secure the sanction of this Grand Lodge or any
of its officers or committees, before it may solicit advertising for its own
publications.
It seems to us to be an anomaly to have in our law the express provision that we do not recognize any but the ftrst three degrees and at the
same time to follow the policy· of attempting to prohibit, or prescribe
conditions under which they will be permitted to do things which are
perfectly legal and moral, namely, put out a publication with advertising
and solicit for that advertising. The mere fact that some or a majority
· of their members may be members of our lodges does not warrant the
continuance of the policy followed this past year any more than it would
warrant a policy of telling the Los Angeles Times or the San Francisco
Examiner that it would have to stop carrying ads because the publisher,
editor and staff were Master Masons.
We therefore recommend a policy of withdrawal from this fteld.
This may be accomplished by adopting the resolution presented by
Brother Alden J. Fulkerson, Past Master, San Diego Lodge No. 35, after
first deleting the seven words "under regulations prescribed by the
Grand Master". His resolution would thus read:
"Resolved that section 127 of Ordinances be amended by adding the
following:
Provided, however, that Master Masons may solicit, sponsor,
insert, place or print advertising in such publications issued offi..
cially by any body, order or organization requiring Masonic
affiliation as a condition to membership."

Your committee does not recommend a policy which would be effected
by repealing the amendment. It believes that the attempt to control
private publications should be continued for the present.
It has considered from the stan'dpoint of policy, the prohibitions of
carrying the trestle boards of constituent lodges in such publications. It
believes that there is no necessity for the prohibitions and that such
lodges as desired to use local. private publications for notices of their
meetings and affairs should be permitted to do so. It has been asserted
to your committee that the carrying of trestle boards by certain of the
publications which have been approved under the terms of the amendment is essential to their continued publication.
By adopting the amendment last year and by action under it during
the year, we have given to these publications something they did not
have previously, namely a measure of approval and a certain standing.
Because of that result, the matter of prohibiting or permitting trestle
boards to be published in approved publications takes on aspects which
it might not have if we had continued to ignore these publications.
Many lodges, it appears, were thus using these magazines. No harm
appears to have "'been suffered as the result. We can see no dire results
if the practice is resumed. There is no secret as to the officers of any lodge
or that each confers the first, second and third degree of Masonry. The
rosters and trestle boards tell no more-and new items are being prohibited.

Masters and Wardens in the Santa Barbara-Ventura area be adopted.

recess of the Grand Lodge, pay a reasonable sum for mailing and
for that purpose mailing lists of lodges may be used.''

Applications to Prerequisite Bodies
The Grand Master held correctly that no member may, within twelve
months after receiving the degree of Master Mason, apply for, receive
any degree or be initiated in any body requiring Masonic affiliation as
a condition of membership therein.
The ruling, however, insofar as it suggests that another Master
Mason may within the twelve-month period propose the brother for
membership in such body, should not be approved.
That the brother who is under the restrictions of his promise does
not himself make the application, should not be the deciding factor.
That which cannot be done directly may not be done indirectly.
We are therefore of the opinion that a Master Mason may not
propose a brother for membership in any concordant body before the
expiration of such brother's waiting period.
Adopted.
Appointment of Trial Master
By ruling No. 32, the Grand Master has held that under Section 301,
of our OrdiBances, the Grand Master, or his representative, is not required to ascertain whether the trial master is qualified to act as such.
We cannot agree with this conclusion. Under this Section, the Master
of the Lodge has no power to act as a trial master simply because he -is
the Master of the Lodge. The power to act as a trial master is derived
from the appointment. The law specifically directs a Grand Master, or
his representative, to appoint as trial master the Master or a Past Master
of this jurisdiction in good standing, and skilled in Masonic law. In
order to comply with this direction, it is the duty of the appointing
officer to ascertain whether or not his appointee meets the requirements
of the law. It is not necessary that his determination of the facts of
qualification be shown in the record.
Adopted.

Ruling No. 34 by Grand Master
What procedure should be followed on a candidate who, during
the obligation of the First Degree. refused to conform to the ritual by a
declared intention not to become bound to assume the penalty thereof?
On the candidate's refusal to conform to the ritual of his initiation, the
Master should direct the senior deacon to reconduct the candidate to
the preparation room in the manner provided in the ritual, and no
further work appearing, close the lodge. At the next regular meeting of
the lodge. the Master should declare the candidate rejected and his fee
should be returned.
· There is abundant written Masonic law which justifies the action
indicated. By Art. III, Sec. 6, R. D .• our Constitution requires "a strict
adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the Order". Landmark Eight-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

331

een requires the qualification of the candidate for initiation. Sec. 650
R. D. enjoins us to remember always that "the ritual itself constitutes
binding law".
Thus, the ritual must be adhered to by all Lodges and Masons.
( R. D. Sec. 247.)
The Committee on Ritual concurs in the above ruling.
Adopted.
Ruling No. 37
By ruling No. 37 the Grand Master held that a lodge cannot receive
an application for the degrees from one who had leased a bar and restaurant reserving an option to buy.
Ordinance No. 210 provides that no lodge shall receive an application for degrees or affiliation from anyone who is engaged either as
principal agent or employee in the saloon business (except in connection
with and as part of the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant).
Because it appears that the applicant is within the exception. your
committee is of opinion that the ruling is erroneous. The answer should
have been "yes."
Adopted.
Discussion of Public Questions
By decision No. 43. the Grand Master ruled:
"Questions relating to a referendum measure to appear on the ballot
of California this fall. might be discussed in meetings of tiled Lodges. or
at social meetings before or after such meetings; but that no action of the
Lodge, endorsing or condemning this or any other measure was to be
taken."
We are of the opinion that our law at the present time does not permit
such discussion within a tiled Lodge room. but that such discussion is
permissible at social meetings held before or after tiled meeting of a
Lodge. We agree with the Grand Master's decision that no action,
endorsing or condemning such a measure can be taken at such a meeting.
The report of the Committee was not adopted.
A minority report of the Committee on Jurisprudence was then presented approving the decision as set forth by the Grand Master in his
annual message.
Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Workmen· s Compensation:
We also concur in the recommendation of the grand Secretary that
the Grand Lodge of California may be assuming unnecessary liability
on account of subordinate lodges failing to carry workmen's compensation insurance as is required by State Law.
Since the California Workmen's Compensation Act provides certain
minimum charges ($39.00 per lodge), the total premium for all lodges
in the State would be in excess of $23,000.00. Investigation shows if the
Workmen's Compensation is carried by the Grand Lodge of California
under a blanket policy for all constituent lodges, Boards of Relief and
Employment, and others, a single minimum premium of approximately
$7.500.00 would be charged. Your Committee on finance concurs with
the recommendation of the Grand Secretary and that his office, or a
special committee on insurance. be authorized to make a survey of the
Workmen's Compensation coverage now carried by each of the subordinate lodges, and if the survey indicates that the lodges are not adequately covered that the Grand Secretary be authorized to obtain
coverage as outlined in his report for the benefit of all subordinate lodges:
and that the premium be paid by the Grand Lodge, and the subordinate
lodges be advised of the effective date in order that they may cancel
any coverage they may have.
Public Liability Coverage:
Much progress has been made in impressing officers of constituent
lodges with the importance of carrying adequate Public Liability and
Property Damage Insurance. It is known that many lodges have no such
protection, even though all are exposed to Public hazard. In discussing
this problem with men of the legal profession and in the light of recent
decision of our Courts, it is felt that men on investigating committees,
or other committees functioning in the interest of the lodge, are agents
of the constituent lodges, and could involve the lodge and Grand Lodge
in a public liability claim.
It is the considered judgment of your Finance Committee that the
whole question of Public Liability Coverage of the Grand Lodge and
constituent lodges be again reviewed, and that the incoming Grand
Master be instructed to appoint a special committee on insurance to investigate the effectiveness and adequacy.
Insurance Coverage for Grand Lodge and Subordinate Lodges, as
respects:
1 ) Workmen's Compensation.
2) General Public Liability and Property Damage.
3) As respects Grand Lodge, personal floater comprehensive
policy covering all personal property of Grand Lodge and
with patricular reference to Regalia, Supplies, Art Gallery, etc.
It is further recommended that if the Committee recommendations
are such that the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, Graad Treasurer,

and the Chairman of the Finance Committee feel it justified, they be
given authority and power. to purchase such coverage as in their judgment is required and desirable.
Your Committee on Finance feels most strongly on the importance
of allowing the constituent lodge the right to manage their own affairs
but where Grand Lodge is in effect partially responsible or could be
joined with a lodge in a suit and the lodge was unable to discharge its
rightful responsibility, we feel Grand Lodge not only has a right to
protect itself, but is morally obligated to do so, either by joining with
the lodge, on an equitable basis, or at least, carrying excess coverage to
protect Grand Lodge in case the constituent lodge has no protection or
insufficient coverage.
