George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the report of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association and also that of
Past Grand Master John R. Moore, State Chairman, setting forth the
progress made by the association and the amounts remaining to be
paid. After a careful study of the existing situation, they have strong
reason to believe that in view of the changes which have been made in
the plans for completing the project, this Grand Lodge may not be called
upon for any further contributions. However, in view of the uncertainties which exist, we recommend that the assessment of l 5c per
member be continued this year.

Morton Estate Bequest
Referring to that portion of the report of the Grand Secretary being
Item 2, under the heading of Unfinished Business "disposition of pro~
ceeds of Estate of Andrew W. Morton, deceased". This amounts to
$25,000.00.
We recommend that this sum be transferred to the Building Fund
account.
Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389
At the 1951 Communication of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Master
was authorized to order the payment of such attorneys' fees, costs and
other expenses as he deemed necessary for the protection of the interests
of Grand Lodge which had been named as defendant in a suit involving
the title to certain stocks held in trust for Palos Verdes Lodge. A total
amount of $642.08 was paid as a result of this authorization, and we
are informed that this is only a portion of the expenses incurred and
that no attorneys' fees have been paid.
Trial has been had and judgment was rendered in favor of the
Lodge and the Grand Lodge, although time for an appeal has not passed.
Past Grand Master, John R. Moore, acted as one of the attorneys for
the Lodge, and Junior Grand Warden, Henry C. Clausen, represented
the Grand Lodge, and it is due largely to the excellent legal work of
these two Brothers that the trial was brought to a successful conclusion.
While it is not the proper time for this matter to be considered, we hope
that eventually all of the costs incurred by the Grand Lodge, as well
as adequate attorneys' fees, will be paid and charged against the corpus
of the trust, which we understand is quite substantial.
Portrait of P.G.M. Benjamin D. Hyam
The matter of a portrait of Past Grand Master Benjamin D. Hyam,
third Grand Master of Masons in California, has been given consideration and this committee concurs with the Policy and General Purposes
Committee that the portrait should be authorized and, therefore, present
the following resolution and move its adoption.
RESOLVED: That the sum of $500.00 be appropriated for the
purpose of commissioni~g an artist to paint a likeness of Hyam from
the photograph that is now in the hands of Grand Lodge. ,

337

Tehachapi and Maricopa Lodge Buildings
The resolutions pertaining to the unfortunate disaster which demolished the Tehachapi and Maricopa Lodge buildings have been referred
to this Committee.
While this Committee is sympathetic to the intent of these resolutions, it feels its hands are tied until the entire situation has been exam~
ined and analyzed by the Committee on Grand Lodge Financing.
This committee, therefore, is confidently content to leave the solution
in the hands of its chairman, the Committee on Lodge Financing and
the incoming Grand Master to resolve it after the matter has been fully
digested by the Committee on Lodge Financing. .
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
That the incoming Grand Master, the chairman of the Committee
on Finance, together with the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge
Financing be hereby authorized to expend such monies of Grand Lodge
to relieve the unfortunate condition of the Tehachapi and Maricopa
Lodges.in their rebuilding projects as may be collectively decided upon.
Memorial Building
Your Committee on Finance has considered with a great deal of
interest the report of the Committee on Memorial Building. It is un~
necessary to recapitulate here the variot,ts studies that have been made
by that committee over the last few years, but it should be emphasized
that, in the thinking of the members of that committee, the erection of a
building which might be termed a memorial building, single purpose in
its character, is not feasible nor within the financial capacity of this
Grand Lodge. Consequently, the work ·of the committee during the
last year has been to find some building which could be adapted for
our purposes and at the same time provide some income which would
·
assist in carrying the financial burden of the project.
While the members of the Finance Committee have not followed
completely all of the work of the Committee on Memorial Building, we

339

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

do know that many investigations have been made and that a great deal
of time and effort has been expended by the members of the committee,
and the proposal which that committee is now making is the very best
that can be made at this time, or is likely to be made in the foreseeable
future. Conseq uently, we feel that the decision which is being asked of
the Grand Lodge is a very important decision and we have approac hed
our consideration of the matter with some hesitation and some reserva tions. One does not lightly enter into the purchas e of a home, nor does
a Lodge consider lightly the matter of entering into a proposal for a new
building.
In considering the purchas e of a new home, either for an individual.
or for a Lodge, ordinar ily it is not considered as to whethe r it will be a
good investment from a financial point of view, but rather as to whethe r
it will meet the needs of the purpose for which it is intended, namely,
that of a home. We believe that this project should be considered from
this same point of view. We do not think it can be recommended as a
sound business investment, neither do we feel that the project is in any
sense unsoun d if we are to consider the objective which is intend edthat of a perman ent home for the Grand Lodge.
. We have no doubt that some of the Master s and officers of Lodges
with us here today, can look back to many frustrations and disappointments as their building program went ahead. We doubt not that if. with
your approval. we go ahead with this program , there will be like disappointments and like frustrations that we cannot now foresee. We
believe, however, that the likelihood of difficulties should not deter us
and that we should take this opportu nity which is offered to us at this
present time.
There are, of course, many considerations which cannot be answere d
at the present time. The plans for the alteratio ns must be carefully considered with a view to the ultimate, maximum comfort of members of the
Grand Lodge. The ultimate method of financing will depend natural ly
upon the completion of those plans. The men who have worked on this
project for many months have believed that these problems can be solved
successfully and if you vote for this project, you are placing your conft~
dence in the officers and committees of the Grand Lodge to solve these
problems. or at least, have them solved sufficiently so that they can be
present ed to the Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication. The
members of your Committee on Finance believe that Grand Lodge is very
fortuna te in having a proposal of this kind present ed to it, and with the
concurrence of the Committee on Policy and Genera l Purpose s approve s
the recommendation of the Committee on the Memorial Building.

for the purchas e of the building described in the report of the
Memorial Building Committee to the owners of the propert y, as is
authorized by the unanimous vote of the elected officers of the
Grand Lodge, and the Chairm an of the Committee on Finance.
Be it resolved further that if such offer is accepted by the
owners of the propert y that the Grand Master or the Deputy
Grand Master, and the Grand Secreta ry, or the Assista nt Grand

Salaries
Your committee has discussed with the Grand Secretary, the salary
needs for the coming year. Total salaries paid during the past year were
$40,541.85. This included $13,200.00 paid to the Grand Secreta ry. and
$7,200.00 paid to the Assista nt Grand Secreta ry. The total salary
expense for Grand Lodge was reduced by $7,500.00, the amount paid
by the Masoni c Homes, making a net of $33,041.85. The Grand Secretary estimates that an increase of $4,500.00 will be needed for the staff
during the' coming year. This includes some increase in the staff as well
as some increase in salaries. This brings us to the salaries of the Grand
Secreta ry and the Assista nt Grand Secreta ry, which have not been
adjusted since the Annual Communication in 1950.
We cannot speak too highly of the services of our Grand Secretary.
An efficient administrative officer, a leader among the Grand Secretaries
of the various jurisdictions of our nation, an authori ty on Masoni c law
and custom, a speaker of outstan ding reputation, it is regretta ble that in
a fraterna l association such as ours that we cannot set his salary on a
scale comparable with those paid in the business world. Our Assista nt
Grand _Secreta ry, likewise represe nts a very high degree of efficiency
and deserves like consideration. We recommend that the salary of the
Grand Secreta ry be increased $3,600.00 per year, and that of the Assistant Grand Secreta ry _$1,800.00, making:

Master. The Most Worshipful Charles M. Wollenberg. Past Grand

Master in her behalf.

to July 31, 1952.
Schedule 4: Statement of Masonic Homes Per Capita Dues and $25.00
Contributions Collected During the Year 1951-52.
COMMENTS

As shown on Exhibit AA of this report, the combined assets of Grand
Lodge, the Masonic Homes and the Endowment Fund now exceed $10,000,000.00. Exhibit BB shows that over $2,000,000.00 was received and a like
amount disbursed by these three. The disbursements were not all for expenses, as the Endowment Fund alone disbursed over $1,000,000.00 for purchase of stocks and bonds. Grand Lodge has set up a series of safe-guards
which, in our opinion, are adequate to insure the safety of this flow of money,
and the safety of the assets on hand.
The revenue from all sources exceeded the expenses and appropriations
by $21,430.89. The expenses include $6,038. 73 which represents the remaining
cost of unsold copies of "100 Years of Freemasonry in California".
Schedules 2 and 4 show proof of the revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1951 annual returns and the $25.00 Homes contribution
reports received up to July 31, 1952. The total amount due, as shown, agrees
with the total cash received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and deposited in the proper bank accounts of the Grand Treasurer. Disbursements were made ·by checks and
supported by properly approved vouchers. The disbursements made by the
Grand Secretary were from his Operating Fund bank account. Reimbursements to the Operating Fund by the Grand Treasurer were not made until
we had audited and approved the bills, which was done monthly. During the
current year, all bills paid by the Grand Secretary were provided for in the
Budget or had the approval of the Grand Master.
Bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries. A
certified list of the securities was received from the Anglo California National

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1952 and submit herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets, July 31, 1952.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1, 1951
to July 31, 1952.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund, July 31, 1952.
Exhibit D: Statement of Income and Capi.tal Accounts, for the Fiscal Year
ended July 31, 1952.
Schedule 1: Regular endowment fund securities owned, July 31, 1952.
Schedule 2: Securities redeemed and sold during the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1952.
COMMENTS
Cash:
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest and dividends due from investments and saving bank accounts
were received by the Grand Treasurer and deposited in the bank accounts
of the Masonic Homes. The total income received by the Homes from the Endowment Fund amounted to $125,715.87.
Securities:
Securities on hand are listed on Schedule 1. Securities redeemed and sold
during the current year are listed on Schedule 2.
Bonds purchased are listed at actual cost. Donated securities are listed
at market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the actual
value is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment Fund
were received from the Anglo California National Bank. The records were
checked to these lists and the securities not listed were inspected by us at
the office of the Grand Secretary.
.
Liabilities:
A check for $150.00 was received from La Habra Lodge, No. 659 attached
to an Endowment Fund collection slip, and deposited in the Endowment
Fund. In August the Lodge claimed the check was an advance payment on
its 1952 annual return, therefore, the Endowment Fund owes the Lodge
$150.00 which we have shown as a liability on the Endowment Fund's State·
ment of Assets, Exhibit A.
Increase in Fund:
The combined assets of the Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund
show the following increase for the current year:

Revenue and Expense:
A detailed audit was made of the revenue and expense accounts and we
satisfied ourselves as to the general correctness of the accounting records.
The Endowment Fund income received by the Homes is in agreement with
the Endowment Fund audit report. All interest and dividends due on the investments were receive<!. The records of the contributions through Lodges
were examined and the amounts received appear to be all that can be collected. All disbursements were made by checks and supported by proper
vouchers.
The 1951 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the $25.00
contributions due thereon, plus the contributions received up to July 31 1952
agree with the amount turned over to the Treasurer by the Grand Sec~etary'.
The per capita on 199,962 members at $1.00, in amount $199,962.00, was also
received ·b y the Treasurer from the Grand Secretary.
The operations of the Masonic Homes resulted in an excess· of revenue
over expense amounting to $112,999.95 as shown by Exhibit B.
Certificate:
In our opinion, the accompanying statements present fairly the financial
position of the Masonic Homes of California at July 31, 1952 and the result
of its operations for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1952, in accordance with
generally accepted accounting principles.
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS & PARKER
Certified Public Accountants

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
· .FOREWORD
Your committee has invariably utilized a topical arrangement in reviewing proceedings of sister jurisdictions. In this report we attempt a
connected Masonic essay constructed from the words uttered by leaders
of the Craft recorded in the printed proceedings of the 1951 Grand
Lodge Communications.

FREEMASONRY IN A CHANGING WORLD

Editorial comment is minimized. Quotation marks were deemed
superfluous. Such connecting and explanatory matter as was essential
is inserted in italics. The ideas expressed are those of the person indicated and not necessarily those of the committee.
Half a century of world turmoil and flux has had its impact on all
institutions, Freemasonry not excepted. The function of this committee
is to keep you informed and in touch with current thought and activity
in other recognized Grand Lodge jurisdictions.
We trust that our work will prove interesting, instructive and stimulating, and that it may better prepare you to perform your responsible
duties in helping to steer the Grand Lodge of California through
troubled waters.

If the Craft is to be perpetual, it must appeal to each time as well
as to all times; it must have in its traditions something that today can
use, although yesterday could not use it and tomorrow need not. We are
a Craft of workmen. It is our glory to be engaged in useful service. Our
rites and usages are not merely a proud possession to be treasured for
their beauty and antiquity. They are instruments imparted to us to be
used. Hence we may properly inquire, what can we make of this wonderful tradition of which we are the custodians that will serve the world
of today? . . . Every world-organization hitherto has been wrecked
ultimately upon its own dogmatism. It has taken the dogmas, the interpretations, the philosophy of its youth for a flxed order of nature. It has
assumed that universality consisted of forcing these dogmas, these interpretations, this philosophy upon all times to come. While it has rested serene in the ruts made by its own prosperity, the world has marched
by it unseen. Masonic Philosophy by Roscoe Pound. Hon. P.G.M.

"I hope Masonry will never become so up to date that it will be
out of date tomorrow f" said Roscoe Pound. Let us hope that Masonry
will never become too big, too modern, too high pressured, too much big
business, too Super-Colossal. too much just another Club. For when
that time comes Masonry will no longer be Masonry. William B. Warner, P.G.M. Nebraska.
When is a man a Mason? The answer is given by Joseph Fort Newton in the paragraph which ends his great book, The Builders: "When
he can look out over the rivers, the hills, and the far horizon with a profound sense of his own littleness in the vast scheme of things, and yet
have faith, hope and courage-which is the root of every virtue. When
he knows that down in his heart every man is as noble, as vile, as divine,
as diabolic, and as lonely as himself, and seeks to know, to forgive, and
to love his fellow man. When he knows how to sympathize with men
in their sorrows, yea, even in their sins--knowing that each man flghts
a hard flght against many odds. When he has learned how to make
friends and to keep them, and above all how to keep friends with himself.... When no voice of distress reaches his ears in vain, and no hand
seeks his aid without response. When he flnds good in every faith that
helps any man to lay hold of divine things and see majestic meanings in
life, whatever the name of that faith may be. . . . When he has kept
faith with himself, with his fellowman, with his God: in his hand a
sword for evil, in his heart a bit of song--glad to live, but not afraid to

die! Such a man has found the only real secret of Masonry, and the one
which it is trying to give to all the world." Lynn R. Brodrick, G.M.
Kansas.

CHAPTER II

Freemasonry is no ivory tower. It is no escape from the problems
and tensions that are inevitable in our kind of world. We must think of
Masonry as that which we can release as a great constructive force in
the world. You are privileged men-men who have seen a vision of what
life can be; men who have dreamed a dream of an ideal life for humanity;
and you are ·therefore forever committed to the task of translating the
vision and the dream into action. Thomas S. Roy, G. M. Massachusetts.

KEEPING MASONS INTERESTED AND ACTIVE

521

Attendance or rather lack of attendance is causing considerable
concern to Grand Masters and, we suspect, it is also a matter of concern
to some Worshipful Masters. The solution is simple and obvious. If
meetings are interesting there will never be a lack of attendance. Business meetings or degree work night after night become monotonous to .
brethren relegated to the role of spectator. Is it any wonder they gradually drift away? To keep them interested give them something to do.
Very few of us are willing to read a book or see the same show over
and over. Are we so naive as to expect Masons to willingly listen to
degree work over and over just because the degrees rendered are beautiful and instructive? Duty to attend lodge means little to some when
other attractions are so plentiful. A Worshipful Master capable of
providing interesting meetings is of far more value to his lodge and
to Masonry than is one who is a proficient ritualist but without organizing ability. Herbert W. Dixon, P.G.M. Wisconsin.
More Masonry in men is our great need, rather than more men in
Masonry. I have made the statement that it would be well if we were
to discontinue receiving new members for a year; we would then be
impelled to offer the Brethren who attend our meetings some of the
instruction that is too often neglected in the rush of ritualistic work we
have had fo1 the past few years. . • • I have no desire to minimize
the importance of good ritual; on the contrary, I laud good degree
work and stress its importance, but we should not concentrate on ritual
to the exclusion of all else. Robert W. Cretney, G.M. Louisiana.
Should talks in Lodge meetings be confined to such subject& as
are purely M81!10nic, or at least carry a Masonic connection 1

Some of the Masonic brethren probably feel that we should permit
only such discussions as connect directly or indirectly with the Order
and are instructive as to its principles, meaning and history. Brothers
so convinced are certainly not a large part of the whole group.
For myself, I do not take that view. I think we should encourage
the intellectual activity of the brothers by covering quite a broad field.
Such subjects as current events, especially in world-wide matters,
scientific developments, literature and history are just as much subjects
for Masonic education as are those that are strictly Masonic. Neither
set of subjects should exclude the other. They should be alternated.
This, I feel, will not only build up the individual member but the Order
also.
For some years it has been a conviction with me that in a ·section of

522

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

this country such as that in which we live, i.e., not in large cities, the
membership of a lodge should represent a cross sect.ion of the thinking
man fn the community. Rich or poor, bankers or barbers-if they think
for themselves and want to progress intellectually they are timber for
the Order.
In a lodge so composed there will be those who can tell their experiences, those who can tell of developments of science, those who can
explain the philosophy and history of the Order, those who can bring
in a good motion picture, and those who can prepare a paper on some
pivotal time in history. Each of these should take part and do or talk of
the thing in which he is interested. It is all Masonic education. Judge
Frederick _C. Loofbourrow. Utah.

The problem of competent and Willing leadership is critical.
Nearly every lodge has its corps of "old faithfuls." They are the small
group who, year after year, shoulder the burdens of the local lodges
and carry them down through the years-while the balance of the membership is, in fact, inactive--indifferent. Yes, to be sure, most of them
pay their dues-but that is the extent of the activity of these indifferent
members.
·
So, this problem of bringing into the leadership circle new, zealous
and younger blood must be solved....
· And may I interject here my sincere conviction that, given proper
leadership--through exercise of care and thought in selection of lodge
officers-we soon can eliminate most of our indifferent members by the
simple process of imbuing them with the conviction that Masonry can
and will make them wiser, happier and better men. Lynn R. Brodrick,
G. M. Kansas.

CHAPTER Ill

MASONIC EDUCATION
We must constantly guard against the idea that a man has been
made a Mason when he has received the degrees--it has · made him
a member but no more a Mason than membership in a musical dub
would have made him a musician. The correct rendition of the ritual is
fundamental and a good knowledge of it is desirable, but we must also
provide ways and means whereby our members as well as our initiates
are taught the essentials of Masonic history and philosophy, the truths
and principles which are embodied in its symbolism and their application
to the building of character and the development of manhood. William
E. Yeager, G. M. Pennsylvania.
We feel that our efforts should be expended in promoting what
might be called primary or elementary education, since there are
available for the true Masonic scholars many volumes of history and
philosophy written thru the years. On the other hand, in the field in
which we feel we ought to work there is a real question of how to issue
reading material which will be read. The experience of the grand secretary's office is that there is relatively little interest in printed material;
... The deputies have an unusual opportunity for disseminating Masonic
information since the meetings which they attend are usually the largest
of the year. F. R. Adams, Chairman, Committee on Masonic Education,
Vermont.

The Claudy Masonic Plays are available to the Lodges. A full set
of the twelve plays have been secured. Worshipful Brother Frank Knoll
is in charge of this activity. Several of the plays have been produced
and lodges are at the present time working on further productions. It
is our judgment that this activity will prove to be of lasting benefit to
the jurisdiction. The plays require no special scenery and use the lodge
set-up. While there are several characters needed, not over two or three
of the parts are heavy. Each of the plays teaches a Masonic lesson.
Harry D. Proudfoot, G. S. Oregon.
A letter has been addressed every month to each lodge which I
have requested them to read at their next stated meeting. These letters
have called attention to various irregularities and suggested ways of
adding interest and variety to Lodge activities. Some of the important
matters discussed in these letters were: ( 1) The evil of the unMasonic
use of the blackball by one, who, because he thinks he is too good to
associate with other good men, or because some friend, or fellow church
or club member, has been rejected, or because he himself has not received
some desired recognition, or because of some religious or political
prejudice, personal jealousy or desire for revenge, has black-balled or
Bled an objection against good men seeking membership in his Lodge.
( 2 ) The malicious practice of participation in the distribution of chain
letters. To mail such letters is a violation of the regulations of the Post
Office Department and to participate in the furtherance of these claims
is highly unMasonic and contrary to the teachings and principles of
Masonry, which are based on faith in a Supreme Architect and not in
any kind of mesmerism or superstition. • . . ( 3) Asking Lodges to hold
a Brotherly Love Night for their own members, seeking to settle personal differences and unite the Lodge in true Masonic fellowship.

Today our beautiful Degrees are being conferred more impressively
and with greater efficiency than ever before. We call attention to this
condition with great pride for this is the very foundation of our Institution. Masonry works in a secret ritual in order to make use of its secrecy
for the dramatization of our ceremonies to make them more impressive,
and not because we have something to hide from the world. Wallace
Phelan Douglas, G. M. Tennessee.

Bookings from the Masonic Film Library to the lodges dropped off

before several courses of action were developed:

2. These Blms and the present films are being grouped into packages
so that the lodges may request Blms for every type of meeting by package.

CHAPTER IV

RESEARCH LODGES
Research Lodges have recently been chartered by 11 of the 49
Grand Jurisdictions in the United States. Such Lodges augment previously existing methods of spreading Masonic light and knowledge.
Their successes have prompted this committee to become enthusiastic
about possibilities in Colorado and to lay groundwork so that like
activities can be started here almost immediately upon approval of this
Grand Lodge.
To the present, over 300 Master Masons from every section of this
Grand Jurisdiction have indicated their desire to become charter members. Incidentally. the charter roll will be open until the date of the
constitution of the Lodge-depend ent, of course, upon favorable consideration by this body of our committee's recommendation. . . . So if
any of you who have not already indicated your desires, do wish to
become charter members of "The Research Lodge of Colorado." if it is
approved, you can do so by seeing some member of the committee before
the close of this session of the Grand Lodge. Gordon R. Merrick. Chairman Special Committee on Lodge of Research, Colorado.

Little did the Grand Lodge of Missouri realize, when it chartered
the Missouri Lodge of Research, the great constructive work it was to
accomplish in the years to follow; yet, in the short space of ten years,
this organization has become the largest Lodge of Research in the
Western Hemisphere. and is exceeded only by the English Lodge
( Quatuor Coronati) which was established more than half a century
ago.
During its existence it has printed volumes containing more than
twenty-five hundred pages, and has distributed other Masonic literature
of value to its members.
Because of the necessity of some form of Masonic Education, I
have attempted in my travel over the State to give as much publicity to
the work of Missouri Lodge of Research as was possible.
During the past year the Lodge has had as its Master, the President
of the United States, and as his part in promoting the work of the Lodge,
he suggested an investigation of all the Masonic books, documents,
photographs and paintings of Masonic interest, now in the Library of
Congress; already that investigation is being carried on by officers of
the Lodge.

Quite naturally. a work of such proportions requires f~nds--funds
beyond the ability of the Missouri Lodge of Research to raise: No ~ne
connected with this work has received any emolument for this service.
It is a work of love. Under these circumstances, I recommen~ that a
reasonable appropriation be made to continue, and to complete this work,
a work which should be of value to the Freemasonry of the world. · • ·
Ray Bond, G. M. Missouri.

The Texas Grand Lodge magazine has been continued in the nature
of a Masonic Digest, giving prominence to Texas matters, and then
attempting to include in each issue outstanding, entertaining and educational articles taken from the many splendid Masonic journals available to us. We, of course, have no editorial policy, and we refrain from
all comment and discussions, feeling that such is not within the jurisdiction of this Committee, but all such matters should. be controlled
entirely by our Grand Master, and this policy, we believe, to be wise,
proper and according to the wishes of Freemasons in Texas....
We have always tried to keep the Magazine on the very highest
level of publications, and for the past three years the cost of publishing
our Magazine has increased 102 per cent. From October 31, 1947, to
August 31, 1948, we sustained a deficit in the publication of the Magazine in the amount of $8,430.19. For a period from November 1, 1949,
to September 30, 1950, we sustained a deficit in the amount of $15,050.77....
Taking this increased cost into consideration, it has been deemed
advisable to increase the price of our Magazine from fifty cents ( 50c)
a year for each subscription to $1.00 a year. This is to become effective
as of January 1, 1951, on any new subscriptions or any renewals there·
after. Rogers Kelley. P.G.M.. Texas.

Some of the controver sial things in Freemaso nry have eased off
a bit. The strenuous and sometimes vehement defense of Mackey' s
eighteenth Landmark about physical perfection has softened in many
quarters. A more sensible view of this outmoded idea seems to · be
gaining ground,-- and wisely so. The Negro Freemaso nry flurry has
subsided, and that, too, is well. However I prophesy again, as I did
last year, that it will rise again and again with ever decreasing violence.
Toleration is a slow process in the evolution of man's thinking. but
eventually will prevail. There now seems to be no real issue about which
Masonic thought differs .. . •
Everywhere, except in the British Isles, are outspoken warnings

CHAPTER VIII

RELIGIOUS AND POLITICAL DISCUSSION
Very rightly partisan politics are a forbidden subject in Masonic
Lodges, but I feel that good citizenship is above partisan politics and
should be discussed freely and often. The situation facing us nationally
is not one that can be cured by force of arms. It is a clash of ideas. On
the one hand we have those who deny the existence of Him whom we
call the Supereme Architect of the Universe and who subordinate the
individual to the state. On the other hand, we have those who acknowledge Him and look to Him for strength and guidance.
The time for apathy and complacency is long since past. As Masons
we have a philosophy which will lead us out of the present confusion if
we only practice it. We have all publicly expressed our faith and belief
in Him. Why not put that faith to work? We sing that grand old hymn,
"Faith of Our Fathers." That is what we need to practice in our daily
lives.
Then, like it or not, we must take part in community and public
affairs. Too many of us too long have taken the easy way out and let
someone else seek public office. As a result, with few exceptions, statesmanship has all but disappeared and been replaced by a lower type of
self-seeking politician to whom honor and country is secondary. Jethro

H. Peckham, G.M., Rhode Island.

What constitutes religious or political discussion before a Masonic Lodge? ... The Jurisprudence Committee gave extended consideration to that subject and presents a written opinion, which we think
covers the matter and answers the question • . •
It is universally understood by Masons that neither politics nor
religion is to be discussed in lodge. The questions prG>pounded are, what
is the meaning of those apparent prohibitions. In order to answer those
questions, it is necessary to go back to the source of the apparent restrictions and to try to ascertain what was meant by the language then used.
This necessitates a consideration of the Ancient Charges.
The first of these Charges, "Concerning God and Religion" is as
follows:
"A Mason is oblig'd, by his Tenure, to obey the moral law, and
if he rightly understands the Art, he will never be a stupid atheist,
nor an irreligious libertine. But though in ancient Times Masons
were charg'd in every Country to be of the Religion of that Country
or Nation, whatever it was, yet 'tis now thought more expedient
only to oblige them to that Religion in which all Men agree, leaving
their particular Opinions to themselves: that is, to be good Men and

541

true, or Men of Honour and Honesty, by whatever Denominations
or Persuasions they may be distinguish'd: whereby Masonry be.comes the Center of Union, and the Means of concilating true
Friendship among Persons that must have remain'd at a perpetual
Distance."
The sixth of these Old Charges, "Of Behavior," has six subheadings.
fhe second is "Behavior after the Lodge is over and the brethren not
gone." It reads as follows:
"You may enjoy yourselves with innocent Mirth. treating one
another according to Ability, but avoiding all excess, or forcing any
Brother to eat or drink beyond his inclination, or hindering him from
going when his Occasion call him, or doing or ·saying a?ything
offensive, or that may forbid an easy and free Conversation: for
that would blast our Harmony, and defeat our laudable Purposes.
Therefore no private Piques or Quarrels must be brought within
the Door of the Lodge, far less any Quarrels about Religion, or
Nations, or State Policy, we being only, as Masons of the Catholick
Religion above-mention'd: we are also of all Nations, Tongues,
Kindreds, and Languages, and are resolved against all Politicks,
as what ever yet conduc'd to the Welfare of the Lodge, nor ever
will. This Charge has been always strictly enjoin'd and observ'd:
but especially ever since the Reformation in Britain or the Dissent
and Secession of these Nations from the Communion of Rome."
These Ancient Charges first found Masonic pronouncement, if not
recognition, as a part of Anderson's Constitutions, in 1722.

. . .• . . .

First, What is the meaning of this prohibition against disC'ussing
religion? Does it put a ban on all religious discussion?
We here quote a brief excerpt from an address delivered by Melvin
Maynard Johnson, Past Grand Master of Massachusetts and Sovere;gn
Grand Commander of the Ancient, Accepted Scottish Rite: Northern
Masonic Jurisdiction, delivered before the Grand Lodge of Indiana
in May of 1948:
Those things about which we can differ in religion were for..
bidden to be discussed within the Lodge but there is nothing in
Anderson's Constitutions, if you consult the dictionaries of that
day and the oldest one is the dictionary of Samuel Johnson: which
was being prepared at about the time that Anderson s Constitutions
were written-if you consult that you will find the definition of
general religion, which is a thing we not only may discuss withi!1
the Lodge but you never attended a Masonic Lodge were it wasn t
discussed. You never attended a Masonic Lodge, which was a
recognized Masonic body, which wasn't either opened by a declara•
tion to the glory of the Grand Architect of the Universe, or by

542

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

prayer to Him that He would guide us in our deliberations, or
both. . . . . .

discussion and by the same token, a study of and speeches about our
Constitution are not prohibited as political discussion. • • . •
The purpose of Masonry is to make its votaries wiser and better and
consequently, happier. We make them wiser, as far as the science of
government is concerned, by study and discussion of political science:
and we make them better by a study and discussion of the. fundamental,
underlying basic principles of religion, or morality, if there is a distinction.
In both fields, the rule and its limitation may be thus summarized:
We may discuss these matters concerning which there can be no honest
difference of opinion; as to matters and systems concerning which there
can be honest differences of opinion among Masons, a different situation
exists. This includes sectarianism and partisan politics. Discussion of
of these is prohibited. • • • •
Masonry is not a crusading institution. It takes no part in public or
private campaigns of any kind. It makes no public appearances except
on state occasions (laying cornerstones, etc.) and for burying its dead.
This does not mean that it is not interested in the commmunity or what
is going on in the commmunity, nor that it does not influence the affairs
of man; but it does iJll this by strengthening and refining individual
character, by teaching and .discussing the eternal verities, by promoting
and stimulating the brotherhood of man based upon the Fatherhood of
God. Walter G. Winslow, P.G.M. Chairman, Jurisprudence Committee, Oregon.
A cautious approach to the problem; I denied a request that Grand
Lodge should issue a circular letter, or otherwise as a lodge make special
effort to induce voters to register or to vote in civil elections: It was my
judgment that by word of mouth, one Mason might solicit such action
on the part of the Masonic brethren, but that officially Masonry keeps
itself out of political measures or meetings. John S. Hedeland, G.M.,
Nebraska.

Here again is the key to the prohibition we are considering. Sectarianism is what is prohibited. In other words, according to this
Ancient Charge, there is no place in Masonry for an "atheist" nor an
irreligious libertine,' but by it a Mason is admonished to have a belief
in God. How he is to worship is not the business of Masonry, and its
discussion is prohibited. This method of worship is, by this fiat of
Masonry and, in the United States, by our Constitution, left to the
dictates of each individual member's conscience. We caU it religious
liberty.
Second: Now let us consider the prohibition against political discussion. The importance, as well as the acuteness, of this question is
emphasized by Mackey. We quote from that eminent Masonic scholar
and authority as follows:
"There is no charge more frequently made against Freemasonry
than that of its tendency to revolution and conspiracy and to political organizations which may affect the peace of society or interfere
with the rights of governments. . . . It is in vain that history
records no instance of this unlawful connection between Freemasonry and politics; it is in vain that the libeler is directed to
the Ancient Constitutions of the Order, which expressly forbad
such connection; the libel is still written, and Freemasoonry is again
and again condemned as a political club."
We think it must be admitted that Masonry is concerned with the
public policy of our nation and of the world.
Prudence is a cardinal virtue. How may a Master Mason emulate
this virtue or be "versed in affairs" without some discussion of the
"s~enc~.of government," the "principles of civil government," "Political
science, etc. . • • • .
In order to be such citizen, he must be intelligent, he must be
informed. These ends are attained by discussion, · by study, that the
member may avoid being a "stupid fool."
The more we study this subject, the more it becomes apparent that
this prohibition, like the prohibition against a discussion of religion, is
not all-inclusive, that it has its limitations, that it is not intended to
prohibit a discussion of things political in the broad meaning of ·that
·
term but only things political in the narrow sense.
As we have pointed out ,the prohibition against religious discussion
was . inten?ed t~ apply .to sectarianism; so this prohibition against
political discussion was intended to apply to partisan politics, not to
the science of government. Certainly no one would contend that a study
of and speeches about the Great Light would be prohibited as a religious

Through the years the intent and mission of Masonry have been
to further by precept and example the application of the principles of
the Fraternity to the problems which affect the welfare of mankind.
While Masonry neither assumes nor aspires to political power, it
cannot be denied that the Fraternity has been a tremendous force in
shaping the political affairs not alone of this country but of the world
as well. And it is equally true that every great political movement for
the advancement of liberty and justice during the past two centuries has
upon it the impress of Masonic influence.
From the founding of our nation to the present time Masonry has
been a dominant, steading force in our national life, for Masonry provides, as does no other institution, a common meeting ground for men
of every faith, race and shade of opinion.

544

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is therefore entirely within the scope and purpose of Masonic
thought and service to turn our attention as Masons to the immediate,
serious and thoughtful considerations of the conditions which confront
us as a nation, as a people and as a Fraternity.

The discussion of partisan political subjects is not to be entered
into in Masonic circles, but Brethren, be warned that if Masons do not
now recognize the dangers that beset us and our nation. we are lost.
Each Masonic grand jurisdiction is a body unto itself, but Masons
everywhere must now unite in the common cause of preserving our way
of life, or we are lost. "What shall we do?" Let us, like our brethren
of old, confront these villainous elements united and unafraid, determined that through our courage the right shall prevail. C. C. Buchanan,
Fraternal Correspondent. Mississippi.
American citiz.ens, as such, can run their affairs through their
well established political media without everybody getting into the act
in as many different capacities as he can find offices to hold. And Freemasonry, specially created and wisely limited as a sanctuary from the
hubbub of the market place, loses much of its finest worth and strength
when it rushes downstairs and out into the street to yell with the mob.
]. Walter Karsner, Chairman, Correspondence Committee, District of
Columbia.

Our Masonic forefathers, when their liberties were endangered, most
certainly did not look upon Masonry as a passive fraternity of form and
ceremonies, rituals and degrees. On the contrary, the bonds of Masonic
brotherhood bound them together into a unified society of Brothers
imbued with the single purpose of safeguarding their rights and liberties
as Americans and Freemasons. James N. Bradford, P.G.M. Missouri.

An edict of the Grand Muter of Wisconsin of 1922 was incorporated in the Masonic Code of that Jurisdiction:
Masonry cannot and does not approve of or ally its.elf with any
organization or movement, secret or public, that proposes to subvert or
supersede the processes of orderly representative government "of the
people, for the people, and by the people:" nor one that appeals to
bigotry and endeavors to foster hatred 0£ any nationality, class, religious
faith or sect, as such . • . •
I cha~ge each and all, that as our Fathers have framed the truly
Masonic principles of Liberty of Conscience, Equality before the law,
and Fraternity among men into the Constitutions of this Nation and
State, we as Freemasons and citizens of this republic are obligated to
perform our full moral and civic duty, to promote and enforce an orderly
administration of justice and equity, acting openly that it may be known
to all men. ·
Furthermore, I charge each and all, that affiliation with any secret
organization {i.e. 1922, Ku Klux Klan; 1952, Communist) that purports
to establish an invisible, intolerant and irresponsible autocracy without
our Commonwealth is unwise, unpatriotic, and in direct violation of the
teachings and traditions of American Masonry and the Constitution of
the United States.

A resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge of Florida in 1950:
"Resolved that Florida Masonry denounces and condemns Communism in all its forms as atheistic and un-American ideology, and that

"And God said, let there be light; and there was light." That
there shall be light is the pledge of Masonry. In a distracted world
. there is an ever-widening field for which Masonry teaches. On all
Masons there is the demand for individual responsibility and service.
In far-flung jurisdictions there is evidence that this duty is recognized
and effort is being made to measurably answer the call.
Some of our best minds are enlisted in this work. This must raise
the standard of our participation in social and public affairs and the
general respect in which Masonry is held. Ernest R. Moore, P.G.M.
Iowa.
New York was one of the first jurisdictions to employ a director of
public relations. Under the direction of Brother Maurice M. Witherspoon a program of public relations with the press, radio and television
has advanced tremendously in the past twelve months.
Among the many special events during the past year, three were
outstanding for the national and international coverage they received.
Last August we commemorated the 68th anniversary of the laying of
the cornerstone of the Statue of Liberty by the New York Grand Lodge
of Masons-and captured national interest with what the papers called
"Miss Liberty's Birthday.''
On Sunday, January 20, Brother Witherspoon and Rear Admiral
Dashiell L. Madiera, USN ( Ret) planned for Independent Royal Arch
Lodge No. 2 to lay wreaths at the statue of Brother John Paul Jones
in the New York University Hall of Fame.
On Sunday, March 2, the Public Relations office arranged to celebrate the lOOth Masonic Birthday of Louis Koseuth, Hungarian patriot,
in front of his statue in Riverside Park.
Grand Lodge has not paid one penny for radio time since 1946,
before the Public Relations department was formed. When television
developed, time on that medium was also obtained free of charge. The
tremendous amount of time and coverage that have been extended to
the Fraternity and the goodwill that has been built up with the personnel
of these mediums, as well as through the press and the consumer magazines, must be laid to the honesty of our presentations, and the complete
follow-through that has always been our rule. We have never attempted
to play one medium against the other, or one newspaper against the
other, but have given the news to all, most of the time. Upon various

our National Constitution, under which the freedom of the American
citizen is guaranteed.
Let us not forget the sixteen basic rights of our peQPle which are:
Right to worship God in one's own way.
Right to free speech and free press.
Right to assemble.
Right to petition grievances.
Right to privacy in our homes.
Right to habeas corpus-n o excessive bail.
Right to trial by jury-inno cent until proved guilty.
Right to move about freely at home and abroad.
Right to own property.
Right to work in callings and localities of our choice.
Right to bargain with our employees.
Right to go into business, compete, make a profit.
Right to bargain for goods and services in a free market.
Right to contract about our affairs.
Right to service of government as a protector and referee.
Right to freedom from "arbitrary " government regulation and
control.

CHAPTER XII

Whether Ught or Darkness will triumph in the present world
struggle depends much upon the courage and realistic vision of the
forces of Light. Sadly we must admit that light is only relative, no
nation enoys its full refulgence, and discreditable nationalism bulks
large as a deterrent to effective unified action. But darkness seems
entire in the Asiastic scene where no outmoded shibboleths hamper in
the ruthless exploitation of millions of slaves who appear to be subsisting on the bare necessities for survival. Denied expression now of
any of their former ideas, they are told only what their masters want
them to hear. The system seems to have achieved unity of a somewhat
precarious kind.
We western peoples must again appraise our programs, purposes,
and politics if disaster is to be avoided. We dare not wait in hope of
the collapse of the soviet regimes. We of America have been benevolent
but demanding, cooperative but condescending, we have attempted to
teach with too little understanding, and we have led arrogantly along
our own "glory road," blind to the bright pathway of humility which
may be the surer way to understanding, brotherhood, and peace. If we
continue to be half generous and half selfish, we cannot hope to win
whole-hearted cooperation from allies. Victory in this struggle may
depend upon the spirit and not on wealth, know-how, or material
abundance. "Know then thyself" should be the motto and watch-word
of us all, soldier and statesman, farmer and artisan, merchant and manufacturer, left and right. In the encroaching darkness let us look well
to our light and let us not be grudging and rebellious if the mighty are
humbled and the weak are strengthened. God's plan is working out and
we must be ready to flt bravely into that plan.
When the victory of Light is secure let-us all work together to bring
about the sixth progressive movement, the Ethical Revolution, wherein
equitable sharing shall be the great objective and men may indeed be
brothers all: not classified and regimented according to the color of their
skins: not required to believe as the rulers for the time being believe:
no church shall impose its creed, but each person shall be free to believe
as his understanding and conscience points the way, and he shall be
free to discard any belief when it no longer satisfies. Albert]. Delange,

FREEMASONRY AND WORLD CRISIS
We can recall the great movements which have affected immeasurable advancement to large portions of humanity and have wrought some
measure of benefit to all mankind. After numerous progressions and
retrogressions, and following the great eclipse known as the Dark Ages,
when the lights glimmered but feebly. came the Renaissance, or revival
of learning, which brightened the light of knowledge to a portion, but
not all, of mankind. Followed then the Reformation which enlightened
the spirit and freed _the conscience of a segment of humanity. The
Pol.it_ical Revolution, led b~ our own country, relighted the lamps of
political freedom, lamps which have flickered and failed in many areas,
but which still burn brightly in favored portions of the world. The
Industrial Revolution increased the material wealth of the world and
resulted in_ ~ more equitable distribution of it, easing the physical burdens of millions of people. We are now in the midst of the Scientific
Revolution which enables men to direct and intensify the forces of nature
to a power undreamed of before and not now fully comprehended.
The five major movements affecting successively the cultural, religious, political, industrial, and technological life of peoples of the
progressive western races now seem to be followed by the threat of a
retrograde movement originating in the hitherto static East, to usher in
an eclipse similar to that which preceded the Dark Ages. Now pure
com~unism is not at all horrible. It is Utopian, and too lovely to exist
outside a dream: but the Capitalistic Dictatorship in Russia (now masquerading as communism) has no lovely or Utopian aspect. The present
hegemonic state of the Moscow dictator and his politburo results from
years of ruthless conniving along a bloody trail and it seems now rather
clearly apparent that nothing less than world dictatorship will satisfy
their greed for power.
A reluctant America, on the other hand, has been forced by circumstances into defensive leadership and in our eagerness to shift that
leadership responsibility to others, we may err as we have erred before.
Heroic sacrificial action by the civilized minority of mankind may be the
price we shall have to pay to preserve our culture and our lives. In this
crisis each individual Mason will have an unique obligation as a citizen to
seek light upon government problems in order to help keep our government respected among governments. And we must remember that party
labels are now more misleading than ever before and we should try to
avoid all "Leftist" and "Rightist" prejudices, because, while we are
thinking of them as "the Left" nevertheless, the Russian oligarchy is
now undeniably the extreme Right, although pure communism (the
Utopian dream) is still the extreme Left.

MASONIC HOMES AND BENEVOLENCE
In Louisiana the Grand Lodge maintains a children·s home. There
has been discussion concerning the advisability of establishing a home
/or the aged. A committee appointed to investigate the matter reported:
During the current year your committee has made a study of Homes
and Benevolent activities in other Jurisdictions and reports of committees
of other states engaged in similar investigations.
Your committee has come to the conclusion that the erection of "A
Home for Aged.. is undesirable and recommends no action be taken at
this time. . • •
·
Your committee further reports that owing to the present policy of
both our State and National Governments of granting pensions and
Social Security relief, the establishment of a relief system by Grand
Lodge is of doubtful necessity, especially so as it seems to be the policy
of government agencies to withdraw or curtail relief when relief is
extended from othe;: sources.
However, your committee feels that there may be some cases not
covered by relief from Government Agencies or cases where the relief
furnished by Government Agencies is inadequate, where it would be
desirable for Grand Lodge or local Lodge, or both, to extend relief or
supplement the relief afforded by Government Agei;icies.
We therefore think that Grand Lodge should set up ••. a Charity
or Benevolent Fund •••"
The following comments concerning various Grand Jurisdictions is
abridged from the Louisiana Report:

Ark811888 as a state is made up principally of rural communities, and
there are no very large cities. but our Arkansas brethren are far ahead
of many of the larger states when it comes to dispensing Masonic
benevolence. It has been the policy of the Board of Charities in that
jurisdiction to maintain aged Masons and the families of deceased
Masons in their own homes and in their own communities in coopera~
tion with their subordinate Lodges •.•
They do not pay a pension or grant a definite monthly allowance
in any case. They found that a pension, no matter how small, would
disqualify the person from receiving State or Federal aid. Under their
plan, they cooperate with the subordinate Lodge. the Lodge being re~
quired to pay a portion of the relief granted ••• The Lodge sends a bill
to the Board of Charities showing the amount advanced. and the Board
reimburses the Lodge for that portion which the Board of Charities has

agreed to assume. All payments to the needy brother ar~ made by the
Lodge, and as far as he, or the family, or the community knows, the
Grand Lodge does not enter the picture at all. The Lod~e ge~ full
credit for having cared for its own and has the further satisfac~on of
having done its duty by helping one who was unable to h~l_p himself.
Freemasonry in general is benefited, since in small comn:iumties, eve~~
body usually knows of what is done to help a needy fallllly .. · · ~n their
program the subordinate Lodge is required to see that an effort ~s ma~e
to obtain State and Federal aid for the applicant before Masonic relief

In cases where hospitalization or sanitarium care is needed. the case

Iowa Plan. Direct relief. in their ~wn homes is given to all applicants who qualify, except those requiring sanitarium care, and these are
cared for in the sanitarium at Bettendorf ... The total number of employees on the staff is 25, 'and tile average number of cases handled is
about 45. The average cost per annum for their maintenance for the
year 1948 was $1,225.10 per patient. The Grand Lodge of Iowa is
definitely committed to the plan of giving outside relief in those cases
where sanitarium care is not required ... Under their plan, the application for relief must come through a subordinate Lodge ... The Grand
Charities Board, in considering an application determines the amount
of relief to be granted, and, at the same time, determines what part of
the relief is to be paid by the subordinate Lodge ... At the end of each
year a new application for relief must be made by each beneficiary, giving the same kind of information as is required in an original application.
This gives the Board an opportunity to determine if the money previously allotted has been wisely used, and whether further relief is
required, and how much ....
Kansas has one of the really fine institutions o~ its kind in this country in its Masonic Home. The grounds are suitably landscaped, the

rooms and parlors well and attractively furnished, and everything is
well maintained and in a clean and orderly condition. The kitchens and
dining rooms are especially well maintained and equipped. The present
population of the Kansas Home consists of -254 adults and 16 children.
The Home is ma.i ntained by a per capita tax of $1.50 per year and the
income from an endowment fund of approximately $1,000,000.00. . . .
Maine does not operate a Masonic Hom~. and they give two very
definite reasons for not doing so. First, their jurisdiction being small,
they do not have the money to carry on an expensive institution of this
kind, and second, they believe that their beneficiaries will be much
happier, and can be assisted in a more satisfactory manner, in their own
homes, in their own community, than in an institutional type of Ho~e.
In that jurisdiction, the subordinate Lodge is expected to render first
aid and relief, when needed, and when a Lodge is unable to meet the
demands, it may call on the Grand Lodge for assistance. To receive such
assistance, a formal application for relief must be filed with the Grand
Lodge Board of Relief.••.

We are, I believe, attempting to follow the trends which lead toward

New York. The Grand Lodge, in addition to their Masonic Home
project some years ago, embarked. on a program .of ~iving direct. relief
to needy Freemasons and their widows, on applications made directly
to, and approved by, the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic. Benevolence....
The amount of money required to maintain this program; it is said,
was so great that it almost broke the Grand .Lodge of New York. The
serious mistake they seem to have made was, that they failed to take
the subordinate Lodge into the picture and require that the applicant be
fully investigated, by his own Lodge, and approved by his Lodge, before
its submission to the Committee on Masonic Benevolences. In 1938,
realizing where this program was leading them, the Grand Lodge voted
to discontinue it.•..

children, she was given the choice of coming into the Home, or receiving assistance in her home and community, and, with two exceptions in six years, every applicant elected to stay in her own home,
and the two families that came into the Home only remained two months.
The system worked so well with the widows and children that they

preferred to remain in their own communities. In each case a budget was
worked out and a definite grant made.

Although this Home is primarily for the benefit of Royal Arch Masons,
their wives and widows, the widows of deceased Master Masons are
also accommodated there, on a per capita cost basis, under an arrangement between the Grand Lodge and the Grand Chapter.... The Texas
Masonic Home and School is owned and operated by the Grand Lodge
of Texas, at Arlington. Here are accommodated children up to and
including high school ages .•.. A trade school is also operated wherein
they train the children so that they may go out into the world and make
their own way. They operate. among other things, a printing shop.
which publishes "The Campus News," a school publication, "The Grand
Lodge Magazine" and does other printing work for the Grand Lodge
and other Grand Bodies of Texas.•.•

Without reference to any particular jurisdiction, generally speaking, all
Homes should be under the direct control of the Grand Lodge within

whatever financial aid the Nation and/or State provides; what he may

if this is not adequate to his support, it should be supplemented by
annuitits from the Grand Lodge .••

New Zealand. Sir Stephen Shepherd Allen, Grand Master, in his
Annua{ Message . after referring to the predominance of Freemasonry
among the English-speaking peoples and its revival in those countries
of Europe which are free from political dictatorship, expressed the hope
that in the near future arrangements might be set in train for representatives from the sovereign Masonic Jurisdictions of the world to
come together at suitable intervals in conference at official high levels
to consider problems .of common interest and point the way to an even
greater unity of purpose and closer ties of brotherhood everywhere. He
exhorted the brethren to press forward along the path of duty. always,
in the words of Lincoln, .. with malice towards none, with charity to all,
and with firmness in the right as God gives us to see the right."

service expected of an officer or members.

CHAPTER XV

STATISTI CS
Uniform 1tati8tic1 are not easy to obtain from the printed proceedings of the 49 Grand Jurisdictions.
.
Many do not publish a consolidated balance sheet, and those that
do follow diverse systems of accounting. Many do not place any valuations on land and buildings. Reports overlap and require close analysis.
In some instances it was necessary to eliminate capital outlay included
in expense accounts.
In the Financial Stati&tics presented herein there may be unintentional omissions and there are undoubtedly some accounting errors. The
figures are presented as an interesting picture of the financial condition
of the American Grand Lodges. Assets and expenditures of individual
Lodges are not included.
·
The membenhi p 1tati8tic1 have been presented in such a way as to
permit comparison between the different jurisdictions.
Using the 1950 United States Census Report it was possible to
compute the number of Masons for each 1000 males in each state. In
the country as a whole it was found that fifty men out of each thousand
are members of the Craft. This includes males of all ages as the breakdown of adult males for 1950 is not yet available. California u below
the national average with only 38 for each thousand while Maine and
Vermont head the lut with the extraordinary number of 98 members for
each thousand males in these two states. The position of the other states
is shown in the membership chart which follows.
